events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1865, Confederate General Stand Watie, a Cherokee Indian, surrendered the last significant Confederate army at Fort Towson, Oklahoma. His surrender marked the end of the Civil War in the Indian Territory.
events.name: Surrender of Stand Watie

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1865, James Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission in Brighton, England, aiming to promote Christian missionary work in the interior of China. This organization played a significant role in the spread of Christianity in China.
events.name: Founding of the China Inland Mission

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1865, Jumbo, a young male African elephant, arrived at the London Zoo, quickly becoming a popular attraction. His fame contributed to the growing interest in exotic animals and conservation efforts in the late 19th century.
events.name: Arrival of Jumbo the Elephant

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1865, Lewis Carroll published his children's novel 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' in England. This whimsical tale has since become a classic of children's literature, celebrated for its imaginative narrative and playful use of language.
events.name: Publication of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1865, the U.S. Secret Service was established in Washington, D.C., originally tasked with investigating and preventing counterfeiting. Over time, its role expanded to include the protection of the President and other high-profile officials.
events.name: Founding of the U.S. Secret Service

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1865, four conspirators involved in the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln were executed by hanging in Washington, D.C. This event marked a significant moment in the aftermath of Lincoln's assassination, reflecting the nation's desire for justice.
events.name: Execution of Lincoln Conspirators

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1865, Edward Whymper led a party of seven to become the first climbers to reach the summit of the Matterhorn in the Alps. Tragically, four members of the party died during the descent, highlighting the dangers of mountaineering.
events.name: First Ascent of the Matterhorn

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1865, Wild Bill Hickok shot 'Little Dave' Davis Tutt dead in the market square of Springfield, Missouri, over a poker debt. This incident is regarded as the first true western fast draw showdown, cementing Hickok's legendary status in American folklore.
events.name: Wild Bill Hickok – Davis Tutt Shootout

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1865, the SS Great Eastern, designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel, embarked from Liverpool on a significant voyage to lay the first transatlantic telegraph cable, which would revolutionize global communication.
events.name: The SS Great Eastern departs on a voyage to lay a transatlantic telegraph cable

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1865, the New Zealand Parliament convened in Wellington for the first time on a permanent basis, establishing the city as the de facto national capital and marking a significant step in the country's political development.
events.name: The New Zealand Parliament first meets in Wellington on a permanent basis

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1865, a group of Welsh settlers arrived in the Chubut Valley of Argentina, establishing a community that would preserve their language and culture in South America, significantly impacting the region's demographic landscape.
events.name: Welsh settlers arrive in Argentina at Chubut Valley

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1865, the steamer Brother Jonathan sank off the coast of Crescent City, California, resulting in the tragic loss of 225 lives, marking one of the deadliest maritime disasters of the time.
events.name: The steamer Brother Jonathan sinks off the California coast

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1865, the first narrow gauge mainline railway in the world was inaugurated at Grandchester, Queensland, Australia, showcasing innovative engineering and paving the way for future railway developments.
events.name: The first narrow gauge mainline railway in the world opens at Grandchester, Australia

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1865, the Dominican Republic successfully regained its independence from Spanish colonial rule, a pivotal moment in the nation's history, largely driven by the efforts of leaders like Gregorio Luperón.

locations.name: Santo Domingo, Santo Domingo Province, Dominican Republic

events.name: The Dominican Republic regains independence from Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1865, the Shergotty meteorite, a significant Mars meteorite, fell in Sherghati, Bihar, India, contributing to the study of extraterrestrial materials and the understanding of planetary geology.
events.name: The Shergotty meteorite falls in Sherghati, Gaya, Bihar, India

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1865, Union Business College was founded in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, later becoming known as Peirce College, and played a crucial role in providing business education in the region.
events.name: Union Business College (now Peirce College) is founded in Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1865, Champ Ferguson became the first person convicted of war crimes in the United States for his actions during the American Civil War, leading to his execution on October 20, 1865.

image.caption: Portrait of Champ Ferguson.
image.credit: Federal Goverment — http://images.worthpoint.com/wp2/cowans/Cowans06242009/thumbnail/yy4920.jpg
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 1865; the description places the image after his capture, not at his conviction on September 26.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Champ Ferguson convicted of war crimes

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1865, Paul Bogle led a significant march of hundreds of black men and women in Morant Bay, Jamaica, in protest against social injustices, which was violently suppressed by British Governor Edward John Eyre, resulting in the execution of 400 individuals.

locations.name: Morant Bay, Saint Thomas Parish, Jamaica

events.name: Morant Bay rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1865, Florida drafted its new constitution in Tallahassee, marking a significant step in the state's reconstruction process following the Civil War.
events.name: Florida drafts its constitution in Tallahassee

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1865, the Standard Oil Company was established in Cleveland, Ohio, by John D. Rockefeller, marking the beginning of a significant chapter in American industrial history and the oil industry.
events.name: The Standard Oil Company opens

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1865, the CSS Shenandoah, the last Confederate warship, surrendered in Liverpool, England, after a long journey from the Pacific, effectively marking the end of the Confederate naval resistance.
events.name: American Civil War: The CSS Shenandoah surrenders in Liverpool

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1865, Captain Henry Wirz, the Confederate superintendent of Andersonville Prison, was hanged for war crimes, becoming one of the few individuals executed for such offenses during the American Civil War.
events.name: Captain Henry Wirz is hanged for war crimes

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1865, the Duar War between Britain and Bhutan concluded with the Treaty of Sinchula, whereby Bhutan ceded control of its southern passes to Britain in exchange for an annual subsidy.
events.name: Duar War ends with the Treaty of Sinchula

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1865, during the Chincha Islands War, a Spanish gunboat was captured by the Chilean tugboat Independencia off the coast of Tomé, marking a significant naval engagement in the conflict.
events.name: Chincha Islands War: Action of 17 November 1865

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1865, during the Chincha Islands War, the Spanish ship Covadonga was captured by Chilean and Peruvian forces north of Valparaíso, highlighting the ongoing maritime conflicts in the region.
events.name: Chincha Islands War: Battle of Papudo

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1865, the United States Congress established the House Committee on Appropriations and the Committee on Banking and Commerce, restructuring legislative responsibilities and enhancing the efficiency of government operations.
events.name: The United States Congress creates the House Committee on Appropriations

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1865, Leopold II ascended to the throne as King of the Belgians following the death of his father, King Leopold I, marking the beginning of a controversial reign that would have lasting implications for Belgium and its colonies.
events.name: Leopold II becomes King of the Belgians

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1865, Secretary of State William H. Seward announced the ratification of the Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, officially abolishing slavery in the United States and marking a pivotal moment in American history.
events.name: Thirteenth Amendment ratified

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1865, the Kappa Alpha Order was founded at Washington College in Lexington, Virginia, establishing one of the oldest college fraternities in the United States, which would promote brotherhood and moral values among its members.

image.caption: Kappa Alpha Order badge reproduced in Baird’s Manual of American College Fraternities.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://www.google.com/books/edition/Baird_s_Manual_of_American_College_Frate/Z1vOAAAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1
image.date_qualification: Badge associated with the fraternity, reproduced in a 1927 reference manual; it is not a contemporary image of the 1865 founding. The badge image creation date is not established.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Kappa Alpha Order is founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1865, Jonathan Shank and Barry Ownby established the Ku Klux Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, as a secret society aimed at resisting Reconstruction efforts and intimidating African Americans and their allies.
events.name: Formation of the Ku Klux Klan

events.enhanced_description: Fisk University, a historically black university, was established in Nashville, Tennessee, in 1866. It became a significant institution for African American education and culture in the post-Civil War United States.
events.name: Establishment of Fisk University

events.enhanced_description: The last issue of The Liberator, an influential abolitionist magazine, was published, marking the end of an important chapter in the fight against slavery in the United States. The publication had played a crucial role in advocating for abolition.
events.name: Last issue of The Liberator published

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, a series of Federalist revolts erupted in Argentina, challenging the central government and reflecting the ongoing political tensions in the country. These revolts were part of a broader struggle between federalists and unitarians that characterized Argentine politics during this period.

locations.historical_name: United Provinces of the Rio de la Plata
locations.name: Argentina

events.name: Federalist revolts in Argentina

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in Germany, revolutionizing the field of explosives and paving the way for advancements in construction and mining. This invention would later contribute to Nobel's fortune and the establishment of the Nobel Prizes.
events.name: Alfred Nobel invents dynamite

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, the foundations of Nestlé S.A. were laid with the establishment of the Anglo-Swiss Milk Company and Farine Lactée Henri Nestlé. This marked the beginning of one of the largest food and beverage companies in the world.
events.name: Foundation of Nestlé S.A.

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, the Minneapolis Milling Company, which would later become General Mills, constructed its own mills in Minneapolis, Minnesota. This development was crucial in establishing Minneapolis as a major milling center in the United States.
events.name: Minneapolis Milling Company builds mills

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, Rabbi Marcus Jastrow arrived in the United States to lead Congregation Rodeph Shalom in Philadelphia. His contributions to Jewish scholarship and community life were significant during a transformative period for Jewish immigrants in America.
events.name: Marcus Jastrow arrives in the United States

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, the recommendations of the state Girls' School Committee in Sweden led to a series of progressive reforms aimed at improving women's rights and education. This initiative was a significant step toward gender equality in the country.
events.name: Girls' School Committee recommendations in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: The Famine of 1866–68 began in Finland, leading to widespread food shortages and suffering among the population. This famine was exacerbated by poor harvests and economic difficulties, significantly impacting Finnish society.
events.name: Famine of 1866–68 begins in Finland

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, Erasmus Jacobs discovered the 21.25-carat Eureka Diamond near Hopetown on the banks of the Orange River in South Africa. This discovery marked the beginning of the diamond rush in South Africa and had lasting economic implications for the region.
events.name: Erasmus Jacobs discovers the Eureka Diamond

events.enhanced_description: In 1866, Magirus Kommanditist was founded in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, laying the groundwork for what would become a major global manufacturer of commercial vehicles, known today as Iveco.
events.name: Foundation of Magirus Kommanditist

events.enhanced_description: Ottoman troops clashed with supporters of Maronite leader Youssef Bey Karam at St. Doumit in Lebanon, resulting in a defeat for the Ottomans. This conflict was part of the broader tensions in the region during the 19th century.
events.name: Clash at St. Doumit

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Aeronautical Society was formed in London as The Aeronautical Society of Great Britain, becoming the world's oldest aeronautical society. It has played a pivotal role in the advancement of aviation and aerospace engineering.

locations.historical_name: The Aeronautical Society of Great Britain
locations.name: London

events.name: Formation of the Royal Aeronautical Society

events.enhanced_description: Wesley College was established in Melbourne, Australia, as an independent school with a strong emphasis on academic excellence and holistic education. It has since become one of the leading educational institutions in the country.
events.name: Establishment of Wesley College

events.enhanced_description: Around 557 BCE, the island of Santorini, known in antiquity as Thera, experienced a catastrophic volcanic eruption. This eruption is one of the largest in recorded history and had significant impacts on the region's geography and climate.
events.name: Volcanic eruption in Santorini

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Abtao took place between a Spanish naval squadron and a combined Peruvian-Chilean fleet near the island of Abtao in the Chiloé Archipelago. This battle was part of the larger War of the Pacific.
events.name: Battle of Abtao

events.enhanced_description: The first daylight bank robbery in United States history during peacetime occurred in Liberty, Missouri. This event is often attributed to Jesse James and his gang, marking a significant moment in American criminal history.
events.name: First daylight bank robbery in peacetime

events.enhanced_description: The Calaveras Skull was discovered in California, initially believed to be evidence of prehistoric humans in North America. However, it was later revealed to be a hoax, raising questions about the authenticity of archaeological finds.
events.name: Discovery of the Calaveras Skull

events.enhanced_description: The United States Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866, marking the first federal legislation aimed at protecting the rights of African Americans. President Andrew Johnson vetoed the bill, but Congress successfully overrode the veto.
events.name: Passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1866

events.enhanced_description: The collapse of Overend, Gurney and Company, a prominent London bank, triggered the Panic of 1866, leading to widespread financial instability. This event underscored the vulnerabilities in the banking system during that period.
events.name: Collapse of Overend, Gurney and Company

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Tuyutí, fought on May 24, 1866, was a significant engagement in the Paraguayan War where the Triple Alliance, consisting of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay, defeated Paraguayan forces. This battle resulted in heavy casualties, with approximately 16,000 soldiers lost, marking a turning point in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Tuyutí

events.enhanced_description: The comic opera 'Cox and Box', written by F. C. Burnand with music by Arthur Sullivan, premiered on May 26, 1866, at Moray Lodge in Kensington. This production marked an important moment in the development of English comic opera, showcasing Sullivan's early musical talent.
events.name: First production of Cox and Box

events.enhanced_description: Bedřich Smetana's comic opera 'The Bartered Bride' premiered on May 30, 1866, in Prague. This opera is celebrated for its nationalistic themes and vibrant melodies, becoming a cornerstone of Czech musical heritage.
events.name: Premiere of The Bartered Bride

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1866, Fenian forces clashed with Canadian militia at the battles of Ridgeway and Fort Erie. These skirmishes were part of the Fenian Raids, which aimed to pressure Britain into granting Ireland independence.
events.name: Skirmishes at Ridgeway and Fort Erie

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1866, calculations indicated that Pluto, which had not yet been discovered, would reach its only aphelion between 1618 and August 2113. This finding reflects the ongoing developments in celestial mechanics and astronomy.
events.name: Pluto's Aphelion Calculations

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1866, the Parliament of Canada convened for the first time in Ottawa, marking a significant step in the establishment of Canadian governance following Confederation in 1867.
events.name: First Meeting of the Parliament of Canada

events.enhanced_description: The Agra High Court was established on June 11, 1866, serving as a significant judicial body in India. It later relocated to Allahabad, where it became known as the Allahabad High Court.
events.name: Establishment of the Agra High Court

events.enhanced_description: The Austro-Prussian War, also known as the Seven Weeks' War, began on June 14, 1866, when Austria and several German states declared war on Prussia. This conflict was pivotal in the unification of Germany under Prussian leadership.
events.name: Beginning of the Austro-Prussian War

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1866, the Kingdom of Italy declared war on Austria, joining the conflict in the Austro-Prussian War. This declaration was part of Italy's efforts to annex territories and assert its national identity.
events.name: Kingdom of Italy Declares War on Austria

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1866, the Riksdag of the Estates in Sweden voted to replace itself with an elected two-chamber parliament. This reform was a significant step towards modern parliamentary democracy in Sweden.
events.name: Riksdag of the Estates Votes for Two-Chamber System

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Langensalza, fought on June 27, 1866, saw Prussian forces defeat the Hanoverian army. This battle was part of the Austro-Prussian War and contributed to the consolidation of Prussian power in Germany.
events.name: Battle of Langensalza

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1866, the Battle of Königgrätz resulted in a decisive victory for the Prussian army under King Wilhelm I and General Helmuth von Moltke against the Austrian forces led by Ludwig von Benedek. This battle was a turning point in the Austro-Prussian War, leading to Prussia's dominance in German affairs.
events.name: Battle of Königgrätz

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1866, Princess Helena, the third daughter of Queen Victoria, married Prince Christian of Schleswig-Holstein in a ceremony held at Windsor. This union was significant in strengthening royal ties across Europe.
events.name: Marriage of Princess Helena

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1866, a Reconstruction Treaty was signed with the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations, completing the abolition of slavery in the United States. This treaty was part of the broader efforts to integrate freedmen into society.

image.caption: Portrait of Henry Crittenden, a formerly enslaved person in the Choctaw Nation.
image.credit: Unknown photographer — The Choctaw Freedmen by Robert Elliott Flickinger
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1914-01-01; this is a later portrait, not a photograph of the 1866 treaty event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Reconstruction Treaty with Choctaw & Chickasaw

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1866, the first Constitution of Romania was issued, establishing a framework for governance and civil rights in the newly unified state. This document laid the groundwork for modern Romanian law and governance.
events.name: First Constitution of Romania

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1866, during the Austro-Prussian War, the Naval Battle of Lissa took place where the Austrian fleet, commanded by Wilhelm von Tegetthoff, defeated the Italian fleet led by Carlo di Persano. This victory solidified Austria's naval dominance in the Adriatic.
events.name: Naval Battle of Lissa

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Blumenau occurred on July 22, 1866, where Austrian forces defended Bratislava against the advancing Prussian army. This battle marked the conclusion of major fighting in the Austro-Prussian War.
events.name: Battle of Blumenau

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1866, Tennessee became the first U.S. state to be readmitted to the Union following the American Civil War. This event was a significant milestone in the Reconstruction era.
events.name: Tennessee Readmitted to the Union

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1866, the United States Congress passed legislation authorizing the four-star rank of General of the Army. Lieutenant General Ulysses S. Grant became the first officer to hold this prestigious rank, reflecting his significant contributions during the Civil War.

image.caption: Rank insignia of General of the Army of the United States for the U.S. Army.
image.credit: Skjoldbro — Own work , based on Uniform of the army of the United States (1882) p. 24.
image.date_qualification: The image is a modern illustration dated 2022-12-09; the insignia is described as used from 1861. The event is dated 1866-07-25.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Authorization of General of the Army Rank

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1866, the SS Great Eastern successfully completed the laying of the transatlantic telegraph cable between Valentia Island, Ireland, and Heart's Content, Newfoundland. This achievement restored a vital communications link between North America and Europe, revolutionizing global communication.

image.caption: Photograph of the SS Great Eastern at Heart’s Content.
image.credit: most likely Robert Edward Holloway (d. 1904) according to source — http://www.library.mun.ca/qeii/cns/photos/
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the scene to July 1866, during the cable-laying expedition; the original image date is 1866-07, while the supported display date is 1866.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Completion of Transatlantic Telegraph Cable

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1866, the Metric Act of 1866 was enacted, legalizing the standardization of weights and measures in the United States. This act was a crucial step towards adopting a more uniform system of measurement.
events.name: Metric Act of 1866

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Prague, signed on August 23, 1866, formally ended the Austro-Prussian War. The treaty resulted in significant territorial changes, including the departure of the Duchy of Limburg from the German Confederation.
events.name: Treaty of Prague

events.enhanced_description: The Great Tea Race of 1866 concluded in September, with the clipper ship Taeping narrowly winning the race to deliver tea to London. This event highlighted the competitive spirit of the tea trade and the significance of maritime trade routes.
events.name: Great Tea Race of 1866

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1866, Paraguayan forces successfully defended Curupayty against the Triple Alliance during the Paraguayan War, inflicting heavy casualties on the attackers while sustaining minimal losses. This battle showcased Paraguay's resilience and strategic defensive capabilities.
events.name: Defense of Curupayty

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Vienna, signed on October 12, 1866, concluded the war between Austria and Italy, formalizing the annexation of Venetia by Italy. This treaty was a critical step in the unification of Italy and the reconfiguration of power in Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1866, French troops under Rear Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze landed on Ganghwa Island, Korea, as part of a punitive expedition following the execution of French Jesuit priests. This marked the first military engagement between Korea and a Western power, highlighting the tensions between Korea and foreign nations during this period.
events.name: French troops land at Ganghwa Island

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1866, the office of State President of the South African Republic was established through a constitutional amendment approved by the Volksraad. This development was significant in shaping the political landscape of the region during a time of colonial expansion and internal strife.
events.name: Creation of the office of State President of the South African Republic

events.enhanced_description: The Ruse–Varna railway line, the first railway in Bulgaria, officially opened on November 7, 1866. This milestone in transportation significantly contributed to the economic development of Bulgaria and facilitated trade and communication within the region.
events.name: Opening of the Ruse–Varna railway line

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1866, the Oaks explosion occurred at the Oaks Colliery in Barnsley, England, resulting in the deaths of 383 miners and rescuers. This disaster remains one of the worst mining accidents in British history, prompting significant changes in mining safety regulations.
events.name: Oaks explosion

events.enhanced_description: The College of Wooster was founded on December 18, 1866, in Wooster, Ohio. It became known for its distinctive approach to undergraduate education, emphasizing independent research and the liberal arts.

image.caption: Retrospective lithograph of the University of Wooster, Ohio.
image.credit: Chicago Lithographing Co. — https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2006677688/
image.date_qualification: Image dated circa 1867; the described founding date is December 18, 1866.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of the College of Wooster

events.enhanced_description: The Covington–Cincinnati Suspension Bridge opened in 1867, connecting Cincinnati, Ohio, and Covington, Kentucky. At the time, it was the longest single-span bridge in the world, showcasing the engineering prowess of its designer, John A. Roebling.
events.name: Opening of the Covington–Cincinnati Suspension Bridge

events.enhanced_description: In July 1867, Reverend Thomas Baker, a Wesleyan Methodist missionary, was tragically killed and cannibalized by the Navatusila tribespeople in Fiji, marking a grim chapter in missionary history. He was the last missionary in Fiji to suffer such a fate, alongside eight of his local followers.
events.name: Death of Reverend Thomas Baker

events.enhanced_description: Pierre Michaux invented the front wheel-driven velocipede, marking the creation of the first mass-produced bicycle. This innovation revolutionized personal transportation and laid the groundwork for the modern cycling industry.
events.name: Invention of the Velocipede

events.enhanced_description: The discovery of diamond fields in South Africa marked the beginning of a diamond rush that would attract thousands of prospectors and lead to significant economic changes in the region. This event played a crucial role in the development of the South African economy and the global diamond trade.
events.name: Discovery of South African Diamond Fields

events.enhanced_description: The Prohibition National Committee was formed in the United States, marking a significant step in the movement towards the prohibition of alcohol. This organization played a pivotal role in the eventual enactment of the 18th Amendment in 1920.
events.name: Formation of the Prohibition National Committee

events.enhanced_description: The Clarke School for the Deaf opened in Northampton, Massachusetts, becoming the first school in the United States to teach deaf children using the oral method. This institution significantly advanced the education and integration of deaf individuals into society.
events.name: Opening of Clarke School for the Deaf

events.enhanced_description: An artesian water spring began to gush continuously at Fountain Point, Michigan, marking a significant natural phenomenon. This event highlighted the geological features of the region and contributed to the understanding of artesian wells.
events.name: Fountain Point Artesian Spring

events.enhanced_description: The introduction of Rosa 'La France' by Jean-Baptiste André Guillot marked the birth of the modern rose. This hybrid rose became a significant development in horticulture and influenced rose cultivation worldwide.
events.name: Introduction of Rosa 'La France'

events.enhanced_description: Gorse was naturalized in New Zealand, where it quickly became one of the worst invasive weeds. This event had significant ecological impacts, affecting native flora and fauna.
events.name: Naturalization of Gorse in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: The Swedish famine of 1867-1869 began, leading to widespread food shortages and suffering across the country. This crisis prompted significant social and political changes in Sweden, including emigration and agricultural reforms.
events.name: Swedish Famine of 1867-1869

events.enhanced_description: A yellow fever epidemic struck New Orleans, resulting in the deaths of 3,093 individuals. This outbreak highlighted the public health challenges of the time and led to changes in sanitation and disease prevention efforts.
events.name: Yellow Fever Epidemic in New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: The Wasps Rugby Football Club was formed in Middlesex, England, contributing to the development of rugby as a popular sport. The club has since become one of the most recognized names in English rugby.
events.name: Formation of Wasps Rugby Football Club

events.enhanced_description: Margarine Unie, originally named Antoon Jurgens United, was founded in the Netherlands, marking the beginning of a significant player in the global food industry. This company would eventually evolve into Unilever, a major multinational corporation.
events.name: Founding of Margarine Unie

events.enhanced_description: Delhaize was founded in Belgium, establishing a major retail group that would grow to become Ahold Delhaize, a significant player in the European grocery market. This event marked the beginning of a long-standing tradition in retail.
events.name: Founding of Delhaize

events.enhanced_description: The game Parcheesi was introduced, becoming a popular board game in the United States. This game, based on the ancient Indian game of Pachisi, contributed to the development of modern board gaming culture.
events.name: Introduction of Parcheesi

events.enhanced_description: The Paraguayan War, a significant conflict in South America, began, involving Paraguay against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. This war had devastating effects on Paraguay, leading to massive casualties and long-term consequences for the nation.
events.name: Paraguayan War

events.enhanced_description: Between 1867 and 1873, Chinese, Scandinavian, and Irish immigrants laid 30,000 miles (48,000 km) of railroad tracks across the United States. This monumental effort was crucial for the expansion of the American railway system and the economic development of the nation.
events.name: Railroad Expansion by Immigrants

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1867, African-American men were granted the right to vote in the District of Columbia, marking a significant step towards civil rights and representation for African Americans in the United States during the Reconstruction era.
events.name: African-American men granted the right to vote in D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1867, Benito Juárez was reinstated as president of Mexico after a tumultuous period marked by foreign intervention and civil strife. His leadership was pivotal in restoring the republic and implementing liberal reforms.
events.name: Benito Juárez becomes president of Mexico again

events.enhanced_description: The London Skating Disaster occurred on January 15, 1867, when the ice broke during a public skating event, resulting in the deaths of 40 people. This tragic incident raised awareness about safety measures during public gatherings.
events.name: London Skating Disaster

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Kōmei of Japan died suddenly on January 30, 1867, at the age of 36, leaving his 14-year-old son to ascend the throne as Emperor Meiji. This transition marked the beginning of the Meiji Restoration, a period of rapid modernization and westernization in Japan.
events.name: Death of Emperor Kōmei of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1867, Maronite nationalist leader Youssef Bey Karam departed Lebanon aboard a French ship for Algeria. His departure symbolized the struggles of Lebanese nationalists during a time of political upheaval and foreign intervention.
events.name: Youssef Bey Karam leaves Lebanon

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1867, Shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu abdicated, allowing Prince Mutsuhito to become Emperor Meiji in a brief ceremony in Kyoto. This event marked the end of the Tokugawa shogunate and the beginning of the Meiji Restoration, which transformed Japan into a modern state.
events.name: Shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu abdicates

events.enhanced_description: West Virginia University was established on February 7, 1867, in Morgantown, West Virginia. It has since grown into a major public research university, contributing significantly to higher education in the region.
events.name: Establishment of West Virginia University

events.enhanced_description: The Covering of the Senne in Brussels began on February 13, 1867, as part of an urban development project aimed at improving the city's infrastructure and aesthetics. This project would have lasting impacts on the urban landscape of Brussels.

image.caption: Buildings and wooden structures along the Senne (Zenne) river in Brussels.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://bbzh.site.voila.fr/belgXIX.htm archive link
image.date_qualification: Before 1870 (as dated in the supplied image metadata); the covering project began in 1867.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Covering of the Senne in Brussels begins

events.enhanced_description: The Augusta Institute was founded on February 14, 1867, in Augusta, Georgia, and later became known as Morehouse College. It played a crucial role in the education of African American men during the Reconstruction era.
events.name: Founding of Augusta Institute

events.enhanced_description: Johann Strauss II's famous waltz, The Blue Danube, was first performed on February 15, 1867, at a concert of the Vienna Men's Choral Association. This piece would go on to become one of the most recognizable and beloved compositions in classical music.

image.caption: Cover of an early edition of Johann Strauss II’s *The Blue Danube*, edited by Carl Anton Spina.
image.credit: Johann Strauss — Collections Walter Anton
image.date_qualification: The image metadata dates the depicted publication to 1867; it does not establish that the image documents the performance on 15 February 1867.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First performance of The Blue Danube

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Inlon River was a significant conflict during the Nien Rebellion, where the Qing Dynasty successfully defeated the Nien rebels in Hubei Province. This battle was part of the larger struggle for control and stability within China during the mid-19th century.
events.name: Battle of Inlon River

events.enhanced_description: The Indiana Daily Student was established at Indiana University in Bloomington, marking a significant development in student journalism. It has since become a key platform for student voices and campus news.

image.caption: Reproduction of the first issue of The Indiana Daily Student.
image.credit: Indiana Daily Student
image.date_qualification: Image date is given as 1867-02; the exact day is not established by the image evidence.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Establishment of The Indiana Daily Student

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political move, the United States Congress forbade taxpayer funding for diplomatic envoys to the Holy See, effectively breaking off relations after nearly two decades. This decision reflected the complex relationship between the U.S. government and the Vatican.
events.name: U.S. Congress forbids funding to the Holy See

events.enhanced_description: The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign was established in March 1867, laying the groundwork for one of the leading public research universities in the United States. It opened its doors to students the following year.

image.caption: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign campus.
image.credit: Kevin Dooley — https://www.flickr.com/photos/pagedooley/52197419694/
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2010-06-26; this is not a contemporaneous image of the 1867 establishment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1867, Nebraska was admitted as the 37th state of the United States, marking a significant expansion of the Union during the Reconstruction era. This admission was part of the broader westward expansion and development of the United States.
events.name: Nebraska admitted as the 37th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: The Fenian Rising broke out in Ireland on March 5, 1867, as members of the Fenian Brotherhood sought to establish an independent Irish Republic. This uprising was part of a series of movements aimed at ending British rule in Ireland.
events.name: The Fenian Rising

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1867, Joseph Lister published a groundbreaking article in The Lancet, outlining his discoveries related to antiseptic surgery. His work laid the foundation for modern surgical practices and significantly reduced post-operative infections.
events.name: Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery article

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1867, William III of the Netherlands accepted an offer from Napoleon III for the sale of Luxembourg, which sparked the Luxembourg Crisis. This event highlighted the geopolitical tensions in Europe during the 19th century.
events.name: Luxembourg Crisis and sale offer

events.enhanced_description: The British North America Act received royal assent on March 29, 1867, leading to the formation of the Dominion of Canada. This act united the Province of Canada, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia, with Ottawa designated as the capital.
events.name: British North America Act and Canadian Confederation

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1867, the United States purchased Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million, a transaction often referred to as 'Seward's Folly.' This acquisition significantly expanded U.S. territory and resources.
events.name: Alaska Purchase

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1867, the Strait Settlement of Singapore transitioned from being ruled from Calcutta to becoming a Crown colony under the jurisdiction of the Colonial Office in London. This marked a significant change in governance for the region.
events.name: Strait Settlement of Singapore becomes a Crown colony

events.enhanced_description: The Exposition Universelle, an international exhibition, opened in Paris on April 1, 1867, showcasing advancements in technology and culture. Notably, it marked the first visit of a Sultan of the Ottoman Empire to Western Europe.
events.name: Exposition Universelle in Paris

events.enhanced_description: I.C. Sorosis, the first women's fraternity founded on the model of men's fraternities, was established at Monmouth College in Monmouth, Illinois, on April 28, 1867. This organization laid the groundwork for future sororities in the United States.
events.name: Founding of I.C. Sorosis

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded political May Day march took place in Chicago on May 1, 1867, marking an important moment in labor rights activism. This event would later contribute to the establishment of International Workers' Day.
events.name: First political May Day march

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1867, Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in the United Kingdom, revolutionizing construction and demolition industries. This invention would later play a significant role in both civil engineering and warfare.

image.caption: Portrait of Alfred Nobel.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://sok.riksarkivet.se/sbl/Presentation.aspx?id=8143
image.date_qualification: Image date: before 1896; it does not depict the patent event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Alfred Nobel patents dynamite

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1867, the Treaty of London was signed, reaffirming the neutrality of Luxembourg and effectively ending the Luxembourg Crisis. This treaty was a significant diplomatic resolution among the great powers of Europe.
events.name: Treaty of London and Luxembourg Crisis

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1867, Robert William Keate was appointed as the Lieutenant-governor of the Colony of Natal, playing a crucial role in the administration of the region during a time of significant change and development.
events.name: Robert William Keate becomes Lieutenant-governor of Natal

events.enhanced_description: The Austro-Hungarian Compromise was enacted on May 29, 1867, establishing the Austro-Hungarian Empire. This agreement allowed for dual monarchy, with Emperor Francis Joseph crowned as King of Hungary on June 8, marking a significant shift in Central European politics.
events.name: Austro-Hungarian Compromise

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1867, the Atlantic Cable Quartz Lode gold mine was named in Montana, reflecting the ongoing gold rush and economic development in the region during the 19th century.
events.name: Atlantic Cable Quartz Lode gold mine named

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1867, Emperor Maximilian of Mexico was executed by a firing squad, marking a pivotal moment in Mexican history. His death symbolized the end of the Second Mexican Empire and the restoration of the Republic.
events.name: Execution of Emperor Maximilian of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1867, the first recorded association football match in Argentina took place in Buenos Aires, marking the beginning of the sport's popularity in the country. This event laid the foundation for Argentina's rich football culture.
events.name: First recorded association football match in Argentina

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1867, the British North America Act came into force, establishing the Dominion of Canada as the first independent dominion in the British Empire. This pivotal moment in Canadian history marked the unification of several provinces under a federal government.
events.name: Canadian Confederation

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1867, Queen's Park Football Club was founded in Glasgow, Scotland, becoming the oldest association football league team in the country. The club played a significant role in the development of football in Scotland.

image.caption: Aerial view of Hampden Park Stadium.
image.credit: Thomas Nugent — From geograph.org.uk
image.date_qualification: Photographed 27 March 2022; the image does not depict the 1867 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Queen's Park F.C.

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1867, France declared Cambodia's independence from Siam, subsequently establishing it as a protectorate under French and British control. This marked the beginning of significant foreign influence in Cambodian affairs.
events.name: Cambodia becomes a French protectorate

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1867, the Harvard School of Dental Medicine was established in Boston, Massachusetts, becoming the first dental school in the United States. This institution has played a crucial role in advancing dental education and practice.
events.name: Establishment of Harvard School of Dental Medicine

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1867, the Battle of Fandane-Thiouthioune took place, where the Serer people successfully defeated the Muslim Marabouts of Senegambia. This battle was significant in the context of the resistance against colonial and religious encroachment.
events.name: Battle of Fandane-Thiouthioune

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1867, Benjamin Disraeli's Second Reform Act was enacted, significantly expanding the electorate in England and Wales by enfranchising many men in cities for the first time. This act added approximately 938,000 voters to an electorate of over a million.
events.name: Second Reform Act

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1867, Emperor Meiji of Japan married Empress Shōken, who was born Masako Ichijō. This union was significant in the context of Japan's modernization and the Meiji Restoration.
events.name: Marriage of Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1867, Sheffield Wednesday Football Club was founded at the Adelphi Hotel in Sheffield, England. This club has a rich history and is one of the oldest football clubs in the world.
events.name: Founding of Sheffield Wednesday F.C.

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1867, Karl Marx published the first volume of 'Das Kapital', a foundational text in communist theory and economics. This work has had a profound impact on political thought and economic theory.
events.name: Publication of Das Kapital

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1867, the first Canadian election was held, resulting in the election of John A. Macdonald's Conservative Party to government. This event was pivotal in shaping the political landscape of the newly formed Dominion of Canada.

image.caption: Map of the 1867 Canadian General Election.
image.credit: Talleyrand6 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Created June 21, 2023; depicts the 1867 election.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: First Canadian election

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1867, the United States took control of Midway Island, a strategic location in the Pacific Ocean. This acquisition was part of the U.S. expansionist policy during the 19th century.

image.caption: Aerial photograph of Midway Atoll.
image.credit: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument Management Plan , Volume IV - Midway Atoll Conceptual Site Plan , p. 12.
image.date_qualification: Site photograph of Midway Atoll, not a contemporary image of the 1867 U.S. control of the island. Image date: 2008.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: U.S. control of Midway Island

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1867, the last convict ship, the Hougoumont, departed from Portsmouth, England, marking the end of penal transportation to Australia. This ship carried 62 Fenians among its transportees, symbolizing the conclusion of a significant chapter in British penal history.
events.name: End of penal transportation from Britain

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1867, Alaska was officially transferred from Russia to the United States, becoming the Department of Alaska. This acquisition expanded U.S. territory significantly and was part of the broader strategy of American expansionism.
events.name: Transfer of Alaska from Russia to the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1867, the Medicine Lodge Treaty was signed near Medicine Lodge Creek, Kansas, requiring southern Great Plains Indian leaders to relocate their tribes to a reservation in western Oklahoma. This treaty was a significant event in the context of U.S. relations with Native American tribes.

locations.name: Medicine Lodge Creek, Kansas, United States

events.name: Medicine Lodge Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1867, Giuseppe Garibaldi's troops marched into the Papal States, a significant event during the Italian unification process. This action was part of the broader struggle to consolidate Italy into a single nation-state.
events.name: Garibaldi's troops march into the Papal States

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1867, the first issue of Harper's Bazaar, a women's fashion magazine, was published in New York City. Initially published weekly, it later transitioned to a monthly format, becoming a significant publication in women's fashion and culture.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Publication of Harper's Bazaar

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1867, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shōgun of Japan, tendered his resignation to Emperor Meiji. This event marked a significant turning point in Japanese history, leading to the end of the Tokugawa shogunate and the restoration of imperial rule.

image.caption: Portrait photograph of Tokugawa Yoshinobu during his time as a duke.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — 東洋文化協会編『幕末・明治・大正回顧八十年史』第3輯、東洋文化協会、1935年。 国立国会図書館 デジタルコレクション：永続的識別子 8797959
image.date_qualification: The image is dated between 1933 and 1934, not to the 1867 resignation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Resignation of Tokugawa Yoshinobu

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1867, American temperance crusader Carrie Nation married Charles Gloyd. Nation would later become famous for her radical activism against alcohol consumption.
events.name: Marriage of Carrie Nation

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1867, the three 'Manchester Martyrs' were hanged in England for their involvement in the murder of a policeman during an attempt to rescue two members of the Irish Republican Brotherhood. Their execution became a rallying point for Irish nationalists.
events.name: Execution of the Manchester Martyrs

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1867, English author Charles Dickens gave his first public reading in a theater in New York City. This event marked the beginning of his successful series of readings in the United States, enhancing his popularity across the Atlantic.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Charles Dickens' first public reading in the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1867, the British expedition to Abyssinia commenced, aimed at rescuing hostages and asserting British influence in the region. This military campaign was part of the broader context of British imperial expansion.
events.name: Beginning of British expedition to Abyssinia

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1867, the Clerkenwell explosion occurred, marking the most infamous action carried out by the Fenians in Britain during the 19th century. This bombing aimed to free imprisoned Irish nationalists and highlighted the tensions between Irish republicans and British authorities.
events.name: Clerkenwell explosion

events.enhanced_description: The Angola Horror was a tragic train wreck that occurred near Angola, New York, resulting in the deaths of 49 people. This disaster prompted John D. Rockefeller to innovate fire-tested burning oil and led George Westinghouse to invent the railway air brake, which became mandatory in the United States in 1893.
events.name: Angola Horror

events.enhanced_description: In March 1868, French geologist Louis Lartet discovered the first identified skeletons of Cro-Magnon, early modern humans, at the Abri de Crô-Magnon rock shelter in Les Eyzies, France. This discovery provided significant insights into human evolution and prehistoric life.
events.name: Discovery of Cro-Magnon skeletons

events.enhanced_description: In March 1868, the Association internationale des femmes was founded as the first transnational women's organization. This group aimed to advocate for women's rights and promote international cooperation among women.
events.name: Founding of the Association internationale des femmes

events.enhanced_description: In May 1868, President Andrew Johnson was acquitted twice during his impeachment trial by the United States Senate, narrowly avoiding removal from office. These events underscored the deep political divisions in the post-Civil War United States.

image.caption: U.S. Senate roll-call record of votes on the impeachment articles against President Andrew Johnson.
image.credit: Edward McPherson, LL.D., Clerk of the House of Representatives of the United States, — "A Handbook of Politics for 1868", Part III Political Manual for 1868, XXIV - The Articles of Impeachment and Reply, Votes in the House, and Judgement of the Senate. Washington City: Philp & Solomons. 1968, p. 282
image.date_qualification: 1868-05-26 (date of the recorded Senate vote; not an upload date)
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Acquittal of Andrew Johnson

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, the first popular bicycle race took place at Parc de Saint-Cloud in Paris, marking a significant moment in the history of cycling as a competitive sport. This event helped to popularize cycling and laid the foundation for future cycling competitions.
events.name: The first popular bicycle race is held

events.enhanced_description: During the Paraguayan War, the Allies captured the fortress of Humaitá in an amphibious operation, marking a pivotal moment in the conflict. This event showcased the strategic military operations undertaken by Brazil and its allies against Paraguay.
figures: Field Marshal Luís Alves de Lima e Silva
events.name: Capture of Humaitá

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, Thomas Henry Huxley, a prominent biologist, claimed to have discovered a primordial matter he named Bathybius haeckelii during his research on the ocean floor. He later retracted this claim in 1871, acknowledging that what he had observed was merely a form of algae.

image.caption: Ernst Haeckel’s illustration of Bathybius haeckelii.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Ernst Haeckel Beitrage zur Plastidentheorie . In: Jenaische Zeitschrift für Medizin und Naturwissenschaft . Band 5, 1870, Plate XVII, Fig 1
image.date_qualification: The depicted illustration dates to 1870, after Huxley’s 1868 report. This is the illustration’s date, not the date of the discovery.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Thomas Henry Huxley discovers bathybius haeckelii

events.enhanced_description: The Académie Julian was established in Paris in 1868 as a significant art school that notably admitted women, providing them with opportunities in the male-dominated art world of the time. It became a prominent institution for artists seeking formal training.
events.name: Establishment of Académie Julian

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, Brisbane Grammar School was founded in Brisbane, Queensland, marking a significant development in the educational landscape of the colony. It provided secondary education opportunities for boys, contributing to the growth of formal education in Australia.
events.name: Founding of Brisbane Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: The Maryland School for the Deaf was established in 1868, providing specialized education for deaf students. This institution played a crucial role in advancing educational opportunities for individuals with hearing impairments in the United States.
events.name: Establishment of Maryland School for the Deaf

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, the Dortmunder Actien Brauerei was founded in Dortmund, Germany, marking the beginning of one of the country's notable breweries. It contributed to the rich brewing heritage of the region and the development of the beer industry in Germany.
events.name: Founding of Dortmunder Actien Brauerei

events.enhanced_description: The Herrenhäuser Brewery was established in 1868 in Hanover, Germany, contributing to the local brewing industry. It became known for its quality beers and played a role in the cultural fabric of the region.
events.name: Establishment of Herrenhäuser Brewery

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, Jamsetji Tata founded the Tata Group in Mumbai, India, initially as a trading company. This organization would grow to become one of India's largest and most respected conglomerates, influencing various sectors including steel, hospitality, and technology.
events.name: Founding of Tata Group

events.enhanced_description: Scottish merchant Thomas Blake Glover developed Japan's first coal mine on Hashima Island in 1868. This venture marked a significant step in Japan's industrialization, providing essential resources for the country's burgeoning economy.
events.name: Development of Japan's first coal mine

events.enhanced_description: The Roman Catholic Diocese of Tucson was established in 1868 as the Apostolic Vicariate of Arizona, taking territory from the former Diocese of Santa Fe. It marked a significant development in the Catholic Church's presence and organization in the American Southwest.
events.name: Establishment of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Tucson

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, Japan's population reached approximately 30 million, reflecting the country's demographic changes during a period of significant political and social transformation. This milestone occurred during the Meiji Restoration, which aimed to modernize Japan.

image.caption: Chart of Japan’s historical population.
image.credit: Max Roser — Our World in Data: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population
image.date_qualification: Image date: 2022-02-15; it is a modern chart, not a contemporary depiction of c.1868.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Population of Japan reaches 30 million

events.enhanced_description: The British Expedition to Abyssinia was led by General Robert Napier to rescue British officials and missionaries captured during the Abyssinian War. This military campaign was notable for its logistical challenges and successful outcome.
events.name: British Expedition to Abyssinia

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Meiji of Japan, at the age of 15, declared the Meiji Restoration, reclaiming full power and initiating a period of rapid modernization and westernization in Japan. This declaration was influenced by supporters from the Chōshū and Satsuma Domains and marked the beginning of the Boshin War.
events.name: Meiji Restoration Declaration

events.enhanced_description: During the Paraguayan War, Brazilian Army commander Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, Duke of Caxias, entered Asunción, the capital of Paraguay, declaring the war over. However, Paraguay's president, Francisco Solano López, prepared guerrilla tactics to continue the fight.
figures: Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, Duke of Caxias
events.name: Duke of Caxias Enters Asunción

events.enhanced_description: The Arkansas constitutional convention convened in Little Rock, addressing the state's governance and legal framework following the Civil War. This convention was a crucial step in the Reconstruction era for Arkansas.
events.name: Arkansas Constitutional Convention

events.enhanced_description: The arrival of the convict ship Hougoumont in Fremantle, Western Australia, marked the end of penal transportation from Britain to Australia after an 89-day voyage. This event signified a shift in British penal policy and the eventual cessation of transportation of convicts to Australia.
events.name: End of Penal Transportation to Australia

events.enhanced_description: Shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu declared the emperor's restoration illegal and prepared to attack Kyoto, escalating tensions that would lead to the Boshin War. This declaration marked a critical moment in the struggle between imperial and shogunate forces in Japan.
events.name: Shōgun's Declaration Against Emperor

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Toba–Fushimi occurred between the forces of the Tokugawa shogunate and the pro-Imperial forces of the Chōshū, Satsuma, and Tosa Domains. This decisive victory for the Imperial forces marked a turning point in the Boshin War.
events.name: Battle of Toba–Fushimi

events.enhanced_description: The Flying Foam massacre was a tragic event where Indigenous Australians were killed by white colonial settlers around Flying Foam Passage in Western Australia. This massacre highlighted the violent conflicts between settlers and Indigenous populations during colonization.
events.name: Flying Foam Massacre

events.enhanced_description: In a meeting in Hyōgo, foreign ministers were persuaded to recognize the restored Emperor Meiji of Japan, with assurances that Japanese harbors would be open in accordance with international treaties. This recognition was crucial for Japan's re-engagement with the world.
events.name: Recognition of Emperor Meiji

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1868, the British War Office officially sanctioned the formation of the Army Post Office Corps, which was established to manage postal services for the British Army. This organization played a crucial role in ensuring communication for military personnel during campaigns.
events.name: Formation of the Army Post Office Corps

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1868, the Jolly Corks, a social organization founded in New York City, was renamed the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks (BPOE). This organization aimed to promote charitable works and community service among its members.

image.caption: Elks National Memorial in Lincoln Park, Chicago, the national headquarters of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks.
image.credit: Smallbones — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2010-02-03; the event is dated 1868-02-16.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Renaming of the Jolly Corks to BPOE

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1868, a Brazilian naval force successfully navigated past the Paraguayan fortress at the Passage of Humaitá, marking a significant turning point in the Paraguayan War. This maneuver allowed Brazilian forces to gain a strategic advantage in the conflict.
events.name: Passage of Humaitá

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1868, the United States House of Representatives voted 126-47 in favor of impeaching President Andrew Johnson, following his dismissal of Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton. This marked a pivotal moment in U.S. history, as Johnson became the first president to be impeached.
events.name: Impeachment of Andrew Johnson

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1868, Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, was shot in the back during a fundraising event in Sydney, Australia, by Irishman Henry James O'Farrell. The Duke survived the attack, while O'Farrell was executed later that year.
figures: Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha

image.caption: Carte-de-visite portrait of Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, in Royal Navy captain’s uniform.
image.credit: Montague Scott — State Library of New South Wales, P1 / 14
image.date_qualification: Circa 1868; the exact date is not stated.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination attempt on Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1868, the University of California was founded in Oakland when the Organic Act was signed into law. This institution has since grown to become one of the leading public university systems in the United States.
events.name: Founding of the University of California

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1868, the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company was established in New York City. It has since become one of the largest life insurance companies in the United States, providing a range of financial services.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Formation of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1868, the Lake Ontario Shore Railroad Company was organized in Oswego, New York. This company played a significant role in the development of transportation infrastructure in the region.
events.name: Organization of the Lake Ontario Shore Railroad Company

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1868, the Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute was established in Hampton, Virginia. This institution focused on providing education and training for African Americans and became a model for similar schools.
events.name: Establishment of the Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1868, during the enthronement of Emperor Meiji, the Charter Oath was promulgated, promising the establishment of deliberative assemblies and the end of feudalism in Japan. This marked a significant step towards modernization in the country.
events.name: Promulgation of the Charter Oath by Emperor Meiji

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1868, Emperor Tewodros II of Ethiopia ordered the massacre of at least 197 prisoners at Magdala, primarily for trivial offenses. This brutal act highlighted the emperor's increasingly tyrannical rule and led to international condemnation.
events.name: Massacre at Magdala by Emperor Tewodros II

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1868, during the Battle of Magdala, a British-Indian task force under General Robert Napier inflicted heavy casualties on the forces of Emperor Tewodros II, resulting in a decisive defeat. Following the battle, Tewodros committed suicide, marking the end of the British Expedition to Abyssinia.

image.caption: Scanned images of the obverse and face of the 1868 Abyssinian Campaign Medal.
image.credit: Richard Harvey — Own work
image.date_qualification: The depicted object is an 1868 campaign medal; the scan is dated 2008-06-19, not to the battle itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Magdala

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1868, the city of Edo surrendered to Emperor Meiji's forces, marking a significant shift in power from the Tokugawa shogunate to the imperial government. This event was pivotal in the Meiji Restoration, which transformed Japan into a modern state.
events.name: Fall of Edo

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1868, General William Tecumseh Sherman brokered the Treaty of Fort Laramie, which aimed to establish peace between the federal government of the United States and the Plains Indians. This treaty was a significant attempt to address the conflicts arising from westward expansion.
events.name: Treaty of Fort Laramie

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1868, during the Boshin War, forces loyal to Emperor Meiji engaged in battle against the retreating troops of the Tokugawa shogunate at Utsunomiya Castle. This battle was part of the broader conflict that ultimately led to the restoration of imperial rule in Japan.
events.name: Battle of Utsunomiya Castle

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1868, Michael Barrett, a Fenian bomber, became the last person to be publicly hanged in the United Kingdom. His execution marked the end of public hangings in the country, leading to significant changes in the penal system.
events.name: Execution of Michael Barrett

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1868, the Parliament of the United Kingdom passed the Capital Punishment Amendment Act, effectively ending the practice of public hanging. This legislative change reflected evolving attitudes towards capital punishment in British society.
events.name: Capital Punishment Amendment Act

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1868, Memorial Day was observed for the first time in the United States, a day dedicated to honoring fallen soldiers. The observance was proclaimed by General John A. Logan and has since become a national holiday.
events.name: First Memorial Day observance

events.enhanced_description: In 1868, Thomas Spence proclaimed himself the president of the Republic of Manitobah, a short-lived and largely symbolic entity that aimed to represent the interests of the Métis and other local populations. His leadership quickly became contentious, leading to alienation among the very communities he sought to represent.
events.name: Thomas Spence declares himself president of the Republic of Manitobah in Canada; he soon alienates the locals

events.enhanced_description: In June 1868, Tītokowaru's War erupted in the South Taranaki District of New Zealand, marking a significant conflict between the Ngāti Ruanui Māori tribe and the New Zealand Government. This war was characterized by guerrilla tactics and highlighted the tensions between Māori land rights and colonial expansion.

locations.name: South Taranaki District, Taranaki, New Zealand

events.name: Tītokowaru's War breaks out

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1868, the Treaty of Bosque Redondo was signed, allowing the Navajo people to return to their ancestral lands in Arizona and New Mexico after years of forced relocation. This treaty marked a significant moment in U.S.-Native American relations, aiming to restore peace and stability in the region.

locations.name: Bosque Redondo, New Mexico, United States

events.name: The Treaty of Bosque Redondo is signed

events.enhanced_description: The first Trades Union Congress convened in Manchester, England, on June 2, 1868, marking a pivotal moment in the labor movement. This gathering brought together various trade unions to discuss workers' rights and collective bargaining, laying the groundwork for future labor reforms.
events.name: The first Trades Union Congress is held

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1868, Mihailo Obrenović, the Prince of Serbia, was assassinated in Košutnjak, Belgrade. His death marked a significant turning point in Serbian politics, leading to a period of instability and the eventual rise of the rival Karađorđević dynasty.
events.name: Mihailo Obrenović is assassinated

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1868, Fort Fred Steele was established near modern-day Sinclair, Wyoming, to protect the western terminus of the Union Pacific Railway. This fort played a crucial role in safeguarding the railroad and facilitating westward expansion during a tumultuous period in American history.
events.name: Fort Fred Steele is established

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1868, the West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway in Manhattan became the first elevated railway in the United States. This innovative transportation system revolutionized urban transit and set the stage for the development of future elevated and subway systems.

image.caption: Charles Thompson Harvey making a southbound test run on the cable-driven West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway.
image.credit: (unknown) — Charles Thompson Harvey testing His Railway . Joseph Brennan . Columbia University. Archived from the original on May 4, 2006 . Retrieved on March 5, 2017 .
image.date_qualification: December 1867; pre-opening test run, not the July 1868 opening date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.historical_name: West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway
locations.name: Manhattan, New York, United States

events.name: The cable-operated West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway becomes the first elevated railway in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1868, the Battle of Ueno took place, where Imperial Japanese troops defeated the Shōgitai, elite forces loyal to the shōgun. This battle was a significant event in the Boshin War, marking a decisive victory for the imperial forces and contributing to the Meiji Restoration.
events.name: Battle of Ueno

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1868, preacher William Booth established the Christian Mission in the East End of London, which later evolved into The Salvation Army. This organization aimed to address social issues and provide aid to the impoverished, becoming a significant force in social reform.

locations.name: East End, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: William Booth establishes the Christian Mission

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1868, the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, establishing citizenship rights and equal protection under the law for all persons. This amendment was a crucial step in the post-Civil War era, aiming to secure civil rights for formerly enslaved individuals.
events.name: The Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution is ratified

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1868, the Navajo people began their long march home from Bosque Redondo, New Mexico, following the signing of the Treaty of Bosque Redondo. This journey marked a significant moment of resilience and cultural revival for the Navajo Nation.

locations.name: Bosque Redondo, New Mexico, United States

events.name: The Navajo people begin their long march home

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1868, Wyoming was officially designated as a United States territory, marking a significant step in the westward expansion and governance of the United States. This designation allowed for the establishment of a territorial government and paved the way for Wyoming's eventual statehood.
events.name: Wyoming becomes a United States territory

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1868, the United States Expatriation Act was adopted, addressing the rights of American citizens abroad and establishing the legal framework for expatriation. This act was significant in defining citizenship and the rights associated with it in a rapidly changing world.

image.caption: Obverse of the Great Seal of the United States.
image.credit: U.S. Government — Extracted from PDF version of Our Flag , available here (direct PDF URL here .)
image.date_qualification: A national emblem used as a contextual symbol for the United States; the saved image date records a basic design from 1782, later design details from 1885, and this file from 2007. It is not a depiction of the 1868 act's adoption.
image.image_date: basic design 1782; many design details 1885; this file 2007
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: insignia

events.name: The United States Expatriation Act is adopted

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1868, the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was adopted, solidifying the legal framework for citizenship and equal protection under the law for all individuals. This amendment was a cornerstone of civil rights legislation in the United States.
events.name: The Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution is adopted

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1868, a devastating earthquake with a magnitude of 8.5–9.0 struck southern Peru, causing widespread destruction and resulting in over 25,000 deaths. The earthquake triggered a massive tsunami that affected coastal areas as far away as Hawaii and New Zealand.
events.name: The Arica earthquake strikes southern Peru

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1868, French astronomer Jules Janssen detected the element later named helium in the spectrum of the Sun's chromosphere during a total solar eclipse in Guntur, India. This groundbreaking discovery expanded the understanding of solar composition and contributed to the field of spectroscopy.
events.name: Helium is first detected in the spectrum of the Sun

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1868, the Abergele rail disaster occurred when an Irish Mail passenger train collided with four cargo trucks loaded with paraffin oil, resulting in 33 fatalities. This incident marked the first major train disaster in Britain and raised concerns about railway safety.
events.name: Abergele rail disaster

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1868, the Yangzhou riot erupted in China, targeting a station of the China Inland Mission. This violent incident nearly escalated into war between Britain and China, highlighting the tensions surrounding foreign missionary activities in the region.
events.name: The Yangzhou riot in China

events.enhanced_description: In September 1868, the Glorious Revolution led to the effective deposition of Queen Isabella II of Spain, who was forced into exile.
