This political upheaval marked a significant shift in Spanish governance and set the stage for the establishment of a provisional government.

image.caption: Chromolithograph titled “Alegoria Revolucionaria La Gloriosa.”
image.credit: 19th century Spanish engraver/printer — 1896 chromolithograph; this copy via https://geoghistoria.blogspot.com/2017/12/actividad-el-sexenio-democratico-la.html
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration related to the 1868 Glorious Revolution; the saved image date is 1896, not the date of the revolution.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Glorious Revolution: Queen Isabella II of Spain is effectively deposed

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1868, Emperor Meiji announced the renaming of the city of Edo to Tokyo, meaning 'Eastern Capital.' This change symbolized the shift of power from the shōgunate to the emperor and marked the beginning of the Meiji Restoration.

image.caption: Colored Photochrom print panorama of Edo (now Tokyo), showing daimyo residences.
image.credit: Felice Beato — Colored Photochrom print version of File:Panorama of Edo bw.jpg . Click the link for the description. http://366days.net/konoe/Edo.jpg
image.date_qualification: Dated 1865 in the supplied image metadata; it predates the 1868 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Emperor Meiji announces the name change of Edo to Tokyo

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1868, during Tītokowaru's War, Māori leader Tītokowaru achieved a significant victory against a New Zealand military force at Te Ngutu o Te Manu. This battle underscored the resistance of Māori tribes against colonial encroachment.

locations.name: Te Ngutu o Te Manu, North Island, New Zealand

events.name: Tītokowaru's War: Māori leader Tītokowaru defeats a New Zealand military force

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1868, the University of the South held its first convocation in Sewanee, Tennessee. This event marked the establishment of the university, which aimed to provide higher education in the Southern United States.

image.caption: Photograph of McClurg Hall at the University of the South in Sewanee.
image.credit: Rex Hammock — https://www.flickr.com/photos/rexblog/3857313092
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2009-08-25; not a contemporary image of the 1868 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The University of the South holds its first convocation

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1868, the Grito de Lares took place when approximately 400-600 rebels, led by Ramón Emeterio Betances, declared Puerto Rico's independence from Spanish rule in the town of Lares. Although the rebellion was quickly suppressed, it became a symbol of the struggle for Puerto Rican autonomy.
events.name: Grito de Lares: Puerto Rico declares independence

events.enhanced_description: The Croatian–Hungarian Settlement, concluded on September 24, 1868, established the political status of Croatia within the Kingdom of Hungary, allowing for a degree of autonomy while remaining under Hungarian rule. This agreement was significant in shaping the political landscape of the Austro-Hungarian Empire until its dissolution in 1918.
events.name: Croatian–Hungarian Settlement

events.enhanced_description: The Opelousas Massacre, occurring on September 28, 1868, was one of the deadliest incidents during the Reconstruction era in the United States, where white supremacist groups attacked African Americans and their allies, resulting in numerous deaths and highlighting the violent resistance to Reconstruction policies.
events.name: Opelousas Massacre

events.enhanced_description: King Chulalongkorn ascended to the throne of Siam on October 1, 1868, initiating a reign that would modernize the country and reform its administrative structures. His leadership is credited with significant advancements in education, infrastructure, and the abolition of slavery.
events.name: Chulalongkorn starts to rule in Siam

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1868, the City of New York granted Mount Sinai Hospital a 99-year lease for a property on Lexington Avenue and 66th Street for the nominal sum of $1. This lease was crucial for the establishment and expansion of one of the city's leading medical institutions.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Mount Sinai Hospital Lease

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1868, Carlos Manuel de Céspedes declared a revolt against Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, an event known as El Grito de Yara. This declaration marked the beginning of the Ten Years' War, a significant struggle for Cuban independence that would last until 1878.
events.name: El Grito de Yara

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1868, English astronomer Norman Lockyer observed and named the D3 Fraunhofer line in the solar spectrum, concluding that it was caused by an unidentified element, which he later named helium. This discovery was pivotal in the field of spectroscopy and the study of solar chemistry.
events.name: Discovery of Helium

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1868, the era name in Japan was officially changed to the Meiji period, marking the end of the Edo period and the beginning of a time of rapid modernization and westernization in Japan. This transition was significant in shaping modern Japanese society and governance.
events.name: Meiji Period Begins

events.enhanced_description: The Uspenski Cathedral, designed by Aleksey Gornostayev, was inaugurated on October 25, 1868, in Helsinki, Finland. This cathedral is notable for its distinctive Russian architectural style and serves as a prominent symbol of the Orthodox Church in Finland.
events.name: Inauguration of Uspenski Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1868, Thomas Edison applied for his first patent for the electric vote recorder, a device designed to improve the efficiency of voting processes. This invention marked the beginning of Edison's prolific career as an inventor and innovator.

locations.name: Menlo Park, New Jersey, United States

events.name: Thomas Edison Patents Electric Vote Recorder

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1868, New Zealand officially adopted a standard time to be observed nationally, a significant step in the organization of timekeeping and scheduling in the country. This move was part of a broader trend towards standardization in the wake of industrialization.
events.name: New Zealand Adopts Standard Time

events.enhanced_description: In the 1868 United States presidential election held on November 3, 1868, Republican candidate Ulysses S. Grant defeated Democrat Horatio Seymour. This election was significant as it reflected the political tensions of the Reconstruction era following the Civil War.
events.name: 1868 United States Presidential Election

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Moturoa, which took place on November 7, 1868, ended in a British defeat due to an underestimation of Māori leader Tītokowaru and his fortifications. This battle was part of the New Zealand Wars, highlighting the ongoing conflict between colonial forces and Māori resistance.
events.name: Battle of Moturoa

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1868, during the American Indian Wars, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led an attack on a Cheyenne village along the Washita River, resulting in the deaths of 103 Cheyenne. This event exemplified the violent conflicts between the U.S. government and Native American tribes during this period.
events.name: Battle of Washita River

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Hakodate began on December 4, 1868, as part of the Boshin War in Japan. This conflict was significant in determining the future of Japan's imperial government and the end of the Tokugawa shogunate.
events.name: Battle of Hakodate

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1868, during the Paraguayan War, Field Marshal Luís Alves de Lima e Silva led 13,000 Brazilian troops against a fortified Paraguayan position at Ytororó. This battle was part of the larger conflict involving Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay against Paraguay.
figures: Luís Alves de Lima e Silva
events.name: Battle of Ytororó

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1868, the world's first traffic signal lights were installed at the junction of Great George Street and Bridge Street in Westminster, London. This innovation was an early attempt to manage urban traffic and improve road safety.
events.name: First Traffic Signal Lights

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1868, King George I established the Greek Presidential Guard as the royal escort. This unit has since become a symbol of national pride and is known for its ceremonial duties at the Greek Parliament.

image.caption: Presidential guards at Syntagma Square, Greece.
image.credit: Robin from England — athens075
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2007-06-10; it does not depict the 1868 establishment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of the Greek Presidential Guard

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1868, U.S. President Andrew Johnson granted an unconditional pardon to all Civil War rebels, a significant act aimed at reconciliation and healing the nation post-Civil War. This decision was controversial and reflected the complexities of Reconstruction policies.
events.name: Unconditional Pardon to Civil War Rebels

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, Children's Hospital Boston was founded by Dr. Francis Henry Brown and other Harvard Medical School graduates as a 20-bed facility in the South End of Boston. It has since grown into a leading pediatric healthcare institution.
events.name: Founding of Children's Hospital Boston

events.enhanced_description: In December 1869, Leo Tolstoy's epic novel War and Peace was published in complete book form in Russia. This monumental work is celebrated for its intricate narrative and profound exploration of history and human experience.

image.caption: Postcard by Elizaveta Bem depicting Natasha Rostova from *War and Peace*.
image.credit: Elisabeth Bem — [1] [2] [3]
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1914, after the novel’s complete publication in 1869.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of War and Peace

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, James Gordon Bennett Jr., the publisher of the New York Herald, commissioned journalist Henry Morton Stanley to locate the missing missionary and explorer Dr. David Livingstone in Africa, who had not been heard from for several years. This expedition would lead to Stanley's famous greeting of 'Dr. Livingstone, I presume?' upon finding Livingstone in Ujiji, Tanzania, in 1871.

image.caption: Portrait of Henry Morton Stanley.
image.credit: Creator:J. Russel & Sons — National Library of Norway
image.date_qualification: The source gives the image date as “before 1902”; it does not establish the date the portrait was made. The upload date is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: James Gordon Bennett Jr asks Henry Morton Stanley to find Dr. David Livingstone

events.enhanced_description: The Co-operative Central Board was established in Manchester in 1869 to support the growing cooperative movement in the UK, which aimed to provide goods and services to members at fair prices. This organization would later evolve into Co-operatives UK, representing the interests of cooperative businesses across the country.

image.caption: Holyoake House, a Classical building on Dantzic Street in Manchester, built for the Co-operative Union.
image.credit: Stephen Richards — From geograph.org.uk
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the organisation’s later headquarters, built in 1911; it is contextual site imagery, not a depiction of the 1869 founding. Photo date: 2011-06-23.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Co-operative Central Board is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, Swiss biochemist Friedrich Miescher isolated a substance he called 'nuclein' from the nuclei of white blood cells, which would later be identified as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). This groundbreaking discovery laid the foundation for modern genetics and molecular biology.

image.caption: Portrait of Professor Friedrich Miescher on his terrace at Augustinergasse 21.
image.credit: Iheggemann25 — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1878; it is not a depiction of the 1869 discovery.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Friedrich Miescher purifies nuclein

events.enhanced_description: The Ladies National Association for the Repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts was founded in 1869 in Great Britain as a response to the controversial laws that allowed for the forced medical examination of women suspected of prostitution. The organization played a crucial role in advocating for women's rights and the repeal of these acts.
events.name: The Ladies National Association for the Repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, French missionary and naturalist Père Armand David received the skin of a giant panda from a hunter, marking the first time this species was known to the Western world. He also described the 'pocket handkerchief tree,' which was later named Davidia involucrata in his honor.
events.name: Père Armand David receives the skin of a giant panda

events.enhanced_description: The University of Otago, established in 1869 in Dunedin, is New Zealand's first university. It has played a significant role in the country's higher education landscape, known for its research and academic programs.

image.caption: Aerial view of the University of Otago campus in Dunedin.
image.credit: ArtNewNZ — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2024-11-13; 155 years after the university was established in 1869.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: University of Otago is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, Thomas Henry Huxley coined the term 'agnostic' to describe a philosophical position of uncertainty regarding the existence of God. This term has since become a significant concept in discussions of faith and knowledge.
events.name: Thomas Henry Huxley coins the word 'Agnostic'

events.enhanced_description: The Campbell Soup Company was founded in 1869 in Camden, New Jersey, and has since become one of the largest food processing companies in the world, known for its soups and other food products.
events.name: Campbell Soup Company is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, Henry John Heinz founded the Heinz company in Sharpsburg, Pennsylvania, which would grow to become a leading global food processing company known for its ketchup and other condiments.
events.name: Heinz founded in Pennsylvania

events.enhanced_description: St. Ignatius College Prep was founded in 1869 in Chicago, Illinois, and is notable for being one of the few buildings that survived the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. The school has a long tradition of academic excellence and Jesuit education.
events.name: St. Ignatius College Prep is founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1869, Abdur Rahman Khan was defeated at Tinah Khan, leading to his exile from Afghanistan. This event marked a significant moment in the power struggles within the region during the late 19th century.
events.name: Abdur Rahman Khan defeated at Tinah Khan

events.enhanced_description: Kilmarnock F.C., Scotland's second oldest professional football team, was founded on January 5, 1869. The club has a rich history and has contributed significantly to Scottish football culture.
events.name: Founding of Kilmarnock F.C.

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1869, Elizabeth Cady Stanton became the first woman to testify before the United States Congress, advocating for women's rights and suffrage. This historic moment marked a significant step in the women's rights movement in the United States.
events.name: Elizabeth Cady Stanton testifies before Congress

events.enhanced_description: The P.E.O. Sisterhood, a philanthropic educational organization for women, was founded on January 21, 1869, at Iowa Wesleyan College in Mount Pleasant, Iowa. The organization has since played a vital role in supporting women's education and empowerment.
events.name: Founding of P.E.O. Sisterhood

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1869, the Republic of Ezo was proclaimed on the northern Japanese island of Ezo by supporters of the Tokugawa shogunate. This short-lived republic was part of the larger conflict during the Meiji Restoration.
events.name: Proclamation of the Republic of Ezo

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1869, prospectors in Moliagul, Victoria, Australia, discovered the largest alluvial gold nugget ever found, known as the 'Welcome Stranger.' This discovery significantly impacted the Australian gold rush and economy.
events.name: Discovery of the Welcome Stranger gold nugget

events.enhanced_description: In February 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev completed his design of the first periodic table, which organized the known chemical elements based on their atomic weights and properties. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for modern chemistry and the systematic study of elements.
events.name: Dmitri Mendeleev finishes his design of the first periodic table

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1869, Ranavalona II, the Merina Queen of Madagascar, was baptized, marking a significant moment in the Christianization of Madagascar. Her conversion had implications for the relationship between the monarchy and missionary activities in the region.
events.name: Baptism of Ranavalona II

events.enhanced_description: The Iron and Steel Institute was formed in London on February 25, 1869, as a professional organization aimed at advancing the knowledge and practice of iron and steel production. It played a crucial role in the industrial development of the United Kingdom.
events.name: Formation of the Iron and Steel Institute

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1869, Mahbub Ali Khan ascended to the throne as the Nizam of Hyderabad, beginning a 42-year reign. His rule was marked by significant developments in the region's administration and culture.
events.name: Mahbub Ali Khan begins reign as Nizam of Hyderabad

events.enhanced_description: In March 1869, the daimyōs of the Tosa, Hizen, Satsuma, and Chōshū Domains returned their domains to Emperor Meiji, facilitating the establishment of a centralized government in Japan. This event was pivotal in the Meiji Restoration, which transformed Japan into a modern state.
events.name: Return of daimyōs to Emperor Meiji

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1869, the North German Confederation issued 10gr and 30gr value stamps printed on goldbeater's skin. This innovation in postal services reflected the growing importance of efficient communication in the rapidly industrializing region.
events.name: Issuance of stamps by North German Confederation

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1869, Ulysses S. Grant was sworn in as the 18th President of the United States. His presidency followed the Civil War and was marked by efforts to reconstruct the nation and address the challenges of the post-war era.
events.name: Ulysses S. Grant sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev made a formal presentation of his periodic table to the Russian Chemical Society in Saint Petersburg. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for modern chemistry and the understanding of chemical elements.
events.name: Dmitri Mendeleev presents periodic table

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1869, Tītoko's War concluded with the surrender of the last Māori troops in the South Taranaki District of New Zealand's North Island. This conflict was part of the broader struggle between Māori and colonial forces during the 19th century.
events.name: End of Tītoko war

events.enhanced_description: The American Museum of Natural History was founded on April 6, 1869, in New York City. It has since become one of the largest and most celebrated museums in the world, known for its extensive collections and research in various fields of natural history.

image.caption: Site photograph of the American Museum of Natural History.
image.credit: Ingfbruno — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2013-04-28; this depicts the museum site, not its 1869 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of the American Museum of Natural History

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1869, the State of Morelos was officially created in Mexico, named after the national hero José María Morelos. This event marked an important step in the political reorganization of the country following the tumultuous period of the Reform War.
events.name: Creation of the State of Morelos

events.enhanced_description: In May 1869, national elections in France saw the opposition, comprising republicans, monarchists, and liberals, garner nearly 45% of the vote. This election reflected the growing political diversity and tensions in France during the Second Empire.
events.name: French National Elections

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1869, the Imperial Japanese Navy achieved a decisive victory over the forces loyal to the Tokugawa shogunate in the Naval Battle of Hakodate. This battle was a significant event in the Boshin War, marking the decline of the shogunate's power.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the Naval Battle of Hakodate, with Kasuga and Kōtetsu of the Imperial Japanese Navy in the foreground.
image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist , ILN Staff, after a sketch by William Henry Webster — From Illustrated London News , 11 September 1869, p. 248 . Description of image is at p. 257
image.date_qualification: The image depicts the May 1869 battle; 11 September 1869 is the publication date, not the battle date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Naval Battle of Hakodate

events.enhanced_description: Purdue University was founded on May 6, 1869, in West Lafayette, Indiana. It has grown to become a leading research institution, known for its engineering and technology programs.
events.name: Founding of Purdue University

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1869, the first transcontinental railroad in North America was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, marked by the driving of the 'golden spike.' This monumental achievement connected the eastern and western United States, revolutionizing transportation and commerce.
events.name: Completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1869, Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton established the National Woman Suffrage Association in New York City. This organization played a crucial role in the women's suffrage movement, advocating for women's right to vote.
events.name: Formation of the National Woman Suffrage Association

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1869, Enomoto Takeaki surrendered at Goryōkaku, marking the collapse of the Republic of Ezo after the land Battle of Hakodate. This event signified the end of the Boshin War and the consolidation of power by the Imperial government.
events.name: Surrender of Enomoto Takeaki at Goryōkaku

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1869, Sainsbury's opened its first store in Drury Lane, London. This marked the beginning of one of the largest supermarket chains in the UK, known for its commitment to quality and customer service.
events.name: Opening of Sainsbury's first store

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1869, John Wesley Powell departed from Green River, Wyoming, with a team of nine men to explore the Green and Colorado Rivers. This expedition would lead to significant discoveries about the geography and geology of the American West.
events.name: John Wesley Powell's expedition

events.enhanced_description: Boston University was chartered by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts on May 26, 1869. It has since grown into a major research university, known for its diverse academic programs and commitment to public service.
events.name: Chartering of Boston University

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1869, the Cincinnati Red Stockings opened the baseball season as the first fully professional baseball team. This event marked a significant milestone in the history of American sports.
events.name: Cincinnati Red Stockings open baseball season

events.enhanced_description: Sherwood College was founded in Nainital, India, on June 2, 1869. It has since become a prominent educational institution, known for its academic excellence and holistic development of students.
events.name: Founding of Sherwood College

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1869, John Wesley Hyatt patented celluloid in Albany, New York. This invention was significant as it became one of the first synthetic plastics, widely used in various applications.
events.name: John Wesley Hyatt patents celluloid

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1869, the fortress of Goryōkaku was turned over to Imperial Japanese forces, marking the end of the Republic of Ezo and concluding the Battle of Hakodate and the Boshin War. This event signified the consolidation of the Meiji Restoration.
events.name: End of the Republic of Ezo

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1869, the first Estonian Song Festival took place in Tartu, celebrating Estonian culture and music. This event has since become a significant tradition in Estonia, fostering national identity and unity.
events.name: First Estonian Song Festival

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1869, a devastating fire destroyed much of Gävle, Sweden, leaving around 8,000 people homeless. This disaster prompted significant changes in fire safety regulations and urban planning in the city.
events.name: Destruction of Gävle by fire

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1869, Hippolyte Mége-Mouriès filed a patent for margarine in France. This invention provided a cheaper alternative to butter and revolutionized the food industry.
events.name: Patent for margarine

events.enhanced_description: In 1869, Mark Twain's travel book, The Innocents Abroad, was published by the American Publishing Company. The book became Twain's bestselling work during his lifetime, offering humorous insights into his travels through Europe and the Holy Land.
events.name: Publication of The Innocents Abroad

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1869, Queen Victoria gave royal assent to the Irish Church Act, disestablishing the Church of Ireland effective January 1, 1871. This act was a significant step in the disestablishment of the Anglican Church in Ireland.
events.name: Royal assent for the Irish Church Act

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1869, August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht founded the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany (SDAP) in Leipzig. This party played a crucial role in the development of socialist politics in Germany.
events.name: Founding of the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1869, the University of Oxford won the first international boat race held on the River Thames against Harvard University. This event marked the beginning of a long-standing tradition of collegiate rowing competitions.
events.name: First international boat race

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1869, Irish scientist Mary Ward was tragically killed by a steam car. Her death highlighted the dangers of early automotive technology and her contributions to science and engineering.
events.name: Death of Mary Ward

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1869, the foundation stone for Neuschwanstein Castle was laid in Bavaria, Germany. This iconic castle, commissioned by King Ludwig II, has become a symbol of romantic architecture and a popular tourist destination.
events.name: Laying of the foundation stone for Neuschwanstein Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Wallace Monument, dedicated to the Scottish hero William Wallace, was completed in Stirling, Scotland. This iconic tower stands as a tribute to Wallace's legacy and offers panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.
events.name: Completion of the Wallace Monument

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1869, the P&O liner SS Carnatic ran aground and sank in the Red Sea, resulting in the tragic drowning of 31 passengers. This incident highlighted the dangers of maritime travel during that era.
events.name: Sinking of the SS Carnatic

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1869, the financial scandal involving James Fisk and Jay Gould led to a significant panic in the United States, known as Black Friday. This event caused widespread financial turmoil and highlighted the vulnerabilities in the financial system of the time.

image.caption: Photograph of the New York Gold Room bulletin board showing the gold-price collapse.
image.credit: James A. Garfield (handwritten note) — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ppmsca.12856 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Dated 1869; described as showing the price collapse on Black Friday, September 24. The handwritten note identifies later use as evidence at 1870 hearings.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Black Friday Financial Panic

events.enhanced_description: In October 1869, the 'Edinburgh Seven', led by Sophia Jex-Blake, became the first women to attend lectures at the University of Edinburgh Medical School. Although they were not allowed to take degrees, their enrollment marked a significant step towards women's education in medicine.
events.name: Edinburgh Seven attend Medical School

events.enhanced_description: The Red River Rebellion broke out on October 11, 1869, against British forces in Canada, led by Louis Riel. This uprising aimed to address the grievances of the Métis people regarding land rights and governance.
events.name: Red River Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1869, the College for Women, the first residential university-level women's college in England, was founded in Hitchin by Emily Davies and Barbara Bodichon. This institution paved the way for women's higher education in the UK.

image.caption: Photochrom print of Girton College, Cambridge.
image.credit: Adam Cuerden — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ppmsc.08082 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: between 1890 and 1900; the college was established in 1869.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of the College for Women

events.enhanced_description: The first issue of the scientific journal Nature was published on November 4, 1869, in London, edited by Norman Lockyer. This journal has since become one of the most prestigious scientific publications in the world.
events.name: Publication of Nature

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1869, the first game of American football between two colleges was played, with Rutgers University defeating Princeton University 6–4. This match is considered a pivotal moment in the development of American football.
events.name: First American Football Game

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1869, the Suez Canal, which links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea, was inaugurated in an elaborate ceremony. This monumental engineering feat significantly shortened maritime travel between Europe and Asia.

image.caption: Édouard Riou’s illustration of the Suez Canal inauguration ceremony at Port Said.
image.credit: Édouard Riou — histoire-image
image.date_qualification: Image date stated as 1869; the description identifies the depicted ceremony as 17 November 1869. This is an illustration, not a photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Inauguration of the Suez Canal

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1869, the Hudson's Bay Company surrendered its claim to Rupert's Land back to the British Crown. This transfer marked a significant moment in Canadian history, paving the way for the expansion of Canadian Confederation.
events.name: Hudson's Bay Company Surrender

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1869, the clipper ship Cutty Sark was launched in Dumbarton, Scotland. It is renowned as one of the last clippers built and the only one to survive in the United Kingdom, symbolizing the golden age of sail.
events.name: Launch of the Cutty Sark

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1869, American outlaw Jesse James committed his first confirmed bank robbery in Gallatin, Missouri. This event marked the beginning of his notorious criminal career and the legend that would follow him.
events.name: Jesse James' First Bank Robbery

events.enhanced_description: The First Vatican Council opened on December 8, 1869, in Rome, under the leadership of Pope Pius IX. This ecumenical council addressed various issues within the Catholic Church, including papal infallibility.
events.name: Opening of the First Vatican Council

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1869, the Wyoming territorial legislature passed a law granting women the right to vote, making it the first such law in the world. This landmark decision was a significant step forward for women's rights and suffrage movements.
events.name: Women's Suffrage in Wyoming

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1869, during the Paraguayan War, Triple Alliance forces captured Asunción, the capital of Paraguay. This event marked a turning point in the conflict, leading to significant changes in the region's political landscape.
events.name: Triple Alliance Takes Asunción

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, the first edition of The Northern Echo newspaper was published in Priestgate, Darlington, England. This publication played a significant role in local journalism and the dissemination of news in the region.
events.name: The first edition of The Northern Echo newspaper is published

events.enhanced_description: In February 1870, Denis Vrain-Lucas was sentenced to two years in prison for multiple counts of forgery in Paris, France. His case drew attention due to the elaborate nature of his forgeries and the public interest in the legal proceedings.
events.name: Denis Vrain-Lucas sentenced for forgery

events.enhanced_description: In March 1870, the Mitsubishi Company was established in Japan as a shipping firm by Iwasaki Yatarō in partnership with Thomas Blake Glover. This company would grow to become one of Japan's largest and most influential conglomerates.
events.name: The Mitsubishi Company is established

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, plans for the Brooklyn Bridge were completed, marking a significant milestone in engineering and architecture. This iconic bridge would later become a vital transportation link between Manhattan and Brooklyn.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Plans for the Brooklyn Bridge are completed

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, it was revealed that the Cardiff Giant, once thought to be a petrified human, was actually a carved gypsum statue. This discovery sparked debates about science and belief, becoming a notable event in American cultural history.
events.name: Cardiff Giant revealed as a hoax

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, the novel The Seven Brothers (Seitsemän veljestä) by Finnish author Aleksis Kivi was published in several thin booklets. This work is considered a cornerstone of Finnish literature and reflects the cultural identity of Finland.

image.caption: A Finnish postage stamp depicting the Seven Brothers of Aleksis Kivi.
image.credit: Published by Posti- ja telelaitos — http://www.datafun.fi/postimerkki/
image.date_qualification: Postage stamp depicting the novel’s characters, not a contemporary image of the novel’s publication. The stamp is dated 1970, a century after the novel’s first publication in 1870.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Seven Brothers novel published

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, the German Commerzbank was founded in Hamburg, Germany. It became one of the leading banks in Germany, playing a significant role in the country's financial sector.
events.name: The German Commerzbank is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, Texas was readmitted to the Union as part of the Reconstruction efforts following the Civil War. This event was significant in restoring the state's political status and representation in Congress.
events.name: Reconstruction: Texas is readmitted to the Union

events.enhanced_description: The Port Adelaide Football Club was founded in 1870, becoming one of the oldest and most successful clubs in Australian rules football. The club has a rich history and a passionate fan base, contributing significantly to the sport's culture in Australia.
events.name: Founding of Port Adelaide Football Club

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, the United States Congress established the Department of Justice to oversee the enforcement of federal laws and ensure fair and impartial administration of justice. This marked a significant development in the U.S. legal framework.
events.name: Creation of the United States Department of Justice

events.enhanced_description: The British government officially admitted the former Hudson's Bay Company territories of Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory into the Dominion of Canada. This event was crucial for the expansion and consolidation of Canadian territory.
events.name: Admission of Rupert's Land and North-Western Territory

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, David Kenyon invented the fireman's pole, a crucial innovation for firehouses that allowed firefighters to descend quickly from upper floors. This invention significantly improved response times during emergencies.
events.name: David Kenyon invents the fireman's pole in Chicago

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, Samuel Graeter began making ice cream in Cincinnati, Ohio, which would eventually lead to the establishment of Graeter's Ice Cream, known for its French pot process and rich flavors. The company has since become a beloved regional brand.
events.name: Graeter's ice cream is originated in Cincinnati, Ohio

events.enhanced_description: In 1870, the Indian Civil Service was predominantly staffed by British officials, with only one Indian among its 916 members. This highlighted the colonial governance structure and the limited opportunities for Indians in administrative roles.
events.name: Just one of the 916 members of the Indian Civil Service is Indian

events.enhanced_description: Construction of the iconic Brooklyn Bridge began on January 3, 1870, in New York City. This engineering marvel would connect Manhattan and Brooklyn, becoming a symbol of innovation and urban development.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Construction of the Brooklyn Bridge begins

events.enhanced_description: The Musikverein, a concert hall in Vienna, Austria, was inaugurated on January 6, 1870. It is renowned for its exceptional acoustics and is home to the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra, making it a central hub for classical music.
events.name: The Musikverein, Vienna, is inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1870, John D. Rockefeller incorporated Standard Oil in New York City, which would grow to dominate the oil industry in the United States and significantly influence global energy markets.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: John D. Rockefeller incorporates Standard Oil

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1870, political cartoonist Thomas Nast published a cartoon in Harper's Weekly that for the first time symbolized the United States Democratic Party with a donkey. This imagery has since become a lasting symbol of the party.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Political cartoon symbolizes the Democratic Party with a donkey

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1870, U.S. soldiers attacked a peaceful camp of the Piegan Blackfeet Indians in what is known as the Marias Massacre, led by Chief Heavy Runner. This tragic event resulted in the deaths of many Native Americans and highlighted the violent conflicts between U.S. forces and indigenous peoples.
events.name: Marias Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1870, during the Reconstruction Era, Virginia rejoined the Union after adopting a new constitution that expanded suffrage to all male citizens over 21, including freedmen. This marked a significant step toward civil rights in the post-Civil War United States.
events.name: Virginia rejoins the Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1870, the British steamship SS City of Boston departed from Halifax, Nova Scotia, on a transatlantic voyage. Tragically, the ship was lost at sea with all 191 aboard, marking one of the maritime disasters of the era.
events.name: SS City of Boston departs Halifax

events.enhanced_description: Goodna State School was founded in February 1870 in Goodna, Queensland, Australia. It has served the local community for over a century, providing education to generations of students.
events.name: Goodna State School is founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1870, it was revealed that the Cardiff Giant, a purported petrified prehistoric man discovered in Cardiff, New York, was actually a carved gypsum statue. This revelation sparked significant public interest and debate about the nature of the hoax.
events.name: Cardiff Giant revealed as forgery

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was passed, guaranteeing African American men the right to vote. This landmark legislation was a significant achievement of the Reconstruction Era, aimed at ensuring civil rights for formerly enslaved individuals.

image.caption: The Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, page 1 of the document.
image.credit: United States Congress — National Archives of the United States
image.date_qualification: The depicted document is dated 1870; the image_date does not establish the date of the passage event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution is passed

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1870, the U.S. Army Weather Bureau was created within the Army Signal Corps, marking the beginning of organized weather forecasting in the United States. This development laid the groundwork for modern meteorological services.
events.name: U.S. Army Weather Bureau is created

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1870, Anaheim, California, was incorporated as a city. Originally founded by German settlers in 1857, Anaheim has since grown into a major urban center known for its tourism and entertainment industry.
events.name: Anaheim, California, is incorporated

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1870, women in the Utah Territory gained the right to vote, making it one of the first places in the United States to grant suffrage to women. This milestone was a significant step in the broader women's suffrage movement.

image.caption: Black-and-white group photograph of Western and national suffrage leaders.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://www.utahwomenshistory.org/2018/02/receiving-losing-and-winning-back-the-vote-the-story-of-utah-womens-suffrage/
image.date_qualification: A later suffrage meeting photograph, not a photograph of the 1870 enfranchisement; the saved image date is given only as the 1870s and conflicts with the described 1895 meeting.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

events.name: Women's suffrage in Utah Territory

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1870, Mississippi was officially readmitted to the Union after a period of military control following the Civil War. This marked a significant step in the Reconstruction era, as the state was able to regain its representation in Congress.
events.name: Military control of Mississippi ends and it is readmitted to the Union

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1870, Hiram Rhodes Revels was sworn in as the first African American senator in U.S. history, representing Mississippi. His election was a landmark event in the Reconstruction era, symbolizing the progress made towards racial equality in the United States.
events.name: Hiram Rhodes Revels is sworn into the United States Senate

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1870, the Beach Pneumatic Transit, the first pneumatic subway system, was opened in New York City. This innovative transportation system utilized air pressure to move cars through underground tunnels, marking a significant advancement in urban transit technology.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First pneumatic subway, Beach Pneumatic Transit, is opened

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1870, the Nisshoki, or 'circle of the sun' flag, was officially adopted as the national flag for Japanese merchant ships by the Daijō-kan. This flag would later become the national flag of Japan, symbolizing the country's identity.
events.name: The Nisshoki flag of Japan is adopted

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1870, the Bulgarian Exarchate was established by decree of Sultan Abdülaziz of the Ottoman Empire. This marked a significant step in the religious and national awakening of the Bulgarian people, allowing for greater autonomy in ecclesiastical matters.
events.name: The Bulgarian Exarchate is established

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1870, the Battle of Cerro Corá took place, marking the final confrontation of the Paraguayan War. Marshal Francisco Solano López's forces were cornered by the Triple Alliance, leading to López's death and the end of the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Cerro Corá

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1870, Thomas Scott was executed by Louis Riel's provisional government during the Red River Rebellion in Manitoba. This event intensified the conflict between the Métis and the Canadian government, highlighting the struggles for rights and recognition.
events.name: Execution of Thomas Scott during the Red River Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1870, the first international Association football match was held between England and Scotland at The Oval in London. This match is considered a pivotal moment in the history of football, contributing to the sport's growing popularity.
events.name: First international Association football match

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1870, Deutsche Bank was founded in Berlin, Germany. It was established to facilitate trade relations between Germany and international markets, eventually becoming one of the world's leading financial institutions.
events.name: Deutsche Bank is founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1870, the Female Infanticide Prevention Act was passed in British India, spearheaded by social reformer Natalia Fish. This legislation aimed to combat the practice of female infanticide, reflecting a growing awareness of women's rights in the region.
events.name: Female Infanticide Prevention Act, 1870, passed in British India

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1870, the Ohio Legislature passed the Cannon Act, establishing the Ohio Agriculture and Mechanical College, which would later become Ohio State University. This act was a significant development in higher education in the United States.
events.name: Cannon Act establishes Ohio State University

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1870, Syracuse University was officially established in Syracuse, New York. It became a prominent institution of higher learning, contributing to the educational landscape of the United States.
events.name: Syracuse University is established

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, granting African American men the right to vote. This amendment was a crucial milestone in the ongoing struggle for civil rights in the United States.
events.name: The Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution is ratified

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1870, Thomas Mundy Peterson became the first African American to vote in an election in the United States. His participation marked a significant moment in the history of voting rights and the Reconstruction era.

locations.name: Perth Amboy, New Jersey, United States

events.name: Thomas Mundy Peterson is the first African American to vote

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1870, a devastating 7.3 magnitude earthquake struck Batang County in Sichuan, China, leading to widespread destruction and a catastrophic fire. The disaster resulted in the tragic loss of approximately 5,000 lives, highlighting the vulnerability of the region to seismic activity.
events.name: Batang Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, one of the largest and most prestigious art museums in the world, was established on April 13, 1870, in New York City. It has since become a cultural landmark, housing an extensive collection of art from various periods and regions.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Establishment of the Metropolitan Museum of Art

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1870, Antonio Guzmán Blanco began his first term as President of Venezuela, a position he would hold multiple times throughout his political career. His leadership was marked by significant modernization efforts and political turmoil in the country.
events.name: Antonio Guzmán Blanco's Presidency

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1870, the Chicago Base Ball Club, which would later become known as the Chicago Cubs, played its inaugural game against the St. Louis Unions. This marked the beginning of a storied franchise in Major League Baseball history.
events.name: First Game of the Chicago Base Ball Club

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1870, the province of Manitoba was officially created in Canada as a response to the Red River Rebellion led by Louis Riel. This event marked a significant moment in Canadian history, addressing the rights of the Métis people and expanding Canadian territory.
events.name: Creation of Manitoba

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1870, the first rugby match in New Zealand was played between the Nelson Football Club and Nelson College. This event marked the beginning of rugby's popularity in New Zealand, which would grow to become a national sport.
events.name: First Rugby Match in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1870, the Fenian Brotherhood launched an attack on Eccles Hill in Ontario, Canada. This event was part of a series of raids aimed at pressuring the British government to grant Ireland independence.
events.name: Fenian Brotherhood Attack

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1870, the final splice of the first telegraph submarine cable between Great Britain and India was completed. This technological achievement revolutionized communication, allowing for faster and more reliable messages across continents.
events.name: Completion of the First Telegraph Submarine Cable

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1870, the renowned English novelist Charles Dickens passed away at Gads Hill Place in Kent. His death left his last novel, 'The Mystery of Edwin Drood,' unfinished, marking the end of an era for Victorian literature.

locations.name: Gads Hill Place, Kent, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Death of Charles Dickens

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1870, the Tianjin Massacre occurred when an angry mob attacked churches in Tianjin, China, resulting in the deaths of 17 foreigners, mostly European Christian priests and nuns, and 40 Chinese converts. This event highlighted the tensions between foreign missionaries and local populations.
events.name: Tianjin Massacre

events.enhanced_description: The office of the Solicitor General of the United States was established in 1870 to supervise and conduct government litigation in the Supreme Court. This office plays a crucial role in representing the federal government in legal matters.
events.name: Establishment of the Solicitor General's Office

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1870, the first message was sent via the electric telegraph using the newly completed submarine cable connecting Great Britain to India. This event marked a milestone in global communication.
events.name: First Message via Submarine Cable

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1870, Richard Wagner's opera 'Die Walküre' premiered at the National Theatre in Munich. This opera is part of Wagner's larger cycle, 'Der Ring des Nibelungen,' and is celebrated for its complex characters and innovative music.
events.name: Premiere of Die Walküre

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1870, President Ulysses S. Grant signed an act establishing federal holidays in the United States, including Independence Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, and New Year's Day. This legislation formalized the observance of these significant national celebrations.
events.name: Federal Holidays Act Signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1870, the Ems Dispatch was published, serving as a catalyst for the Franco-Prussian War. The dispatch, which reported on a diplomatic encounter between France and Prussia, inflamed tensions and led to the declaration of war.

image.caption: Photograph of Wilhelm I and Nikolaus Wilhelm zu Nassau in Bad Ems.
image.credit: Anonymous Unknown author — Preussen 1701-1871 (?)
image.date_qualification: circa 1870 (as stated in the image date; not an exact date of the dispatch’s publication)
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of the Ems Dispatch

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1870, Georgia became the last former Confederate state to be readmitted to the Union during the Reconstruction Era. This event marked a significant step in the reintegration of Southern states following the Civil War.
events.name: Georgia Readmitted to the Union

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1870, Pope Pius IX declared papal infallibility in matters of faith and morals during the First Vatican Council. This declaration solidified the authority of the papacy within the Catholic Church and has had lasting implications for Catholic doctrine.
events.name: Papal Infallibility Declared

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1870, France officially declared war on Prussia, marking the beginning of the Franco-Prussian War. This conflict would have significant consequences for both nations and alter the balance of power in Europe.

image.caption: Map of the Franco-Prussian War.
image.credit: Edited by A.W.Ward, G.W.Prothero, and Stanley Leathes — Cambridge Modern History Atlas
image.date_qualification: Map dated 1912; it provides context for the war that began in 1870 and does not depict the declaration itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: France Declares War on Prussia

events.enhanced_description: The Solar Saros 153 began on July 28, 1870, marking the start of a series of solar eclipses that will continue until 3114. This astronomical event is part of a cycle that has been studied for centuries.
events.name: Start of Solar Saros 153

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1870, the 'Diggers' Republic' was proclaimed at Klipdrift in South Africa by diamond miners, with Stafford Parker as president. This short-lived republic was a response to the influx of miners and the demand for self-governance in the diamond-rich region.
events.name: Proclamation of the Diggers' Republic

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1870, the Tower Subway, the world's first underground passenger 'tube' railway, officially opened beneath the River Thames in London. This innovative engineering feat demonstrated the potential of underground transportation systems.
events.name: Opening of the Tower Subway

events.enhanced_description: The Republic of Ploiești was a short-lived uprising against Domnitor Carol I of Romania, which ultimately failed. The revolt reflected the growing discontent among various social classes in Romania during this period.
events.name: The Republic of Ploiești uprising

events.enhanced_description: The Red River Rebellion concluded with the arrival of the Wolseley Expedition, leading to the flight of its leader, Louis Riel. This rebellion was a pivotal moment in Canadian history, highlighting the tensions between the Métis people and the Canadian government.
events.name: End of the Red River Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: During the Franco-Prussian War, the Battle of Sedan resulted in a decisive victory for Prussian forces, capturing Emperor Napoleon III and around 100,000 French soldiers. This defeat marked a significant turning point in the war and led to the fall of the Second French Empire.

image.caption: Retrospective painting by Wilhelm Camphausen depicting Napoleon III at Sedan.
image.credit: Wilhelm Camphausen — [1]
image.date_qualification: The Battle of Sedan was fought 1–2 September 1870; the image description identifies the painting as a work by Camphausen, who died in 1885, but supplies no painting date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Sedan

events.enhanced_description: Following his capture at Sedan, Emperor Napoleon III was deposed, leading to the declaration of the Third Republic in France. This event marked the end of imperial rule and the beginning of a new republican era.
events.name: Deposition of Napoleon III

events.enhanced_description: Louisa Swain made history by becoming the first woman in the United States to legally cast a vote since 1807, marking a significant milestone in the women's suffrage movement. This event took place in Laramie, Wyoming, which was at the forefront of women's voting rights.

image.caption: Portrait of Louisa A. Swain.
image.credit: Alice Stone Blackwell — Blackwell, Alice Stone (November 1918) The Woman Citizen (Public domain ed.), Leslie Woman Suffrage Commission
image.date_qualification: Published November 1918; the image metadata dates the depicted portrait to by 1880. This is not an image of the 1870 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Louisa Swain's historic vote

events.enhanced_description: During the Washburn–Langford–Doane Expedition, Old Faithful Geyser was observed and named by Henry D. Washburn. This event contributed to the scientific understanding and appreciation of geothermal features in Yellowstone National Park.

image.caption: Photograph of Old Faithful Geyser erupting in Yellowstone National Park.
image.credit: Dietmar Rabich — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2022 photograph of the geyser erupting; it does not depict the 1870 observation and naming event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, United States

events.name: Observation of Old Faithful Geyser

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Paris commenced during the Franco-Prussian War, leading to a prolonged blockade of the city. This siege would have significant implications for the war and for the French populace.
events.name: Beginning of the Siege of Paris

events.enhanced_description: The capture of Rome by Bersaglieri soldiers at Porta Pia marked the completion of Italian unification, effectively ending the Papal States and diminishing papal temporal power. This event was a crucial step in the establishment of Italy as a unified nation.
events.name: Capture of Rome

events.enhanced_description: A plebiscite held in Rome overwhelmingly supported the annexation of the city by Italy, with 133,681 votes in favor and only 1,507 against. This event solidified Rome's status as part of the newly unified Italy.
events.name: Plebiscite in Rome

events.enhanced_description: Following the annexation of Rome, the city was declared the capital of unified Italy. This decision marked a significant moment in the establishment of the Italian state.
events.name: Rome becomes the capital of unified Italy

events.enhanced_description: Léon Gambetta famously escaped besieged Paris in a hot-air balloon, a dramatic event during the Franco-Prussian War. His escape allowed him to continue to rally support for the French cause against the Prussian forces.
events.name: Gambetta's escape from Paris

events.enhanced_description: Wade Perrin was assassinated on October 20, 1870, in Joanna, South Carolina, in a politically charged atmosphere following the Civil War. His murder was emblematic of the violent struggles for power and influence in the Reconstruction-era South.
events.name: Assassination of Wade Perrin

events.enhanced_description: The First Vatican Council, which addressed issues of church authority and infallibility, officially adjourned. This council was significant in shaping the modern Catholic Church's structure and doctrine.
events.name: Adjournment of the First Vatican Council

events.enhanced_description: The leaders responsible for the Tianjin Massacre, which targeted foreign nationals, were executed by the Imperial government of China. This event highlighted the tensions between foreign powers and Chinese authorities during this period.
events.name: Execution of Tianjin Massacre leaders

events.enhanced_description: The newly established Weather Bureau, which would later become the National Weather Service, issued its first official meteorological forecast, predicting high winds in Chicago and Milwaukee. This marked a significant development in weather forecasting.
events.name: First official meteorological forecast

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish Cortes Generales proclaimed Amadeo de Saboya as King Amadeo I of Spain, marking a brief period of monarchy during the turbulent years following the Spanish Revolution of 1868.
events.name: Proclamation of Amadeo I of Spain

events.enhanced_description: Joseph H. Rainey of South Carolina made history by becoming the second black U.S. congressman, following Hiram Rhodes Revels. His election represented a significant step forward in the representation of African Americans in government.

image.caption: Portrait of Joseph Rainey, member of the United States House of Representatives, painted by Simmie Knox.
image.credit: Simmie Knox — Black Americans in Congress. Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2004, not the 1870 event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Joseph H. Rainey becomes congressman

events.enhanced_description: Juan Prim, the prime minister of Spain, was shot by unknown assassins as he left the Cortes, dying two days later. His assassination had significant political repercussions during a tumultuous period in Spanish history.
events.name: Assassination of Juan Prim

events.enhanced_description: Sir Henry Barkly was appointed Governor of the Cape of Good Hope and High Commissioner for Southern Africa, a position that placed him at the forefront of colonial administration during a critical period in the region's history.

locations.name: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Appointment of Sir Henry Barkly

events.enhanced_description: The Bonnet Carré Crevasse in 1871 was a catastrophic levee failure along the Mississippi River, leading to widespread flooding and significant damage in the surrounding areas. This event prompted discussions about infrastructure and flood management in the region.
events.name: Bonnet Carré Crevasse

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, John Campbell, Marquess of Lorne, married Princess Louise, the daughter of Queen Victoria, at Windsor. This historic union marked the first time a legitimate daughter of a British monarch married a commoner since 1515.
events.name: John Campbell, Marquess of Lorne marries Princess Louise

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, the United States Army issued an order for the abandonment of Fort Kearny in Nebraska, reflecting the changing military strategies and the decline of the fort's strategic importance.
events.name: The United States Army issues an order for the abandonment of Fort Kearny

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1871, the Royal Albert Hall was officially opened by Queen Victoria, featuring a grand organ by Henry Willis & Sons, which was the largest in the world at that time. This venue has since become a significant cultural landmark in London.
events.name: The Royal Albert Hall in London is opened

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1871, British Columbia officially joined the confederation of Canada, becoming the sixth province. This significant political move was aimed at enhancing economic stability and development in the region.
events.name: British Columbia joins Canada

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, C. W. Alcock proposed the establishment of a Challenge Cup for Association football, leading to the creation of the FA Cup, the oldest football competition in the world. This initiative marked a pivotal moment in the history of football in England.
events.name: FA Cup Proposal

events.enhanced_description: In November 1871, John D. Rockefeller and a group of major railroad interests formed the South Improvement Company in Pennsylvania. This organization aimed to control and organize the burgeoning American petroleum industry, setting the stage for Rockefeller's future dominance in the field.
events.name: Formation of the South Improvement Company

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, the Società degli Spettroscopisti Italiani was founded in Rome, marking the establishment of the world's first scientific organization dedicated to astrophysics. This organization played a crucial role in advancing the study of spectroscopy and its applications in astronomy.
events.name: The Società degli Spettroscopisti Italiani is established

events.enhanced_description: John O'Neill, a prominent Fenian leader, was arrested by U.S. authorities in 1871, effectively ending the Fenian raids aimed at liberating Ireland from British rule. His capture marked a significant turning point in the Fenian movement, which had sought to use military action to achieve Irish independence.
events.name: John O'Neill (Fenian) is arrested

events.enhanced_description: Continental AG, originally known as Continental-Caoutchouc und Gutta-Percha Compagnie, was founded in Hanover, Germany, in 1871. The company has grown to become one of the leading automotive suppliers in the world, specializing in tire manufacturing and other automotive technologies.
events.name: Continental AG is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, British forces marched into the Klipdrift Republic, annexing the territory and establishing it as the Griqualand West Colony. This military action was part of the broader context of British expansion in southern Africa during the 19th century.
events.name: British forces march into the Klipdrift Republic

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, Henri, Count of Chambord, refused to accept the crown as 'King Henry V of France' unless the French government abandoned the tricolor flag in favor of the Bourbon flag. This refusal highlighted the ongoing tensions between royalists and republicans in post-Franco-Prussian War France.

image.caption: Portrait of Henri, Count of Chambord.
image.credit: Étienne Neurdein — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Henri, Count of Chambord; the saved evidence gives no image date. It is not a depiction of the refusal itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Henri, Count of Chambord, refuses to be crowned

events.enhanced_description: William M. Tweed, known as Boss Tweed, was arrested in 1871 for bribery and corruption, marking the decline of his powerful influence over New York City politics. His arrest was a significant moment in the fight against political corruption in the United States.
events.name: Boss Tweed of Tammany Hall is arrested

events.enhanced_description: The National Rifle Association of America was granted a charter by the state of New York in 1871. Founded to promote rifle shooting and marksmanship, the organization has evolved into a significant political force in the United States, advocating for gun rights.
events.name: The National Rifle Association of America is granted a charter

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, astronomer George Biddell Airy presented his groundbreaking discovery that astronomical aberration is independent of the local medium. This finding contributed significantly to the understanding of light and its behavior in space.
events.name: George Biddell Airy presents his discovery

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, gold was discovered at Pilgrim's Creek in the Pilgrim's Rest area of South Africa, sparking a gold rush that attracted many prospectors. This discovery significantly impacted the local economy and led to the establishment of the town of New Rush.
events.name: Gold is discovered at Pilgrim's Creek

events.enhanced_description: In 1871, an 83.50-carat diamond was discovered in the Pilgrim's Rest area of South Africa, leading to a diamond rush. This event significantly influenced the region's development and attracted numerous miners and fortune seekers.
events.name: An 83.50-carat diamond is discovered

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1871, during the Franco-Prussian War, the Prussian forces achieved a strategic victory at the Battle of Bapaume. This battle was part of the larger campaign that ultimately led to the unification of Germany.
events.name: Franco-Prussian War: Battle of Bapaume – Prussians win a strategic victory

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1871, the German Empire was proclaimed at the Palace of Versailles, marking the unification of various German states under Prussian leadership. Wilhelm I was declared the first German Emperor, solidifying Prussia's dominance in German affairs.
events.name: Proclamation of the German Empire

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dijon was a decisive conflict where a coalition of Franks and Burgundians defeated the forces of Gundobad. Following the battle, King Clovis I pursued Gundobad, leading to his surrender and the establishment of Frankish dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Dijon

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1871, the first legislative election of the French Third Republic was held, resulting in a significant majority for monarchists who favored peace with the newly established German Empire. The National Assembly convened in Bordeaux to address the nation's future.
events.name: 1871 French legislative election

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1871, the United States Commission on Fish and Fisheries was established to address the declining fish populations and promote sustainable fishing practices. This marked an important step in the conservation movement in the U.S.
events.name: United States Commission on Fish and Fisheries is founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1871, U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant signed the District of Columbia Organic Act, which reorganized the government of the District of Columbia and established a single municipal government for the city.
events.name: District of Columbia Organic Act of 1871 signed into law

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1871, the Danish Women's Society was founded in Copenhagen to advocate for women's rights and promote gender equality in Denmark. This organization played a significant role in the women's suffrage movement in the country.
events.name: Danish Women's Society founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1871, U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant signed the first civil service reform legislation into law, establishing the United States Civil Service Commission to oversee the hiring of government employees based on merit rather than political affiliation.
events.name: First American civil service reform legislation signed into law

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1871, José Paranhos, Viscount of Rio Branco, was appointed Prime Minister of the Empire of Brazil, serving for four years. He was instrumental in implementing significant reforms during his tenure.
figures: José Paranhos, Viscount of Rio Branco

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: José Paranhos, Viscount of Rio Branco, becomes Prime Minister of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1871, the Mokrani Revolt erupted in French Algeria as a response to colonial rule, led by local Berber leaders. This uprising was part of a broader resistance against French imperialism in North Africa.
events.name: Mokrani Revolt breaks out in French Algeria

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1871, the events leading to the Paris Commune began when French troops, ordered by Adolphe Thiers, attempted to seize cannons from Montmartre. The troops fraternized with civilians, leading to a revolutionary uprising.
events.name: Origin of the Paris Commune

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1871, Otto von Bismarck was appointed as the first Chancellor of the newly proclaimed German Empire, where he would play a pivotal role in shaping the empire's policies and direction.
events.name: Otto von Bismarck becomes the first Chancellor of the German Empire

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1871, William Holden became the first governor of a U.S. state to be removed from office by impeachment in North Carolina, reflecting the turbulent political climate of the Reconstruction era.
events.name: William Holden impeached in North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1871, the Paris Commune was formally established in response to the Franco-Prussian War and the perceived failures of the French government. It represented a radical socialist government that lasted until May 1871.
events.name: The Paris Commune is formally established

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1871, the first international rugby match was played between Scotland and England at Raeburn Place in Edinburgh, resulting in a 1-0 victory for Scotland. This match marked the beginning of international rugby competitions.
events.name: First Rugby Union International

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1871, John Maynard Woodworth was appointed as the first Surgeon General of the United States, tasked with overseeing public health and medical affairs within the military and civilian populations.
events.name: John Maynard Woodworth appointed as first Surgeon General of the United States

events.enhanced_description: The Stockholms Handelsbank, one of the first banks in Sweden, was established in April 1871, marking a significant development in the Swedish banking sector and contributing to the modernization of the country's financial system.
events.name: The Stockholms Handelsbank is founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1871, the New Jersey Detective Agency was chartered, establishing a formal organization for law enforcement and investigation in the state, which played a crucial role in the development of modern policing.
events.name: The New Jersey Detective Agency is chartered

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1871, P. T. Barnum opened his three-ring circus in Brooklyn, New York, promoting it as "The Greatest Show on Earth," which revolutionized the circus industry and entertainment in America.
events.name: P. T. Barnum opens his three-ring circus

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1871, U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant signed the Civil Rights Act of 1871, aimed at protecting the civil rights of citizens and addressing the issues of racial discrimination and violence in the post-Civil War era.
events.name: Ulysses S. Grant signs the Civil Rights Act of 1871

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1871, the murder of Jane Clouson, a servant girl in Eltham, England, captured public attention, particularly due to the acquittal of her probable murderer, highlighting issues of justice and societal norms of the time.

image.caption: Illustrated Police News depiction of Edmund Walter Pook.
image.credit: Unknown illustrator for the Illustrated Police News . Extracted from File:Front cover of the Illustrated Police News, 27 May 1871.png by User:Jarry1250 . — This image has been extracted from another file
image.date_qualification: Portrait-style depiction of Pook published in 1871; it is contextual to the murder case, not a photograph of the crime.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Murder of Jane Clouson

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1871, the first supposedly Major League Baseball game was played in America, marking a pivotal moment in the history of professional baseball and the establishment of organized sports in the country.
events.name: First supposedly Major League Baseball game played
