events.enhanced_description: The Washington Monument was completed on December 6, 1884, becoming the tallest structure in the world at that time. This iconic obelisk honors George Washington and symbolizes the nation's enduring values.
events.name: Completion of the Washington Monument

events.enhanced_description: Mark Twain's classic novel, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, was first published in London on December 10, 1884. The book is celebrated for its exploration of themes such as race and identity in pre-Civil War America.
events.name: Publication of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

events.enhanced_description: The World Cotton Centennial, a world's fair, opened in New Orleans on December 16, 1884, showcasing the importance of cotton in the economy and culture of the Southern United States. It celebrated advancements in agriculture and industry.
events.name: World Cotton Centennial world's fair opens

events.enhanced_description: Anton Bruckner's Symphony No. 7 premiered in Leipzig on December 30, 1884, marking a significant moment in the history of classical music. The symphony is noted for its emotional depth and innovative orchestration.
events.name: Premiere of Anton Bruckner's Symphony No. 7

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Cut Knife, fought in 1885, was a significant engagement during the North-West Rebellion where Cree and Assiniboine warriors achieved their largest victory over Canadian forces. This battle highlighted the resistance of Indigenous peoples against colonial encroachment.
events.name: North-West Rebellion - Battle of Cut Knife

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, Karl Benz produced the Benz Patent-Motorwagen, which is regarded as the first automobile. This groundbreaking invention was patented and publicly launched the following year, revolutionizing personal transportation.
events.name: Production of the Benz Patent-Motorwagen

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, John Kemp Starley demonstrated the Rover safety bicycle, which is regarded as the first practical modern bicycle. This design significantly improved safety and comfort for cyclists, influencing bicycle design for years to come.
events.name: Demonstration of the Rover Safety Bicycle

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, the Home Insurance Building in Chicago, designed by William Le Baron Jenney, was completed. It is regarded as the first skyscraper, featuring a fireproof weight-bearing metal frame and ten floors, marking a significant advancement in architectural design.
events.name: Completion of the Home Insurance Building

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, Bicycle Playing Cards were first produced, becoming a popular brand in card games and contributing to the culture of playing cards in America.
events.name: Production of Bicycle Playing Cards

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families Association was established in the United Kingdom to provide charitable assistance to the families of military personnel. This organization has played a crucial role in supporting those affected by military service.
events.name: Establishment of the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families Association

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, Camp Dudley was founded in Westport, New York, becoming the oldest continually running boys' camp in the United States. This camp has been instrumental in shaping outdoor education and youth development.
events.name: Founding of Camp Dudley

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, John Ormsby published his acclaimed English translation of Miguel de Cervantes' 'Don Quixote', which was recognized for its scholarly accuracy and literary quality. This translation would remain in print and influence English-speaking readers for decades.
events.name: John Ormsby publishes his new English translation of Don Quixote

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, Michigan Technological University, originally known as the Michigan Mining School, opened its doors in Houghton, Michigan. This institution was established to provide education in mining engineering and has since evolved into a comprehensive technological university.
events.name: Michigan Technological University opens its doors

events.enhanced_description: Chuo Law College was founded in 1885 in Kanda, Tokyo, Japan, marking the beginning of what would later become Chuo University. This institution played a significant role in legal education in Japan.
events.name: Chuo Law College founded

events.enhanced_description: Before November 1, 1885, a violent crackdown in Cochinchina resulted in the deaths of more than 24,000 Christians, alongside the destruction of 225 churches, 17 orphanages, and 10 convents. This tragic event highlighted the religious tensions in the region during this period.
events.name: Mass killings of Christians in Cochinchina

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1885, during the Sino-French War, French troops under General Oscar de Négrier achieved a decisive victory against a numerically superior Qing Chinese force at the Battle of Nùi Bop in northern Vietnam. This battle was part of the larger conflict over control in Indochina.
events.name: Battle of Nùi Bop

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1885, during the Mahdist War in Sudan, British troops defeated Mahdist forces at the Battle of Abu Klea. This battle was significant in the context of British colonial military campaigns in Africa.
events.name: Battle of Abu Klea

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1885, American inventor LaMarcus Adna Thompson patented a roller coaster, marking a pivotal moment in amusement park history. His design laid the groundwork for the development of modern roller coasters, which have become a staple of entertainment worldwide.
events.name: LaMarcus Adna Thompson patents roller coaster

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1885, Irish rebels caused significant damage to Westminster Hall and the Tower of London using dynamite. This act of rebellion highlighted the tensions between Irish nationalists and British authorities during this period.
events.name: Irish rebels damage Westminster Hall and the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1885, during the Mahdist War in Sudan, troops loyal to Mahdi Muhammad Ahmad captured Khartoum, resulting in the death of British commander Charles George Gordon. This event marked a significant turning point in the conflict and British colonial interests in the region.
events.name: Fall of Khartoum

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1885, King Leopold II of Belgium established the Congo Free State as his personal possession. This act marked the beginning of a brutal regime characterized by exploitation and atrocities against the Congolese people.

locations.name: Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Establishment of the Congo Free State

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1885, the first Japanese immigrants arrived in Hawaii, marking the beginning of significant Japanese influence in the islands. This migration contributed to the cultural diversity of Hawaii and shaped its social landscape.
events.name: First Japanese arrive in Hawaii

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1885, Charles Dow published the first edition of the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which stood at a level of 62.76 and represented the dollar average of 14 stocks. This index became a key indicator of the stock market's performance and economic health.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First edition of the Dow Jones Industrial Average

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1885, the Richmond Football Club was officially formed at the Royal Hotel in the Melbourne suburb of Richmond, Victoria. This club has since become one of the most successful teams in Australian rules football history.
events.name: Formation of the Richmond Football Club

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1885, U.S. President Chester A. Arthur dedicated the Washington Monument, a tribute to the first president of the United States, George Washington. This iconic structure symbolizes national pride and the country's history.
events.name: Dedication of the Washington Monument

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1885, during the Sino-French War, France secured an important victory over China at the Battle of Đồng Đăng in the Tonkin region of modern-day Vietnam. This battle was crucial in establishing French colonial control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Đồng Đăng

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1885, the final act of the Berlin Conference was signed, regulating European colonization and trade in Africa during the scramble for Africa. This agreement had lasting implications for the continent's political landscape.
events.name: Final act of the Berlin Conference

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, February concluded without having a full moon, a rare occurrence that happens approximately once every 19 years. This event is of interest to astronomers and those studying lunar cycles.
events.name: February concludes without a full moon

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1885, American Telephone and Telegraph (AT&T), a subsidiary of the American Bell Telephone Company, was incorporated in New York. This marked a significant development in the telecommunications industry.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Incorporation of AT&T

events.enhanced_description: Grover Cleveland was sworn in as the 24th President of the United States, marking his return to the presidency after having served from 1885 to 1889, making him the only U.S. president to serve two non-consecutive terms.
events.name: Grover Cleveland sworn in as president

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1885, the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Madrid was founded, establishing a significant ecclesiastical jurisdiction in Spain. This foundation played a crucial role in the religious landscape of the country.

image.caption: Coat of arms of the Archdiocese of Madrid.
image.credit: Ansunando — This vector image includes elements that have been taken or adapted from this file:
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 2016-03-19; it dates the symbol image, not the 1885 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Madrid

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1885, Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Mikado premiered at the Savoy Theatre in London. This operetta became one of the duo's most popular works and remains a staple of musical theatre.
events.name: Opening of The Mikado

events.enhanced_description: In 1885, the Prussian government, under the influence of Otto von Bismarck, initiated a campaign to expel all ethnic Poles and Jews who lacked German citizenship from Prussia. This act was part of a broader policy aimed at Germanization and consolidation of national identity.
events.name: Prussian deportations

events.enhanced_description: The North-West Rebellion began on March 26, 1885, with the Battle of Duck Lake, where Métis forces led by Louis Riel engaged Canadian government troops. This conflict was a significant uprising against the Canadian government, driven by grievances over land rights and cultural recognition.
events.name: North-West Rebellion - Battle of Duck Lake

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1885, Jeanette Pickersgill became the first person to be legally cremated in England at the Woking Crematorium, established by the Cremation Society. This event marked a significant shift in attitudes towards cremation in Victorian England, reflecting changing cultural and religious views.
events.name: First legal cremation in England

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1885, the Battle for Kushka triggered the Panjdeh Incident, which nearly led to war between the British Empire and the Russian Empire. This conflict highlighted the geopolitical tensions in Central Asia during the Great Game.
events.name: Battle for Kushka and the Panjdeh Incident

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1885, the United Kingdom established the Bechuanaland Protectorate, marking a significant step in British colonial expansion in southern Africa. This protectorate would later become part of modern-day Botswana.
events.name: Establishment of the Bechuanaland Protectorate

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1885, during the North-West Rebellion, Cree warriors led by Wandering Spirit attacked Frog Lake, resulting in the deaths of nine settlers. This incident exemplified the tensions between Indigenous peoples and settlers in Canada during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Frog Lake Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1885, Gottlieb Daimler was granted a German patent for his innovative single-cylinder, water-cooled engine design. This invention was pivotal in the development of the modern automobile and laid the groundwork for Daimler's future successes in the automotive industry.
events.name: Gottlieb Daimler patent

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1885, Luton Town Football Club was formed through the merger of Luton Wanderers F.C. and Luton Excelsior F.C. This event marked a significant development in the history of football in England, contributing to the establishment of professional football clubs.
events.name: Formation of Luton Town Football Club

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1885, French forces achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Kép, compelling Chinese troops to withdraw from Tonkin. This battle marked the conclusion of the Sino-French War, which had significant implications for French colonial expansion in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Sino-French War - Battle of Kép

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1885, Antonín Dvořák's Symphony No. 7 premiered at St James's Hall in London. This symphony is regarded as one of Dvořák's most significant works, showcasing his unique blend of Czech folk influences with classical forms.
events.name: Premiere of Dvořák's Symphony No. 7

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1885, a bill was signed into law by the New York State legislature, establishing Niagara Falls State Park. This marked the first state park in the United States, aimed at preserving the natural beauty of the falls and promoting tourism.

image.caption: Niagara Falls, with the American Falls in the foreground and Horseshoe Falls in the background.
image.credit: Ad Meskens — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph taken 2009-09-05; this is not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Formation of Niagara Falls State Park

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1885, Good Housekeeping magazine was published for the first time in the United States. The magazine would go on to become a significant publication, influencing domestic life and consumer culture in America.
events.name: Good Housekeeping magazine launch

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1885, during the North-West Rebellion, Canadian government forces decisively defeated Métis rebels at the Battle of Batoche. This battle effectively ended the rebellion, leading to the capture of Louis Riel and the suppression of Métis resistance.
events.name: North-West Rebellion - Battle of Batoche

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1885, after a protracted legislative battle, John A. Logan was re-elected to the United States Senate. Logan was a prominent figure in American politics, known for his military service and advocacy for veterans' rights.
events.name: John A. Logan re-elected to U.S. Senate

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1885, the first public train departed from Swanage railway station on the newly constructed Swanage Railway in England. This event marked a significant development in local transportation and tourism.
events.name: First public train departs Swanage railway station

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1885, the Battle of Loon Lake marked the last skirmish of the North-West Rebellion, where the Canadian North-West Mounted Police and their allies forced a group of Plains Cree warriors to surrender. This battle symbolized the end of armed resistance by the Métis and Indigenous peoples in the region.
events.name: Battle of Loon Lake

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1885, the Statue of Liberty arrived in New York Harbor, a gift from France symbolizing freedom and democracy. This monumental statue would become an iconic representation of the United States and its values.
events.name: Arrival of the Statue of Liberty

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1885, Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, was appointed Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. His leadership would be marked by significant political challenges and the expansion of the British Empire.
events.name: Robert Gascoyne-Cecil becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: In July 1885, Japan Brewery, the predecessor of Kirin Holdings, was founded in Yokohama, Japan. This establishment marked the beginning of a significant brewing industry in Japan, which would grow to become internationally recognized.
events.name: Japan Brewery founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1885, Louis Pasteur and Émile Roux successfully tested their rabies vaccine on Joseph Meister, a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog. This groundbreaking achievement marked a significant advancement in medical science and public health.
events.name: Louis Pasteur rabies vaccine test

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1885, Sarah E. Goode became the first African-American woman to receive a patent for her invention of the hideaway bed. This achievement was a significant milestone in the history of innovation and women's contributions to technology.
events.name: Sarah E. Goode patent

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1885, the Reservation at Niagara Falls was opened, allowing public access to the natural wonder for free. Thomas V. Welch was appointed as the first Superintendent of the Park, which would become a major tourist attraction.
events.name: Niagara Falls Reservation opens

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1885, BHP (Broken Hill Proprietary) was founded in New South Wales, Australia. This company would grow to become one of the world's largest mining and natural gas producers, significantly impacting the global resources market.
events.name: BHP founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1885, the Football Association officially recognized professional players in England. This decision marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of football, leading to the establishment of professional leagues and clubs.
events.name: Football Association recognizes professional players

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1885, the trial of Louis Riel for treason began in Regina. Riel, a key figure in the North-West Rebellion, faced charges that would ultimately lead to his execution, symbolizing the tensions between the Canadian government and Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Louis Riel's trial for treason

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1885, astronomer Robert Innes discovered S Andromedae, marking it as the only supernova observed in the Andromeda Galaxy to date and the first supernova noted outside the Milky Way. This discovery significantly advanced the understanding of stellar phenomena and the universe's structure.
events.name: Discovery of S Andromedae

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1885, Gottlieb Daimler was granted a German patent for the Daimler Reitwagen, which is regarded as the first motorcycle. This invention represented a significant milestone in the development of motorized vehicles and laid the groundwork for the modern automotive industry.
events.name: Patent for the Daimler Reitwagen

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1885, the Rock Springs massacre occurred when 150 white miners attacked their Chinese coworkers in Rock Springs, Wyoming, resulting in the deaths of 28 individuals and injuries to 15 others. This violent event highlighted the racial tensions and labor disputes prevalent in the American West during this period.
events.name: Rock Springs Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1885, the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia united, marking a significant step towards national unification and independence from Ottoman rule. This event was celebrated as a triumph of Bulgarian nationalism and played a crucial role in the country's history.
events.name: Bulgarian unification

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1885, Eastern Rumelia declared its union with Bulgaria, effectively completing the unification of the Bulgarian state. This political move was a significant step towards the consolidation of Bulgarian national identity and sovereignty.
events.name: Union of Eastern Rumelia with Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1885, Saint Thomas Academy was founded in Saint Paul, Minnesota. This institution has played a significant role in the education of young men in the region, emphasizing both academic excellence and moral development.
events.name: Founding of Saint Thomas Academy

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1885, Arbroath FC defeated Bon Accord FC with a staggering score of 36-0, marking the highest score ever recorded in professional football history. This match remains a significant moment in the annals of sports, showcasing the dominance of Arbroath FC during that era.
events.name: Arbroath FC vs Bon Accord FC

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1885, a train wreck involving the P. T. Barnum Circus resulted in the death of Jumbo, a giant elephant, in St. Thomas, Ontario. Jumbo was a beloved attraction and his death was a significant event in the history of circus entertainment.
events.name: Jumbo the Elephant's Death

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1885, the union of Eastern Rumelia with Bulgaria was officially proclaimed in Plovdiv. This event was pivotal in the establishment of a unified Bulgarian state and was met with both national pride and international scrutiny.
events.name: Proclamation of Union of Eastern Rumelia with Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1885, a British force abolished the Boer republic of Stellaland, incorporating it into British Bechuanaland. This action was part of the broader British imperial strategy in southern Africa during the late 19th century.

image.caption: First flag of Stellaland.
image.credit: Samhanin — Own work , source: worldstatesmen.org
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the flag to 1883. The 2021 date is the file's metadata date, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Abolition of Stellaland

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1885, Millwall F.C. was founded by workers on the Isle of Dogs in London, originally known as Millwall Rovers. The club has since become a significant part of English football history.
events.name: Founding of Millwall F.C.

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1885, the city of Fresno, California, was incorporated. This event marked the beginning of Fresno's development as a significant urban center in the San Joaquin Valley.
events.name: Incorporation of Fresno

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1885, the Georgia Institute of Technology was established in Atlanta as the Georgia School of Technology. This institution has since become a leading technological university in the United States.
events.name: Establishment of Georgia Institute of Technology

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1885, Johannes Brahms conducted the premiere of his Symphony No. 4 in Meiningen, Germany. This symphony is regarded as one of Brahms' masterpieces and a significant contribution to the symphonic repertoire.
events.name: Premiere of Brahms' Symphony No. 4

events.enhanced_description: In November 1885, the Third Anglo-Burmese War began, marking a significant conflict between the British Empire and the Kingdom of Burma. This war ultimately led to the annexation of Burma into British India.
events.name: Beginning of the Third Anglo-Burmese War

events.enhanced_description: The Tacoma riot of November 3, 1885, was an anti-Chinese riot that resulted in the expulsion of Chinese immigrants from Tacoma, Washington. This event reflected the racial tensions and xenophobia prevalent in the United States during the late 19th century.
events.name: Tacoma riot of 1885

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1885, construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was completed in Craigellachie, British Columbia. Prime Minister John A. Macdonald viewed this railway as crucial for national unity and military mobility across Canada.
events.name: Completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1885, Serbia declared war against Bulgaria, initiating the Serbo-Bulgarian War. The conflict culminated in the Battle of Slivnitsa from November 17-19, where Serbia was decisively defeated.
events.name: Serbo-Bulgarian War Declaration

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1885, Louis Riel, the Canadian rebel leader of the Métis, was executed for high treason in Regina, Saskatchewan. His death marked a pivotal moment in Canadian history, symbolizing the struggle for Métis rights and identity.
events.name: Execution of Louis Riel

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1885, the U.S. Patent Office acknowledged this date as the first time Dr Pepper was served, although the exact date of its invention remains unknown. This soft drink has since become a cultural icon in the United States.
events.name: First Serving of Dr Pepper

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1885, 72 Indian lawyers, academics, and journalists gathered in Bombay (now Mumbai) to form the Indian National Congress. This organization would become a pivotal force in the Indian independence movement against British rule.
events.name: Formation of the Indian National Congress

events.enhanced_description: In January 1886, Upper Burma was formally annexed to British Burma following its conquest during the Third Anglo-Burmese War. This event marked a significant expansion of British colonial rule in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Formal annexation of Upper Burma

events.enhanced_description: The earlier ruling of Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific Railroad in 1886 established the precedent for corporate rights, influencing future legal interpretations of corporate personhood.
events.name: Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific Railroad (earlier ruling)

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Motherwell Football Club was founded in Scotland, contributing to the rich history of football in the region and becoming a significant part of Scottish football culture.
events.name: Motherwell Football Club founded

events.enhanced_description: The Great Vancouver Fire, which occurred in 1886, was a catastrophic event that reshaped the city and its infrastructure, leading to significant urban development in the aftermath.
events.name: The Great Vancouver Fire (earlier mention)

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, a significant log jam formed on the St. Croix River near Taylors Falls, Minnesota, impacting local navigation and commerce in the region.
events.name: Log jam on the St. Croix River

events.enhanced_description: In November 1886, the United States experienced an extremely harsh winter that would last until 1887, resulting in the deaths of tens of thousands of cattle across the Great Plains. This environmental disaster had significant economic repercussions for the cattle industry and the livelihoods of ranchers.
events.name: Harsh winter of 1886-87 begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Addis Ababa was founded as the capital of the Ethiopian Empire. Established under Emperor Menelik II, the city has since grown into a vibrant metropolis and a center of culture and politics in Ethiopia.
events.name: Foundation of Addis Ababa

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, the village of Skorenovac was founded in Serbia, primarily by Székely Hungarians. This settlement reflects the migration patterns and cultural influences in the region during this period.
events.name: Foundation of Skorenovac

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, William Grant & Sons was founded in Dunfermline, Scotland, marking the beginning of one of the most renowned Scotch whisky distilleries in the world. The company has since become synonymous with quality and craftsmanship in whisky production.
events.name: Foundation of William Grant & Sons

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Yorkshire Tea was established in Harrogate, England, becoming a staple brand in the British tea market. The brand is known for its commitment to quality and has gained a loyal following over the years.
events.name: Foundation of Yorkshire Tea

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Johnson & Johnson was founded in New Brunswick, New Jersey, beginning its journey to become a multinational brand in healthcare products. The company is recognized for its innovations in medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and consumer health products.

locations.name: New Brunswick, New Jersey, United States

events.name: Foundation of Johnson & Johnson

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Avon Products was founded in New York City, United States, establishing itself as a worldwide cosmetics and household brand. The company pioneered the direct-selling model, empowering individuals to sell products directly to consumers.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Foundation of Avon Products

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Del Monte Foods was founded in California, United States, becoming a significant player in the food product and processing industry. The brand is known for its canned fruits and vegetables, as well as its commitment to quality.
events.name: Foundation of Del Monte Foods

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Emily Ruete published her landmark memoir, 'Memoirs of an Arabian Princess: An Autobiography.' This work provides a unique perspective on the life of a woman in the Arabian Peninsula during the 19th century and has been influential in understanding the region's history.

image.caption: Portrait of Emily Ruete (Sayyida Salme) in traditional dress.
image.credit: Plate, Heinrich Friedrich (* 1824, † 1895), Fotograf in Hamburg — Photo probably taken between 1856-1880. Original print in possession of the oostersinstituut.nl Foundation Eastern Institute in Leiden . Consulted on 3 April 2023.
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Emily Ruete; the credit estimates the original photograph between 1856 and 1880. It is not an image of the memoir publication, and the optional display date is omitted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Memoirs of an Arabian Princess

events.enhanced_description: In 1886, Bedford Rugby Club was formed in England, contributing to the growth of rugby as a popular sport in the country. The club has since become an integral part of the local community and the rugby union landscape.
events.name: Formation of Bedford Rugby Club

events.enhanced_description: The Punjab Chiefs' College was formed on 2 January 1886 in British India and renamed Aitchison College on 13 November 1886.

image.caption: A commemorative postage stamp issued by Pakistan Post for Aitchison College.
image.credit: Saad Ullah Bhatti — Own work
image.date_qualification: Commemorative stamp created in 2021, long after the college’s 1886 founding; it is a symbolic representation, not a contemporary image of the founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Formation of Punjab Chiefs' College (later Aitchison College)

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1886, Robert Louis Stevenson's novella 'Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde' was published simultaneously in New York and London. This work explored the duality of human nature and has since become a classic of Gothic literature.

locations.name: New York, New York, United States

events.name: Publication of Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1886, the German Parliament passed a resolution condemning the Prussian deportations, a politically motivated mass expulsion of ethnic Poles and Jews initiated by Otto von Bismarck. This event highlighted the ethnic tensions and political struggles within the German Empire.
events.name: Resolution condemning Prussian deportations

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1886, The Hockey Association was formed in England, marking the birth of modern field hockey. This organization standardized the rules of the game and promoted its growth in the UK and beyond.
events.name: Formation of The Hockey Association

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1886, Karl Benz patented the Benz Patent-Motorwagen, recognized as the first successful gasoline-driven automobile. This invention laid the groundwork for the modern automotive industry.
events.name: Karl Benz patents the first successful gasoline-driven automobile

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1886, anti-Chinese sentiments erupted into riots in Seattle, Washington, reflecting the racial tensions and economic anxieties of the time. This event was part of a broader wave of anti-Asian violence in the United States.
events.name: Seattle riot of 1886

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1886, the West End Riots occurred in London following a popular meeting in Trafalgar Square. These riots were indicative of the growing social unrest and demand for political reform in Victorian England.
events.name: The West End Riots

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1886, the first trainload of oranges departed from Los Angeles via the United States transcontinental railroad. This event marked a significant development in agricultural transportation and commerce in California.
events.name: First trainload of oranges leaves Los Angeles

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1886, the Anglo-Chinese School was founded by Bishop William Fitzjames Oldham at 70 Amoy Street, Singapore. This institution played a crucial role in the education of Chinese and English-speaking students in the region.
events.name: Anglo-Chinese School founded

events.enhanced_description: In March 1886, Gottlieb Daimler assembled his first automobile in Germany, marking a significant milestone in automotive engineering. This innovation contributed to the development of the modern automobile industry.
events.name: Gottlieb Daimler assembles his first automobile

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1886, the Treaty of Bucharest was signed, officially ending the Serbo-Bulgarian War. This treaty established new borders and marked a significant moment in Balkan politics.
events.name: Treaty of Bucharest ends the Serbo-Bulgarian War

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1886, a law was adopted in the German Empire establishing the Kiel Canal, a significant engineering project that would enhance maritime trade by connecting the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
events.name: Law establishing the Kiel Canal adopted

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1886, the Carrollton Massacre occurred in Mississippi, where 20 African Americans were killed in a racially motivated attack. This event underscored the violent racial tensions prevalent in the post-Reconstruction South.
events.name: Carrollton Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1886, Wilhelm Steinitz was recognized as the first official World Chess Champion after defeating Johannes Zukertort in a match held in New York City. This victory established Steinitz as a leading figure in the history of chess.

locations.name: New York, New York, United States

events.name: Wilhelm Steinitz becomes first World Chess Champion

events.enhanced_description: In April 1886, the Swedish Dress Reform Society was established, advocating for changes in women's clothing to promote health and comfort. This movement was part of a broader trend in the late 19th century towards reforming women's fashion.
events.name: Establishment of the Swedish Dress Reform Society

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1886, William Ewart Gladstone introduced the First Irish Home Rule Bill in the Parliament of the United Kingdom. Although it was ultimately defeated on June 8, this bill represented a significant attempt to address Irish self-governance.
events.name: First Irish Home Rule Bill introduced

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1886, the settlement of Vancouver, British Columbia, was incorporated, marking its official recognition as a city. This event laid the foundation for Vancouver's growth into a major urban center in Canada.
events.name: Incorporation of Vancouver

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1886, Father Augustine Tolton was ordained in Rome, becoming the first Roman Catholic priest from the United States to publicly identify as African American. His ordination was a significant milestone in the history of the Catholic Church in America.
events.name: Father Augustine Tolton ordained

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1886, a general strike began across the United States, advocating for labor rights and the eight-hour workday. This movement escalated into the Haymarket affair in Chicago on May 4, which became a pivotal moment in labor history.

image.caption: Wood engraving by Thure de Thulstrup depicting the Haymarket riot.
image.credit: Thure de Thulstrup — de Thulstrup, Thure ( May 15, 1886 ). " The Anarchist riot in Chicago: a dynamite bomb exploding among the police ". Harper's Weekly 30 (1534): 312-313.
image.date_qualification: The May 15, 1886 date is the illustration’s publication date, not the date of the May 1 strike or the May 4 Haymarket rally.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: General strike in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1886, Emile Berliner began his work that would lead to the invention of the gramophone, revolutionizing the way sound was recorded and played back. This innovation laid the foundation for the modern music industry.
events.name: Emile Berliner begins work on the gramophone

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1886, American pharmacist Dr. John Pemberton invented a carbonated beverage that would be named 'Coca-Cola'. This drink would go on to become one of the most recognized brands in the world.

image.caption: Early Coca-Cola bottling machine at Biedenharn Museum and Gardens in Monroe, Louisiana.
image.credit: Billy Hathorn — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2014-11-12; not contemporaneous with the 1886 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Coca-Cola invented

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1886, Portugal and France formalized an agreement to delineate the borders of their respective colonies in Guinea, which was crucial for colonial administration and resource management in West Africa.
events.name: Portugal and France agree to regulate the borders of their colonies in Guinea

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1886, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific Railroad that corporations are entitled to the same legal rights as individuals, a landmark decision that has had lasting implications for corporate personhood in American law.
events.name: Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific Railroad

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1886, John Pemberton began advertising Coca-Cola in The Atlanta Journal, marking the beginning of what would become one of the most recognized brands in the world.

image.caption: A late-19th-century Coca-Cola coupon offering a free glass of the drink.
image.credit: Coca-Cola Company — Scanned by uploader from Wired magazine (Nov 2010), Vol. 18, No. 11, p. 104.
image.date_qualification: Circa 1888, later than the event date of May 29, 1886.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: trademarked

events.name: John Pemberton begins to advertise Coca-Cola

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1886, U.S. President Grover Cleveland married Frances Folsom in a ceremony at the White House, making him the only sitting president to marry in the executive mansion.
events.name: Grover Cleveland marries Frances Folsom

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1886, Charles Lwanga and 12 other Catholic boys and men, along with 9 Anglicans, were executed by Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda in Namugongo, an event that is commemorated as the Uganda Martyrs' Day.

image.caption: Reliquary containing relics of the Ugandan Martyrs, including Charles Lwanga and Matthew Maluba, at the Museum of Catholic Art and History in Columbus, Ohio.
image.credit: Maximilian775 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2025-01-03; the depicted relics are associated with the martyrs, not a contemporary image of their executions.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Uganda Martyrs

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1886, the Mount Tarawera volcano erupted in New Zealand, leading to the destruction of the Pink and White Terraces and resulting in over 150 fatalities, marking one of the most significant volcanic events in New Zealand's history.
events.name: Mount Tarawera eruption

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1886, King Ludwig II of Bavaria was detained and subsequently drowned under mysterious circumstances, an event that led to widespread speculation and intrigue surrounding his death.
events.name: Death of King Ludwig II of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1886, the Great Vancouver Fire devastated much of the city, destroying thousands of buildings and leading to significant changes in urban planning and fire safety regulations in the region.
events.name: The Great Vancouver Fire

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1886, renowned conductor Arturo Toscanini made his conducting debut with an Italian opera company in Rio de Janeiro, marking the beginning of a distinguished career in classical music.
events.name: Arturo Toscanini's conducting debut

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1886, Queen Victoria officially opened the Royal Holloway College for women near London, England, promoting women's education and empowerment during a time when such opportunities were limited.
events.name: Royal Holloway College opened

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1886, Karl Benz officially unveiled the Benz Patent Motorwagen, widely regarded as the first true automobile, marking a pivotal moment in the history of transportation.

image.caption: An 1888 Benz Patent-Motorwagen Model No. 3 on display at the Automuseum Dr. Carl Benz in Ladenburg, Germany.
image.credit: Bahnfrend — Own work
image.date_qualification: Depicted vehicle dated 1888; photograph dated 2014-07-05; not contemporaneous with the July 3, 1886 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Karl Benz unveils the Benz Patent Motorwagen

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1886, American inventor Charles Martin Hall filed a patent for an inexpensive method of refining aluminum, a process that was independently discovered around the same time by French chemist Paul Héroult, leading to the Hall–Héroult process.
events.name: Charles Martin Hall files a patent for aluminium refining

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1886, Steve Brodie was reported to have jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge, a claim that sparked public interest and controversy, although it was later disputed.
events.name: Steve Brodie's Brooklyn Bridge jump

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1886, Robert Cecil, 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, became Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, leading a Conservative government during a period marked by imperial expansion and domestic reform.
events.name: Robert Cecil becomes Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1886, the Nagasaki Incident occurred when Chinese troops rioted during shore leave in Nagasaki, Japan, reflecting the tensions of foreign military presence in the region.
events.name: Nagasaki Incident

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1886, the Christian Union (Church of God) was established, contributing to the growth of religious movements in the United States during the late 19th century.
events.name: Establishment of the Christian Union (Church of God)

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1886, a massive hurricane struck and demolished the town of Indianola, Texas, leading to significant loss of life and property, and ultimately contributing to the town's decline.
events.name: Hurricane demolishes Indianola, Texas

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1886, a 7.0 Mw earthquake struck Charleston, South Carolina, causing extensive damage and resulting in approximately 60 fatalities, marking one of the most significant seismic events in U.S. history.

image.caption: A fissure and a wrecked brick house on Tradd Street, Charleston, South Carolina.
image.credit: John Karl Hillers — US Geological Survey Photographic Library
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies the scene with the Charleston Earthquake of August 31, 1886; the supplied image date is 1886.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Charleston earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1886, Grasshopper Club Zürich was founded as the first football club in the Swiss city of Zürich, playing a pivotal role in the development of football in Switzerland.
events.name: Grasshopper Club Zürich founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1886, Apache leader Geronimo surrendered to General Nelson Miles at Skeleton Canyon, Arizona, effectively marking the end of the Apache Wars and a significant moment in U.S. military history.
events.name: Geronimo surrenders

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1886, the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works was signed, establishing important international standards for copyright protection.
events.name: Berne Convention signed

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1886, American physicist William Stanley Jr. patented the first practical alternating current transformer device, known as the induction coil. This invention played a crucial role in the development of electrical engineering and the widespread use of alternating current for power distribution.
events.name: William Stanley Jr. patents the induction coil

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1886, Spain officially abolished slavery in Cuba, marking a significant step towards social reform in the region. This decision was influenced by both internal pressures from abolitionist movements and external pressures from the United States and other nations advocating for human rights.
events.name: Spain abolishes slavery in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1886, the British merchant vessel Normanton sank off the coast of Japan, leading to a diplomatic incident known as the Normanton incident. The sinking raised tensions between Britain and Japan, highlighting issues of maritime safety and international relations.
events.name: The Normanton incident

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1886, U.S. President Grover Cleveland dedicated the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor, a gift from France symbolizing freedom and democracy. The event sparked spontaneous celebrations in New York City, leading to the first ticker tape parade in history.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Dedication of the Statue of Liberty

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1886, Ananda College, the largest Buddhist boys' school in Sri Lanka, was founded in Colombo. The institution has since played a pivotal role in the education of Buddhist youth and has contributed significantly to the cultural and educational landscape of the country.
events.name: Foundation of Ananda College

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1886, German physicist Heinrich Hertz successfully verified the existence of electromagnetic waves at the University of Karlsruhe. His groundbreaking experiments laid the foundation for modern wireless communication and significantly advanced the field of electromagnetism.
events.name: Heinrich Hertz verifies electromagnetic waves

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1886, German inventor Friedrich Soennecken developed the first hole puncher, an office tool designed to create small holes in paper. This invention revolutionized office organization and remains a staple in workplaces worldwide.
events.name: Friedrich Soennecken develops the hole puncher

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1886, Robert Bosch founded the Werkstätte für Feinmechanik und Elektrotechnik in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. This workshop would eventually evolve into the globally recognized brand Robert Bosch GmbH, known for its innovations in engineering and technology.
events.name: Foundation of the Workshop for Fine Mechanics and Electronics

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1886, the Folies Bergère staged its first revue in Paris, marking the beginning of a new era in entertainment. This iconic venue became famous for its extravagant performances and remains a symbol of Parisian nightlife.
events.name: First revue at the Folies Bergère

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1886, the London Association football club Arsenal, originally founded as Dial Square, played its first match on the Isle of Dogs. This match marked the beginning of what would become one of the most successful football clubs in England.
events.name: Arsenal Football Club's first match

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1886, English adventurer Thomas Stevens concluded his historic journey, becoming the first person to circumnavigate the globe by bicycle. He had set out from San Francisco in 1884 on a penny-farthing, demonstrating the possibilities of long-distance travel and adventure.
events.name: Thomas Stevens concludes first bicycle circumnavigation

events.enhanced_description: In 1887, the United States Senate approved the leasing of Pearl Harbor as a naval base. This decision was pivotal in establishing Pearl Harbor as a strategic military location in the Pacific, which would later play a crucial role in World War II.

image.caption: Aerial view of Ford Island and ships at Pearl Harbor during Operation RIMPAC ’86.
image.credit: PH2 Thompson, USN — U.S. DefenseImagery photo VIRIN: DN-SC-87-04122
image.date_qualification: Photographed 1986-06-30; depicts the site nearly a century after the 1887 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: United States Senate allows leasing of Pearl Harbor

events.enhanced_description: In 1887, the British emigrant ship Kapunda sank after a collision off the coast of Brazil, resulting in the tragic loss of 303 lives, with only 16 survivors. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during that era.
events.name: Kapunda shipwreck

events.enhanced_description: The Amateur Athletic Union (AAU) was formed in 1887 in the United States to promote and coordinate amateur sports. This organization has played a significant role in the development of athletics and youth sports programs across the country.
events.name: Amateur Athletic Union formed

events.enhanced_description: In 1887, Brisbane experienced a record one-day rainfall of 465 millimeters (18.3 inches), setting a benchmark for precipitation in any Australian capital city. This extreme weather event underscored the region's susceptibility to heavy rainfall.
events.name: Brisbane rainfall record

events.enhanced_description: In 1887, construction work began on the foundations of the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France. This iconic structure, designed by Gustave Eiffel, would later become a symbol of French engineering and a major tourist attraction.
events.name: Construction of the Eiffel Tower begins

events.enhanced_description: Zululand was formally annexed and became a British colony, marking a significant expansion of British imperial control in Southern Africa. This event was part of the broader context of colonialism and the subjugation of indigenous peoples in the region.
events.name: Zululand Becomes a British Colony

events.enhanced_description: The earliest constituent of the U.S. National Institutes of Health was established at the Marine Hospital on Staten Island as the Laboratory of Hygiene. This institution would play a vital role in public health research and policy in the United States.

locations.name: Staten Island, New York, United States

events.name: Establishment of the Laboratory of Hygiene

events.enhanced_description: The Michelson–Morley experiment's results were published, demonstrating that the speed of light is independent of the motion of the observer. This groundbreaking finding challenged existing theories of ether and paved the way for Einstein's theory of relativity.
events.name: Results of the Michelson–Morley experiment are published

events.enhanced_description: Sherlock Holmes, the iconic detective character created by Arthur Conan Doyle, made his first appearance in the novel 'A Study in Scarlet.' This character would go on to become one of the most famous figures in literature and popular culture.
events.name: Sherlock Holmes makes his first appearance

events.enhanced_description: Laos and Cambodia were incorporated into French Indochina, a colonial territory established by France in Southeast Asia. This expansion marked a significant period of French colonial rule and had lasting impacts on the region's political and cultural landscape.

locations.name: French Indochina (modern-day Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia)

events.name: Laos and Cambodia are added to French Indochina

events.enhanced_description: Heinrich Hertz discovered the photoelectric effect while experimenting with electromagnetic waves, marking a pivotal moment in the study of quantum mechanics. His work laid the foundation for future developments in physics and technology.
events.name: Heinrich Hertz discovers the photoelectric effect

events.enhanced_description: Franz König published 'Über freie Körper in den Gelenken' in the Deutsche Zeitschrift für Chirurgie, where he described and named the disease Osteochondritis dissecans for the first time. This publication contributed significantly to the field of orthopedics.
events.name: Franz König publishes on Osteochondritis dissecans

events.enhanced_description: Teachers College, which later became part of Columbia University, was founded to improve the quality of education and teacher training in the United States. It has since played a crucial role in educational reform and research.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Teachers College is founded

events.enhanced_description: The first English-language edition of Friedrich Engels' influential study 'The Condition of the Working Class in England' was published in New York City, translated by Florence Kelley. This work provided critical insights into the lives of the working class during the Industrial Revolution.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First English edition of Engels' study is published

events.enhanced_description: Enrique Gaspar's novel 'El anacronópete,' the first work of fiction to feature a time machine, was published in Barcelona. This innovative story laid the groundwork for future science fiction literature.
events.name: Publication of El anacronópete

events.enhanced_description: The publication of Futabatei Shimei's 'The Drifting Cloud' (Ukigumo) began, marking it as the first modern novel in Japan. This work played a significant role in the development of Japanese literature.
events.name: Publication of The Drifting Cloud begins

events.enhanced_description: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in London, becoming one of the most influential organizations in the study of the occult and esotericism. The order attracted many notable figures and contributed to the revival of interest in mysticism and magic.
events.name: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn is founded

events.enhanced_description: Nagase Shoten, the predecessor of the Japanese cosmetics and toiletry brand Kao Corporation, was founded in Nihonbashi, Tokyo. This company has played a significant role in the development of the cosmetics industry in Japan.
events.name: Nagase Shoten is founded

events.enhanced_description: Tokyo Fire Insurance, which later became part of Sompo Japan Nipponkoa Insurance, was founded in Tokyo. This company has been a key player in the insurance industry in Japan.
events.name: Tokyo Fire Insurance is founded

events.enhanced_description: Taiwan was designated as a province of China, marking a significant shift in its political status. This change had lasting implications for Taiwan's history and its relationship with mainland China.
events.name: Taiwan becomes a Chinese province

events.enhanced_description: Skanska, a global construction and real estate development company, was founded in Malmö, Sweden. It has since grown to become one of the largest construction firms in the world, known for its commitment to sustainability.
events.name: Skanska is founded

events.enhanced_description: A. G. Edwards, a financial services company, was founded by General Albert Gallatin Edwards in St. Louis, Missouri. The firm became known for its customer service and investment advice.
events.name: A. G. Edwards is founded

events.enhanced_description: Heyl & Patterson Inc., a pioneer in coal unloading equipment, was founded by Edmund W. Heyl and William J. Patterson in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The company played a significant role in the coal industry and manufacturing technology.
events.name: Heyl & Patterson Inc. is founded

events.enhanced_description: The first battery rail car was introduced on the Royal Bavarian State Railways, marking a significant advancement in railway technology. This innovation paved the way for electric trains, which would later revolutionize public transportation.
events.name: The first battery rail car is used on the Royal Bavarian State Railways

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1887, Dr. Joseph Grancher defended Louis Pasteur's anti-rabies treatment in the Académie Nationale de Médecine in Paris. This defense was crucial in gaining acceptance for Pasteur's groundbreaking work in immunology and public health.
events.name: Defense of Pasteur's anti-rabies treatment

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1887, the United States Senate approved the lease of Pearl Harbor as a naval base. This strategic decision would later play a significant role in U.S. military operations in the Pacific, especially during the Spanish-American War and World War II.
events.name: U.S. Senate allows lease of Pearl Harbor

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1887, the Amateur Athletic Union (AAU) was formed in the United States to promote and regulate amateur sports. The organization has played a vital role in the development of athletics and has been instrumental in the establishment of various sporting events.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Formation of the Amateur Athletic Union

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dogali was fought on January 24, 1887, between the forces of the Kingdom of Italy and the Ethiopian Empire. The battle resulted in a decisive victory for the Ethiopian troops, marking a significant setback for Italian colonial ambitions in East Africa.

image.caption: Michele Cammarano’s retrospective painting depicting the Battle of Dogali.
image.credit: Michele Cammarano — http://www.artesuarte.it/articolo.php?id=55
image.date_qualification: Painting dated 1896; it depicts the battle of 26 January 1887, not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Dogali

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1887, during a snowstorm at Fort Keogh, Montana, the largest snowflakes on record were reported, measuring 15 inches (38 cm) wide and 8 inches (20 cm) thick. This extraordinary meteorological event remains a notable record in the study of weather phenomena.
events.name: Largest snowflakes recorded at Fort Keogh

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1887, the first Groundhog Day was observed in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania. This event marked the beginning of a unique American tradition where a groundhog is said to predict the weather based on whether it sees its shadow.
events.name: First Groundhog Day observed

events.enhanced_description: The Interstate Commerce Act was signed into law by President Grover Cleveland on February 4, 1887. This landmark legislation aimed to regulate the railroad industry and prevent monopolistic practices, marking a significant step in the establishment of federal regulatory authority.
events.name: Interstate Commerce Act signed into law

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1887, Giuseppe Verdi's opera 'Otello' premiered at La Scala in Milan. This opera, based on Shakespeare's tragedy, is celebrated for its powerful music and dramatic intensity, solidifying Verdi's reputation as one of the greatest composers of the 19th century.
events.name: Premiere of Verdi's Otello

events.enhanced_description: The Dawes Act, also known as the General Allotment Act, was enacted on February 8, 1887. This legislation aimed to assimilate Native Americans into American society by allotting them individual plots of land and promoting farming, ultimately leading to significant loss of tribal land.
events.name: Dawes Act enacted

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1887, a large earthquake struck the French Riviera, resulting in the deaths of approximately 2,000 people along the Mediterranean coast. This disaster highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity and led to changes in building regulations.
events.name: Earthquake hits the French Riviera

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1887, at the Sydney Cricket Ground, George Lohmann became the first bowler to take eight wickets in a Test innings. This achievement set a significant milestone in the history of cricket and showcased Lohmann's exceptional talent.
events.name: George Lohmann's bowling record

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1887, Anne Sullivan began teaching Helen Keller, who was deaf and blind. This pivotal moment in Keller's life led to her remarkable achievements and advocacy for people with disabilities, showcasing the impact of dedicated education.
events.name: Anne Sullivan begins teaching Helen Keller

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1887, North Carolina State University was established, originally known as the North Carolina College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts. The university has since grown into a major research institution and a key player in the state's educational landscape.

locations.historical_name: North Carolina College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts
locations.name: Raleigh, North Carolina, United States

events.name: North Carolina State University established

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1887, Chester Greenwood patented earmuffs in Farmington, Maine. This invention provided a practical solution for protecting ears from cold weather, and Greenwood's design has influenced the development of winter headgear.
events.name: Chester Greenwood patents earmuffs

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1887, the final of the first All-Ireland Hurling Championship was held, marking a significant moment in the history of Irish sports. This event helped to promote hurling as a national sport and fostered a sense of Irish identity.
events.name: First All-Ireland Hurling Championship final

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1887, Susanna M. Salter was elected as the first female mayor in the United States in Argonia, Kansas. Her election was a significant milestone in the women's suffrage movement, demonstrating the growing political involvement of women in American society.
events.name: Susanna M. Salter elected as first female mayor

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1887, the Catholic University of America was founded in Washington, D.C. This institution was established to provide higher education in the Catholic tradition and has since become a prominent center for Catholic scholarship.
events.name: Catholic University of America founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1887, Occidental College was founded in Los Angeles, California. This liberal arts college has played a significant role in higher education in California and continues to be known for its diverse academic programs.

image.caption: Herrick Memorial Chapel and fountain at Occidental College.
image.credit: The original uploader was Geographer at English Wikipedia . — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by IngerAlHaosului using CommonsHelper .
image.date_qualification: Campus-site photograph described as taken on July 15, 2005; the chapel was built in 1964 and the fountain in 1979. It depicts the later campus, not the college’s 1887 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 1.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 1.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Occidental College founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1887, the Schnaebele incident occurred, nearly leading to war between France and Germany. This border incident highlighted the tensions between the two nations during a period of rising nationalism in Europe.
events.name: Schnaebele incident

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1887, an earthquake struck Sonora, Mexico, causing significant damage and loss of life. This natural disaster underscored the region's vulnerability to seismic activity and prompted discussions on disaster preparedness.
events.name: Earthquake in Sonora, Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1887, Ricardo Palma founded the Peruvian Academy of Language in Lima, Peru. This institution was established to promote and preserve the Spanish language and literature in Peru, contributing to the cultural heritage of the nation.
events.name: Peruvian Academy of Language founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1887, the cornerstone of Stanford University was laid in northern California. This prestigious institution would later open in 1891 and has since become one of the leading universities in the world.
events.name: Stanford University cornerstone laid

events.enhanced_description: The Hells Canyon massacre occurred when 34 Chinese gold miners were ambushed and murdered by local vigilantes in a racially motivated attack. This tragic event highlighted the intense racial tensions and violence faced by Chinese immigrants during the Gold Rush era in the United States.
events.name: Hells Canyon Massacre

events.enhanced_description: Herman Hollerith received a U.S. patent for his punched card calculator, a significant innovation that laid the groundwork for modern data processing and computing. His invention was pivotal in the efficient processing of census data and later influenced the development of early computers.
events.name: Herman Hollerith's Patent

events.enhanced_description: The Reinsurance Treaty was a secret agreement between Germany and Russia, orchestrated by Otto von Bismarck to maintain peace in Europe and counterbalance the Franco-Russian Alliance. This treaty was crucial in the complex web of alliances that characterized European politics leading up to World War I.
events.name: Reinsurance Treaty

events.enhanced_description: The British Empire celebrated Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, marking the 50th anniversary of her reign. This event was a grand celebration of British imperial power and unity, featuring parades, ceremonies, and public festivities across the empire.

image.caption: William Ewart Lockhart’s painting depicts the Golden Jubilee thanksgiving service at Westminster Abbey.
image.credit: William Ewart Lockhart — [2] (earlier versions from [3] and [4] ).
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting depicting the 21 June 1887 service; the saved image date gives a creation range from 1887 to 1890, not a photograph date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee

events.enhanced_description: The Rocky Mountains Park Act was enacted in Canada, establishing Banff National Park as the first national park in the country. This landmark legislation marked a significant step in the conservation movement and the recognition of the natural beauty of Canada's landscapes.
events.name: Rocky Mountains Park Act

events.enhanced_description: Minot, North Dakota, was incorporated as a city, reflecting the growth and development of urban centers in the American West during the late 19th century. This incorporation marked a significant milestone in the city's history and its role in regional development.
events.name: Incorporation of Minot

events.enhanced_description: The United Retail Federation was established in Brisbane, Australia, representing a significant development in the organization of retail businesses in the region. This federation aimed to advocate for the interests of retailers and improve the business environment.
events.name: United Retail Federation Established

events.enhanced_description: James Blyth operated the first working wind turbine at Marykirk, Scotland, marking a significant advancement in renewable energy technology. This pioneering work laid the foundation for future developments in wind energy generation.
events.name: James Blyth's Wind Turbine

events.enhanced_description: Construction of the iron structure of the Eiffel Tower began in Paris, France, designed by engineer Gustave Eiffel. This iconic landmark would later become a symbol of French ingenuity and a major tourist attraction.
events.name: Construction of the Eiffel Tower

events.enhanced_description: King Kalākaua of Hawai'i was forced to sign the 'Bayonet Constitution', which significantly reduced the powers of the monarchy and disenfranchised many native Hawaiians and other groups. This event marked a turning point in Hawaiian history and the eventual overthrow of the monarchy.
events.name: Bayonet Constitution

events.enhanced_description: Odense Boldklub was founded as the Odense Cricket Club, marking the establishment of one of Denmark's oldest football clubs. This club would go on to play a significant role in the development of football in Denmark.
events.name: Odense Boldklub Founded

events.enhanced_description: Dorr Eugene Felt received the first U.S. patent for his comptometer, an early mechanical calculator that revolutionized data entry and calculation processes. This invention played a crucial role in the evolution of office technology.
events.name: Dorr Eugene Felt's Patent

events.enhanced_description: L. L. Zamenhof published "Unua Libro", the first description of Esperanto, a constructed international auxiliary language aimed at fostering communication between people of different native languages. This publication marked the beginning of the Esperanto movement.
events.name: Publication of Unua Libro

events.enhanced_description: Hibernian F.C. of Scotland defeated Preston North End F.C. of England to win the 'Championship of the World', a title awarded to the winners of the respective national cup competitions. This match was significant in the early history of football and showcased the growing popularity of the sport.
events.name: Hibernian F.C. Championship Win

events.enhanced_description: The British Empire formally took control of Balochistan, further expanding its colonial reach in South Asia. This annexation was part of the broader imperial strategy to secure trade routes and resources in the region.
events.name: British Empire Takes Over Balochistan

events.enhanced_description: Florida A&M University was established in Tallahassee, Florida, as a historically black university. It has since played a crucial role in providing higher education opportunities for African Americans in the region.
events.name: Florida A&M University Opens

events.enhanced_description: Yamaha Corporation was founded in Hamamatsu, Japan, originally as Yamaha Organ Manufacturing. The company has since grown into a global leader in musical instruments and audio equipment, significantly influencing the music industry.
events.name: Yamaha Corporation Founded

events.enhanced_description: The Coimbra Academic Association was established as the students' union of the University of Coimbra, one of the oldest universities in Europe. This organization aimed to represent student interests and foster a sense of community among the student body.
events.name: The Coimbra Academic Association is founded

events.enhanced_description: Celtic Football Club was founded in Glasgow by Irish Marist Brother Walfrid to raise funds for the Poor Children's Dinner Table charity. The club quickly became a significant part of Scottish football and a symbol of the Irish immigrant community in Scotland.
events.name: Celtic F.C. is formed

events.enhanced_description: Emile Berliner was granted a U.S. patent for the Berliner Gramophone, a significant advancement in sound recording technology. This invention laid the groundwork for the modern music industry and the way sound was recorded and played back.
events.name: Emile Berliner is granted a U.S. patent for the Berliner Gramophone

events.enhanced_description: Louis Lingg, facing execution for his alleged involvement in the Haymarket affair, committed suicide using dynamite in his jail cell. His death highlighted the tensions surrounding labor rights and the radical movements of the time.
events.name: Louis Lingg's suicide

events.enhanced_description: August Spies, Albert Parsons, Adolph Fischer, and George Engel were executed by hanging for their roles in the Haymarket affair, a pivotal event in labor history that underscored the struggle for workers' rights in the United States.
events.name: Hanging of August Spies and others

events.enhanced_description: On Bloody Sunday, police clashed with radical and Irish nationalist protesters in London, leading to significant violence and highlighting the growing tensions between the government and various social movements. This event became a symbol of the struggle for civil rights in the UK.
events.name: Bloody Sunday in London

events.enhanced_description: Örgryte IS, a prominent Swedish football club, was founded by Wilhelm Friberg in Gothenburg. The club has a rich history in Swedish football and has contributed significantly to the development of the sport in the region.
events.name: Örgryte IS is founded

events.enhanced_description: The International Bureau of Intellectual Property was established to promote the protection of intellectual property rights globally. This organization played a crucial role in the development of international treaties and agreements regarding intellectual property.
events.name: International Bureau of Intellectual Property is established

events.enhanced_description: Glenfiddich single malt Scotch whisky was first produced in Dufftown, Scotland, marking the beginning of one of the most famous whisky brands in the world. Glenfiddich has since become synonymous with quality and tradition in whisky production.
events.name: Glenfiddich single malt Scotch whisky is first produced

events.enhanced_description: In 1888, the Brighton Beach Hotel in Coney Island, New York, was moved 520 feet (160 meters) using six steam locomotives, a remarkable feat of engineering aimed at protecting it from ocean storms. This event showcased innovative techniques in civil engineering during the period.
events.name: Brighton Beach Hotel moved

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1888, American writer Ernest Thayer's baseball poem 'Casey at the Bat' was first published in The San Francisco Examiner under the pen name 'Phin'. This poem has since become a classic of American literature, celebrated for its vivid depiction of baseball culture.
events.name: Casey at the Bat published

events.enhanced_description: In 1888, Letitia Alice Walkington made history by becoming the first woman in the United Kingdom to earn a Bachelor of Laws degree from the Royal University of Ireland at Queen's College, Belfast. This milestone marked a significant advancement for women's rights in education and paved the way for future generations of female lawyers.
events.name: Letitia Alice Walkington becomes the first woman in the United Kingdom to receive a degree of Bachelor of Laws

events.enhanced_description: In 1888, Gideon Daniel Searle founded G.D. Searle in Omaha, Nebraska, establishing a company that would become a significant player in the pharmaceutical industry. This venture contributed to the growth of healthcare innovations in the United States.
events.name: Founding of G.D. Searle

events.enhanced_description: In 1888, Dr. Wallace C. Abbott established Abbott Laboratories, originally known as Abbott Alkaloidal, in Illinois. This company would grow to become a leading global healthcare company, known for its innovative medical products and pharmaceuticals.
events.name: Founding of Abbott Laboratories

events.enhanced_description: Katz's Delicatessen was founded in 1888 in the Lower East Side of Manhattan, New York City. It has since become an iconic establishment known for its classic Jewish deli fare, particularly its pastrami sandwiches, and is a significant part of New York's culinary history.

image.caption: Katz's Delicatessen in New York City.
image.credit: ajay_suresh — Katz's Delicatessen
image.date_qualification: Image date: 2021-10-23 16:06; this is not the founding date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of Katz's Delicatessen

events.enhanced_description: The first British rugby union tour of Australia and New Zealand took place in 1888, marking a significant moment in the history of rugby. This tour helped to popularize the sport in the Southern Hemisphere and laid the foundation for future international competitions.
events.name: First British rugby union tour of Australia and New Zealand
