events.name: BOVESPA stock exchange founded

events.enhanced_description: Bohemian Football Club was founded on September 6, 1890, in the Gate Lodge of Phoenix Park, Dublin. As one of the oldest football clubs in Ireland, Bohemian F.C. has played a significant role in the development of football in the country.
events.name: Foundation of Bohemian F.C.

events.enhanced_description: Salisbury, now known as Harare, was founded on September 12, 1890, during the period of British colonial expansion in Southern Africa. The establishment of Salisbury marked the beginning of significant urban development in the region, which would later become the capital of Zimbabwe.
events.name: Foundation of Salisbury, Rhodesia

events.enhanced_description: The University of North Texas was founded on September 19, 1890, originally established as the Texas Normal College and Teacher Training Institute. It has since grown into a major public research university, contributing significantly to education in Texas.

locations.historical_name: Texas Normal College and Teacher Training Institute
locations.name: Denton

events.name: Foundation of the University of North Texas

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1890, Wilford Woodruff, the President of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, issued the 1890 Manifesto, which officially ended the practice of polygamy within the church. This landmark declaration was a significant turning point in the history of the LDS Church and its relationship with the United States.
events.name: 1890 Manifesto

events.enhanced_description: Yosemite National Park was established on October 1, 1890, as one of the first national parks in the United States, preserving its stunning natural beauty and diverse ecosystems. The park has since become a symbol of conservation efforts and a popular destination for outdoor enthusiasts.
events.name: Establishment of Yosemite National Park

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1890, Clément Ader's steam-powered fixed-wing aircraft, Ader Éole, made its first brief flight in Satory, France, achieving an uncontrolled takeoff of approximately 50 meters. This event is recognized as one of the earliest instances of powered flight, contributing to the development of aviation technology.
events.name: First flight of Clément Ader's Ader Éole

events.enhanced_description: The Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) was founded on October 11, 1890, in Washington, D.C., as a lineage-based membership organization for women. The DAR played a significant role in promoting patriotism, historical preservation, and education in the United States.
events.name: Founding of the Daughters of the American Revolution

events.enhanced_description: The Uddevalla Suffrage Association was founded in Sweden on October 12, 1890, advocating for women's rights and suffrage. This organization was part of the broader movement for gender equality in Sweden, contributing to the eventual granting of voting rights to women.
events.name: Foundation of the Uddevalla Suffrage Association

events.enhanced_description: Delta Chi fraternity was founded on October 13, 1890, by 11 law students at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. The fraternity has since grown to become a prominent national organization, emphasizing brotherhood, scholarship, and service.
events.name: Foundation of Delta Chi fraternity

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1890, the City and South London Railway officially opened, becoming the first deep-level underground railway in London. This innovative transportation system revolutionized urban travel and set the stage for the expansion of the London Underground network.
events.name: Opening of the City and South London Railway

events.enhanced_description: Edward King, the Anglican bishop of Lincoln, was convicted of using ritualistic practices, which sparked significant controversy within the Church of England and raised questions about the direction of Anglican worship during a time of religious change.
events.name: Conviction of Edward King

events.enhanced_description: The death of King William III of the Netherlands without a male heir led to his daughter, Princess Wilhelmina, ascending to the throne, marking a significant transition in Dutch monarchy and ending the personal union with Luxembourg.
events.name: Death of King William III of the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: The Meiji Constitution was enacted in Japan, establishing a constitutional monarchy and convening the first Diet, which marked a pivotal moment in Japan's modernization and political reform.
events.name: Meiji Constitution goes into effect

events.enhanced_description: Sitting Bull, the renowned Hunkpapa Lakota leader, was killed by police on the Standing Rock Indian Reservation, an event that marked a tragic moment in Native American history and the ongoing struggles against U.S. government policies.

events.name: Sitting Bull's death

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1890, the Oklahoma territorial legislature established three institutions of higher learning: the University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma State University, and the University of Central Oklahoma, laying the foundation for higher education in the state.

image.caption: Bizzell Memorial Library on the University of Oklahoma campus in Norman, Oklahoma.

events.enhanced_description: The Wounded Knee Massacre occurred on December 29, 1890, when the U.S. 7th Cavalry Regiment attempted to disperse a Lakota camp practicing the Ghost Dance, resulting in the deaths of 153 Lakota Sioux and 25 soldiers, marking a tragic end to the Indian Wars.

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, a strike involving 500 Hungarian steel workers occurred, leading to 3,000 men being out of work, highlighting the labor struggles and economic tensions of the time.
events.name: Hungarian steel workers' strike

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, a strike involving 500 Hungarian steel workers occurred, leading to 3,000 men being out of work. This labor unrest was part of the broader labor movement in Hungary, reflecting the struggles of workers during this period.
events.name: Hungarian Steel Workers Strike

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, Germany formally took possession of its new African territories, expanding its colonial empire. This event was part of the broader scramble for Africa, where European powers competed for control over African lands and resources.
events.name: Germany Takes Possession of African Territories

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, the Australian shearers' strike began, which would eventually lead to the foundation of the Australian Labor Party. This strike was a significant event in the history of labor movements in Australia, highlighting the struggles of workers for better conditions.
events.name: Australian Shearers' Strike Begins

events.enhanced_description: In January 1891, tensions escalated between the United States government and the Lakota Sioux near the Pine Ridge Reservation, leading to violent confrontations. This conflict was part of the broader struggles of Native Americans against U.S. expansion and policies.
events.name: A fight between the United States and Lakotas breaks out near Pine Ridge agency

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, a violent clash occurred in Motherwell, Scotland, between railway strikers advocating for better working conditions and police attempting to suppress the protest. This incident highlighted the growing tensions between labor movements and authorities during the Industrial Revolution.
events.name: A fight between railway strikers and police breaks out at Motherwell, Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In early 1891, General Nelson A. Miles led U.S. forces to surround the Lakota Sioux in the Pine Ridge Reservation, marking a significant moment in the conflict between Native Americans and the U.S. government. This military action was part of the larger context of the Indian Wars.
events.name: General Miles' forces surround the Lakota in the Pine Ridge Reservation

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, Secretary of the Navy Benjamin F. Tracy relieved Commander Reiter of his command due to the controversial Barrundia Affair, which involved the U.S. Navy's actions in Central America. This incident raised questions about U.S. foreign policy and military conduct.
events.name: Secretary Tracy relieves Commander Reiter of his ship, on account of the Barrundia Affair

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, the Inter-American Monetary Commission convened in Washington, D.C., to discuss monetary policies and economic cooperation among American nations. This meeting was significant in shaping future economic relations in the Americas.
figures: Members of the Inter-American Monetary Commission
events.name: The Inter-American Monetary Commission meets in Washington DC

events.enhanced_description: In early 1891, approximately 3,000 Lakota Sioux approached the Pine Ridge Reservation with intentions to surrender, reflecting the dire circumstances faced by Native Americans amidst U.S. military pressure. This event marked a pivotal moment in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: 3,000 Lakotas approach Pine Ridge with a view to surrender

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, the shutdown of sixteen blast furnaces in Mahoning Valley, Ohio, resulted in the loss of jobs for approximately 10,000 workers. This event underscored the volatility of the industrial economy and the struggles faced by laborers during this period.
events.name: Mahoning Valley, Ohio, sixteen blast furnaces shut down, putting 10,000 men out of work

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, Canada initiated legal proceedings against the United States before the Supreme Court regarding the seizure of Canadian vessels in the Bering Sea. This case highlighted tensions over maritime rights and international law.
events.name: Canada brings suit before the United States Supreme Court in re-seizures of vessels in the Bering Sea

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, St. Mary's Cathedral was dedicated in San Francisco, becoming a significant landmark for the Catholic community in the region. The cathedral's architecture and design reflected the growing influence of the Catholic Church in California.
events.name: St. Mary's Cathedral dedicated in San Francisco

events.enhanced_description: In early 1891, General Nelson A. Miles declared the end of the Lakota uprising at Pine Ridge Reservation, commending his troops for their efforts. This announcement marked a significant moment in the U.S. government's campaign against Native American resistance.
events.name: General Miles officially announces the end of the native outbreak and congratulates his troops

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, the British government ordered a naval squadron to Chile amidst rising tensions during the Chilean Civil War. This deployment underscored Britain's strategic interests in Latin America during a period of political instability.
events.name: A British squadron ordered to Chile

events.enhanced_description: In May 1891, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad proclaimed himself as the Promised Messiah and Mahdi, a significant claim in the Ahmadiyya movement within Islam. This declaration had profound implications for Islamic theology and sectarian dynamics.
events.name: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad claims to be the Promised Messiah

events.enhanced_description: In June 1891, the clipper ship Cromdale was completed, marking the end of an era for fully rigged ships built for the Australian wool trade. This vessel represented the peak of sailing technology before the advent of steam-powered ships.
events.name: The clipper ship Cromdale is completed

events.enhanced_description: In July 1891, Arthur Conan Doyle's iconic detective Sherlock Holmes made his debut in The Strand Magazine, captivating readers with his brilliant deductive reasoning. This introduction laid the foundation for one of the most enduring characters in literary history and popular culture.
events.name: Sherlock Holmes appears in The Strand Magazine

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, the Wrigley Company was founded in Chicago by William Wrigley Jr., initially starting as a chewing gum manufacturer. The company would go on to become a leading global brand in the confectionery industry.
events.name: The Wrigley Company is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, the London–Paris telephone system was inaugurated, allowing for direct communication between the two major cities for the first time. This advancement in telecommunications represented a significant leap forward in connecting people across distances.
events.name: The London–Paris telephone system is opened

events.enhanced_description: During a May Day demonstration in 1891, troops opened fire on workers in Fourmies, France, resulting in the deaths of nine individuals and injuring thirty others. This tragic event highlighted the tensions between labor movements and government authorities during a period of social unrest.
events.name: Troops fire on a workers' May Day demonstration

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, Giuseppe De Felice Giuffrida founded the first Fascio dei lavoratori (Workers League) in Catania, Sicily. This organization aimed to unite workers and advocate for their rights, marking an important step in the labor movement in Italy.
events.name: The first Fascio dei lavoratori is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, Skansen was established as the world's first open-air museum by Artur Hazelius on the island of Djurgården in Stockholm, Sweden. This innovative museum showcased Swedish culture and history through reconstructed buildings and exhibits.
events.name: Skansen is established

events.enhanced_description: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a prominent nationalist leader, initiated a vigorous campaign for Indian self-rule, laying the groundwork for the Indian independence movement. His efforts mobilized public opinion and inspired future generations of leaders in the struggle against British colonial rule.
events.name: Brahmin teacher and nationalist Bal Gangadhar Tilak begins agitation for Indian Home Rule

events.enhanced_description: James Naismith, a physical education instructor, invented basketball as a new indoor sport to keep his students active during the winter months. The game quickly gained popularity and evolved into one of the major professional sports in the United States and around the world.

image.caption: Portrait of James Naismith with a soccer ball and a basket.

events.name: James Naismith invents basketball in the United States

events.enhanced_description: Seattle University was founded as the Immaculate Conception school, marking the beginning of a significant educational institution in the Pacific Northwest. It has since grown into a prominent Jesuit university known for its commitment to social justice and community service.
events.name: Seattle University is established as the Immaculate Conception school

events.enhanced_description: Nikola Tesla invented the Tesla coil, a high-voltage transformer that produces high-frequency alternating current. This invention played a crucial role in the development of radio technology and wireless transmission, significantly impacting the field of electrical engineering.

events.enhanced_description: Édouard Michelin patented the removable pneumatic bicycle tire, revolutionizing the cycling industry by making tire changes easier and enhancing the overall riding experience. This innovation laid the foundation for modern tire manufacturing and contributed to the growth of the automotive industry.
events.name: Michelin patents the removable pneumatic bicycle tire

events.enhanced_description: Victorinox began the production of the Swiss Army Knife, a versatile multi-tool that has become an iconic symbol of Swiss craftsmanship. This innovative tool was designed to meet the needs of soldiers and has since evolved into a popular everyday carry item worldwide.
events.name: Production of the Swiss Army Knife by Victorinox begins

events.enhanced_description: Philips was founded in Eindhoven, focusing on the production of carbon-filament lamps and other electro-technical products. The company grew to become one of the largest electronics manufacturers in the world, known for its innovation and quality.
events.name: Philips founded in Eindhoven, Netherlands, for the production of carbon-filament lamps and other electro-technical products

events.enhanced_description: The New Mexico Military Institute was established in Roswell, originally known as the Goss Military Institute. This institution has played a significant role in military education and training in the region.
events.name: New Mexico Military Institute is founded (as Goss Military Institute) in Roswell, New Mexico Territory

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1891, the Earl of Zetland issued a declaration regarding the famine affecting the western counties of Ireland, drawing attention to the ongoing social and economic issues faced by the Irish population.
events.name: Earl of Zetland's declaration on Irish famine

events.enhanced_description: The Australian shearers' strike began on January 5, 1891, leading to significant labor unrest and indirectly contributing to the foundation of the Australian Labor Party.
events.name: Australian shearers' strike

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1891, General Miles' forces surrounded the Lakota in the Pine Ridge Reservation, a critical moment in the aftermath of the Wounded Knee Massacre and the ongoing tensions between Native Americans and the U.S. government.

locations.name: Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota, United States

events.name: General Miles surrounds Lakota

events.enhanced_description: The great shoe strike in Rochester, New York, was called off on January 9, 1891, ending a significant labor dispute that had implications for workers' rights and labor relations in the region.
events.name: End of the great shoe strike

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1891, Irish Nationalist leaders convened a significant conference in Boulogne-sur-Mer, France, to discuss strategies for Irish self-governance. The French government supported their cause by providing a loan, reflecting the international dimensions of Irish nationalism during this period.
events.name: Irish Nationalist Conference at Boulogne

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1891, approximately 3,000 Lakota people approached Pine Ridge Reservation with intentions to surrender, marking a significant moment in the aftermath of the Ghost Dance movement and the Wounded Knee Massacre. This event underscored the desperate situation of Native Americans in the face of U.S. military pressure.

locations.name: Pine Ridge, South Dakota, United States

events.name: Lakota Surrender at Pine Ridge

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1891, Canada initiated a lawsuit before the United States Supreme Court regarding the seizure of vessels in the Bering Sea, which was a pivotal moment in international maritime law and fisheries management. This case highlighted tensions between the two nations over resource rights in the North Pacific.
events.name: Canada vs. United States Supreme Court Case

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1891, a conference took place at Pine Ridge Reservation where Lakota chiefs met with General Nelson A. Miles. During this meeting, the Lakota agreed to surrender, signaling a critical moment in the U.S. government's efforts to quell Native American resistance.

locations.name: Pine Ridge, South Dakota, United States

events.name: Lakota Chiefs Conference with General Miles

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1891, railway strikers in Scotland attempted to wreck a train near Greenock as part of their protest against poor working conditions and wages. This incident highlighted the growing labor unrest in the UK during the late 19th century.
events.name: Scottish Railway Strikers Attempt Train Wreck

events.enhanced_description: The Chilean Civil War broke out on January 16, 1891, primarily between supporters of President José Manuel Balmaceda and those favoring congressional authority. This conflict marked a significant turning point in Chilean politics, leading to a shift in power dynamics.
events.name: Chilean Civil War of 1891

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1891, General Nelson A. Miles officially announced the end of the Native American outbreak, congratulating his troops for their efforts. This declaration marked a significant moment in U.S. military history regarding Native American relations.

locations.name: Pine Ridge, South Dakota, United States

events.name: General Miles Announces End of Native Outbreak

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1891, Jim Hogg was inaugurated as the first native Texan to serve as governor of Texas. His election represented a significant milestone in Texas politics and reflected the growing influence of local leaders.
events.name: Jim Hogg Becomes Governor of Texas

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1891, Liliuokalani was proclaimed Queen of Hawaii, becoming the first and only reigning queen of the Hawaiian Kingdom. Her reign would later be challenged by American interests, leading to significant political turmoil.
events.name: Liliuokalani Proclaimed Queen of Hawaii

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1891, the Portuguese Republican Revolution broke out in Porto, marking a significant challenge to the monarchy and a push towards establishing a republic in Portugal. This event was part of a broader wave of republican movements across Europe.
events.name: Portuguese Republican Revolution

events.enhanced_description: In February 1891, the Tobacco Protest began in Iran, led by merchants against the government's concession to a foreign company for the production and sale of tobacco. This movement was significant in mobilizing public opinion against foreign influence and contributed to the constitutional revolution.
events.name: Tobacco Protest in Iran

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1891, during an FA Cup quarter-final match, a goal was deliberately stopped by handball on the goal line, leading to an indirect free kick being awarded. This incident played a crucial role in changing public perception regarding the implementation of penalty kicks in football.
events.name: FA Cup Quarter Final Incident

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1891, Allmänna Idrottsklubben (AIK) was founded in Stockholm, Sweden, marking a significant development in Swedish sports culture. AIK would go on to become one of the most successful and popular sports clubs in Sweden.
events.name: AIK Sports Club Founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1891, a serious mining disaster occurred in Springhill, Nova Scotia, resulting in significant loss of life and highlighting the dangers faced by miners during this period. This tragedy prompted discussions on mine safety regulations.
events.name: Springhill Mining Disaster

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1891, the International Copyright Act was passed by the 51st United States Congress, establishing protections for foreign authors and creators. This act was a significant step in the development of international copyright law.
events.name: International Copyright Act of 1891

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1891, Sir John A. Macdonald, the first Prime Minister of Canada, secured a fourth consecutive parliamentary victory over the Liberal Party. His continued leadership was pivotal in shaping Canada's early political landscape.
events.name: Sir John A. Macdonald's Fourth Victory

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1891, the Great Blizzard struck southern and western England, causing extensive snow drifts and powerful storms. The severe weather resulted in the sinking of 14 ships and approximately 220 fatalities, marking it as one of the most devastating weather events of the time.
events.name: The Great Blizzard of 1891

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1891, Djurgårdens IF, a prominent sports club, was founded in Stockholm, Sweden. The club has since become a significant part of Swedish sports culture, participating in various sports including football and ice hockey.
events.name: Djurgårdens IF Founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1891, a lynch mob stormed the Old Parish Prison in New Orleans, lynching 11 Italians who had been arrested but found innocent of the murder of Police Chief David Hennessy. This event highlighted the racial tensions and mob violence prevalent in the United States during this era.
events.name: Lynching of Italians in New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1891, the British steamship SS Utopia sank in the inner harbor of Gibraltar after colliding with the battleship HMS Anson, resulting in the tragic loss of 564 lives. This maritime disaster raised concerns about shipping safety and regulations.
events.name: SS Utopia Sinks

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1891, the London-Paris telephone system was officially opened, marking a significant advancement in telecommunications and enhancing communication between the two major cities. This development was part of the broader technological innovations of the late 19th century.
events.name: London-Paris Telephone System Opens

events.enhanced_description: In April 1891, William Wrigley Jr. founded the Wrigley Company in Chicago, which would become famous for its chewing gum products. This marked the beginning of a significant American brand in the confectionery industry.
events.name: The Wrigley Company is founded in Chicago

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1891, the United Kingdom conducted a census revealing that 15.6 million people lived in cities of 20,000 or more in England and Wales. This data highlighted urbanization trends and demographic shifts during the late 19th century.
events.name: Census in the United Kingdom: 15

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1891, the first official match of the Argentine Primera División took place in Caballito, Buenos Aires, marking the beginning of organized football in Argentina. This event laid the foundation for the country's rich football culture.
events.name: The first official game in the Association football league of Argentina (1891 Argentine Primera División) is held in Caballito, Buenos Aires

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1891, during the Chilean Civil War, the ironclad Blanco Encalada was sunk at the Battle of Caldera Bay by self-propelled torpedo boats. This event marked a significant moment in naval warfare and the conflict between government and rebel forces.
events.name: Chilean Civil War of 1891: Chilean ironclad Blanco Encalada is sunk at the Battle of Caldera Bay by torpedo boats

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1891, French troops opened fire on a May Day demonstration in Fourmies, resulting in the deaths of nine workers and injuries to thirty others. This tragic event highlighted the violent repression of labor movements in France during this period.
events.name: Troops fire on a workers' May Day demonstration in support of the 8-hour workday in Fourmies, France, killing 9 and wounding 30

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1891, the Jamaica International Exhibition was held, showcasing the island's cultural and economic development. This event was significant for promoting Jamaica's identity and attracting international attention.
events.name: Jamaica International Exhibition

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1891, Carnegie Hall in New York City held its grand opening with a performance conducted by the renowned composer Peter Tchaikovsky. This event marked the establishment of one of the most prestigious concert halls in the world.

image.caption: Carnegie Hall, a concert venue in Midtown Manhattan.
image.credit: Ajay Suresh from New York, NY, USA — Carnegie Hall - Full
image.date_qualification: Contemporary photograph of the Carnegie Hall site, taken in 2019; it does not depict the 1891 grand opening or performance.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Music Hall in New York (later known as Carnegie Hall) has its grand opening and first public performance, with Peter Tchaikovsky as guest conductor

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1891, Tsesarevich Nikolay Alexandrovich, the future Czar Nicholas II of Russia, survived an assassination attempt while visiting Ōtsu, Japan. This incident strained Russo-Japanese relations and highlighted the tensions between the two nations.

image.caption: A Le Petit Journal gravure depicting the Ōtsu incident.
image.credit: H. Meyer (?) [likely the initials refer to Henri Meyer], published in the 30 May 1891 issue of 'Le Petit Journal' — SPCollection
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration published 19 days after the 11 May 1891 assassination attempt; the description notes that its depiction is inaccurate.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ōtsu incident: Tsesarevich Nikolay Alexandrovich survives an assassination attempt while visiting Japan

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1891, Pope Leo XIII issued the encyclical Rerum novarum, addressing the rights and duties of capital and labor. This document laid the groundwork for modern Catholic social teaching and influenced the formation of Christian Democratic parties in Europe.
events.name: Pope Leo XIII issues the encyclical Rerum novarum

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1891, Thomas Edison showcased his prototype kinetoscope at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey, during a convention of the National Federation of Women's Clubs. This invention was pivotal in the development of motion picture technology.
events.name: Thomas Edison's prototype kinetoscope is first displayed at Edison's Laboratory

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1891, Tsesarevich Nikolay Alexandrovich inaugurated the construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway in Vladivostok, marking a monumental project in Russian infrastructure that would connect the vast country from west to east.
events.name: Inauguration of construction work on the Trans-Siberian Railway

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1891, the Johnstown Inclined Plane was opened in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, as an innovative solution for transporting people and goods up the steep hills of the region. This engineering marvel became a significant local transportation system.

image.caption: The Johnstown Inclined Plane in Johnstown, Pennsylvania.
image.credit: Niagara — Own work
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the inclined plane, not an image of its 1891 opening. The saved image date is 2010-11-28.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Johnstown Inclined Plane opens in Johnstown, Pennsylvania

events.enhanced_description: In June 1891, the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais was officially granted its status, reflecting the political restructuring occurring in Brazil during this period. This development was significant for the governance and administration of the region.
events.name: Minas Gerais was granted in 1891

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1891, Lucien and Paul Nunn successfully transmitted alternating current over a distance of 10 miles from the Ames Power Plant near Telluride, Colorado. This groundbreaking achievement marked a significant milestone in the development of electrical engineering and the use of alternating current for power distribution.
events.name: The first long-distance transmission of alternating current

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1891, the Springboks rugby union team of South Africa played their first international test match against the British Lions, losing by a score of 4-0. This match marked the beginning of South Africa's rich rugby history.
events.name: The Springboks play their first international test match

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1891, the first American Express traveler's cheque was cashed, revolutionizing the way travelers managed their finances abroad. This innovation provided a safer and more convenient alternative to carrying cash.
events.name: The first American Express traveler's cheque is cashed

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1891, France and Russia formalized a defensive alliance, a strategic partnership that would shape European politics leading up to World War I. This alliance was a response to the growing threat posed by Germany and its allies.
events.name: France and Russia conclude a defensive alliance

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1891, John Heath scored the first penalty kick in an Association football match for Wolverhampton Wanderers. This event marked a significant moment in the history of football, establishing a new rule that would become integral to the game.
events.name: The first penalty kick in Association football

events.enhanced_description: The Chilean Civil War of 1891 concluded on September 18 with the suicide of deposed President José Manuel Balmaceda, leading to the victory of the Congressional party. This event marked the beginning of a new political era in Chile known as the Parliamentary Era.
events.name: The Chilean Civil War of 1891 ends

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1891, Finland's first hydropower plant was commissioned along the Tammerkoski rapids in Tampere. This development marked a significant advancement in the use of renewable energy in Finland.
events.name: The first hydropower plant of Finland is commissioned

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1891, Club Atlético Peñarol was founded in Montevideo, originally named the Central Uruguay Railway Cricket Club (CURCC). This club would become one of the most successful and storied football clubs in South America.
events.name: Club Atlético Peñarol is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1891, Thyssen was founded in Duisburg, Germany, laying the groundwork for what would become the ThyssenKrupp conglomerate, a major player in the global steel and industrial sectors.
events.name: Thyssen is founded

events.enhanced_description: In October 1891, Eugène Dubois discovered the first fragmentary bones of Pithecanthropus erectus, later reclassified as Homo erectus, at Trinil along the Solo River in Indonesia. This discovery was pivotal in the study of human evolution and the understanding of early hominids.

image.caption: Comparative cross-sections of Sinanthropus and Pithecanthropus skulls, credited to Franz Weidenreich.
image.credit: Franz Weidenreich — https://archive.org/details/TheSkullOfSinanthropusPekinensisAComparativeStudyOnAPrimitive/page/n477/mode/2up
image.date_qualification: The image is a 1943 skull cross-section illustration, not a photograph of Dubois’s 1891 discovery.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Eugène Dubois finds the first fragmentary bones of Pithecanthropus erectus

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1891, Stanford University opened its doors in California, founded by Leland and Jane Stanford in memory of their son. The university has since become one of the leading institutions of higher education in the world.
events.name: Stanford University opens its doors

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1891, the Mino–Owari earthquake, measuring 8.0 on the moment magnitude scale, struck the Gifu region of Japan. This devastating event resulted in over 7,200 deaths and left more than 17,000 injured, causing significant destruction and altering the landscape.
events.name: The Mino–Owari earthquake strikes Japan

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1891, Lion Corporation was founded in Japan, originally known as Kobayashi Tomijirō Shōten. The company has since grown to become a leading manufacturer of personal care and household products in Asia.
events.name: Lion Corporation is founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1891, the Jindandao Incident occurred in Inner Mongolia, where the Chinese Juu Uda League massacred tens of thousands of Mongols. This violent uprising was eventually suppressed by government troops, highlighting ethnic tensions in the region.
events.name: Jindandao Incident

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1891, the constitution of the First Brazilian Republic was promulgated, establishing a republican form of government in Brazil. This document laid the foundation for the country's political structure and governance.
events.name: The constitution of the First Brazilian Republic is promulgated

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1891, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers was organized in St. Louis, Missouri. This labor union aimed to represent electrical workers and advocate for their rights in the burgeoning electrical industry.
events.name: The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers is organized

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1891, Drexel University was inaugurated in Philadelphia as the Drexel Institute of Art, Science and Industry. The institution has since evolved into a prominent university known for its focus on experiential learning and research.

locations.historical_name: Drexel Institute of Art, Science and Industry
locations.name: Drexel University

events.name: Drexel University is inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1891, Asteroid 323 Brucia became the first asteroid to be discovered using photography. This milestone in astronomy demonstrated the advancements in observational techniques and contributed to the study of celestial bodies.
events.name: Asteroid 323 Brucia is discovered

events.enhanced_description: Ellis Island officially began processing immigrants, serving as the gateway for millions seeking a new life in the United States. This facility became a symbol of American immigration and the diverse cultural fabric of the nation.

image.caption: Photograph of immigrants aboard a ferry boat near Ellis Island.
image.credit: mákvirágok — https://www.flickr.com/photos/fekete-feher/42396619972/
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 1920, 28 years after the first inspection station opened in 1892.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Ellis Island, New York, United States

events.name: Ellis Island begins processing immigrants to the United States

events.enhanced_description: The Johnson County War erupted in Wyoming, a violent conflict between small farmers and large ranchers over land and cattle grazing rights. This struggle highlighted the tensions in the American West during the late 19th century and had lasting implications for land use and ranching practices.
events.name: The Johnson County War breaks out between small farmers and large ranchers in Wyoming

events.enhanced_description: In September 1892, Yale University made a historic decision to admit women to its graduate school for the first time. This milestone represented a significant step towards gender equality in higher education in the United States.
events.name: Women admitted to Yale's graduate school

events.enhanced_description: Rudolf Diesel applied for a patent for his innovative compression ignition engine, which would later be known as the Diesel engine. This invention revolutionized the transportation and industrial sectors, providing a more efficient alternative to steam engines.
events.name: Rudolf Diesel applies for a patent on his compression ignition engine (the Diesel engine)

events.enhanced_description: St. Petersburg was officially incorporated as a town, marking its development into a significant urban center in Florida. The city has since grown into a popular destination known for its beaches and cultural institutions.

image.caption: Antique postcard depicting St. Petersburg, Florida.
image.credit: Foley and Fisher, Real Estate — 1906 antique postcard
image.date_qualification: Circa 1906 (postcard date; not the 1892 event date).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: St. Petersburg, Florida is incorporated as a town

events.enhanced_description: Theodoros Deligiannis concluded his term as Prime Minister of Greece, paving the way for Konstantinos Konstantopoulos to assume office. This political transition reflected the ongoing struggles and changes within the Greek political landscape during the late 19th century.
events.name: Theodoros Deligiannis ends his term as Prime Minister of Greece and Konstantinos Konstantopoulos takes office

events.enhanced_description: The rulers of the Trucial States, including Abu Dhabi and Dubai, signed an agreement establishing themselves as de facto British protectorates. This agreement marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the region, influencing its future development.
events.name: "Exclusive Agreement": Rulers of the Trucial States sign an agreement, becoming de facto British protectorates

events.enhanced_description: The first public basketball game was played at the Springfield YMCA, featuring students against faculty. This historic match, which ended with a score of 5-1, showcased the new sport invented by James Naismith and marked the beginning of basketball's rise in popularity.
events.name: The first basketball game is played in public at the Springfield YMCA

events.enhanced_description: Ernest Louis ascended to the title of Grand Duke of Hesse and the Rhine following the death of his father, Grand Duke Louis IV. His reign would be marked by significant political and social changes in the region during the late 19th century.
events.name: Ernest Louis becomes Grand Duke of Hesse and the Rhine

events.enhanced_description: Liverpool Football Club was founded by John Houlding after a dispute with Everton FC over rent at Anfield. The club has since become one of the most successful and storied teams in football history, known for its passionate fanbase and rich heritage.
events.name: The Liverpool Football Club is founded

events.enhanced_description: The St. Patrick's Day Snowstorm struck Tennessee, bringing record snowfall of up to 26 inches. This unusual weather event caused significant disruptions and established snowfall records that have endured over the years.
events.name: The St. Patrick's Day Snowstorm besieges Tennessee

events.enhanced_description: Sir Frederick Stanley, the Governor General of Canada, announced his intention to donate the Stanley Cup, which would become the championship trophy for ice hockey in North America. This gesture significantly contributed to the growth and popularity of the sport.
events.name: Sir Frederick Stanley announces his intention to donate the Stanley Cup for ice hockey

events.enhanced_description: The inaugural French rugby championship final was held in Paris, with Racing Club de France defeating Stade Français. This match marked a significant milestone in the history of rugby in France, contributing to the sport's growing popularity.
events.name: The first ever French rugby championship final takes place in Paris

events.enhanced_description: The world's first fingerprinting bureau was officially opened in Buenos Aires, having operated unofficially since the previous year. This pioneering initiative laid the groundwork for modern forensic science and criminal identification methods.
events.name: The world's first fingerprinting bureau is formally opened in Buenos Aires

events.enhanced_description: The General Electric Company was formed through the merger of the Thomson-Houston Electric Company and the Edison General Electric Company, marking a significant consolidation in the electrical industry. This company would go on to play a pivotal role in technological innovation and industrial development.

image.caption: General Electric shops in Schenectady, New York.
image.credit: Horace L.Arnold — "Modern Machine-Shop Economics." in Engineering Magazine 11. 1896
image.date_qualification: 1896; depicts the shops after GE’s establishment in 1892, not the merger event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The General Electric Company is established through the merger of the Thomson-Houston Electric Company and the Edison General Electric Company

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Yemoja River, British troops successfully defeated the Ijebu infantry using a maxim gun, marking a significant event in the context of British colonial expansion in Nigeria. This battle exemplified the military superiority of colonial forces over local resistance.
events.name: Battle of Yemoja River: British troops defeat Ijebu infantry in modern-day Nigeria

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1892, the last broad gauge train operated by the Great Western Railway departed from Paddington Station in London, marking the end of an era in British railway history. The broad gauge, which had been a significant feature of the railway system since its inception, was gradually replaced by the standard gauge.
events.name: The last broad gauge train runs from Paddington on the Great Western Railway of England

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1892, British forces captured Ijebu Ode, a significant event in the expansion of British colonial power into the Nigerian interior. This conquest was part of a broader campaign to establish control over the Yoruba territories and facilitated further British dominance in West Africa.
events.name: The British conquest of Ijebu Ode

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1892, Prince George was formally appointed as the Duke of York, a title that would later be associated with his reign as King George V of the United Kingdom. This title was part of the British royal tradition of granting noble titles to members of the royal family.
events.name: Prince George becomes Duke of York

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1892, a catastrophic oil fire broke out in Oil City, Pennsylvania, resulting in the tragic deaths of 130 individuals. This disaster highlighted the dangers associated with the burgeoning oil industry in the United States during the late 19th century.
events.name: Oil City fire

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1892, the Chicago 'L' (short for 'elevated') transit system commenced operations, providing a new mode of public transportation for the city's residents. This innovative rail system significantly improved urban mobility and set a precedent for future public transit developments.
events.name: Chicago 'L' begins operation

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1892, Homer Plessy was arrested for sitting in a whites-only railroad car in New Orleans, Louisiana. This act of civil disobedience led to the landmark Supreme Court case Plessy v. Ferguson, which upheld the constitutionality of racial segregation under the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
events.name: Homer Plessy's arrest

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1892, the Limelight Department was officially established in Melbourne, Australia, becoming one of the world's first film studios. This institution played a crucial role in the early development of the film industry and the production of motion pictures.
events.name: Establishment of the Limelight Department

events.enhanced_description: The Homestead Strike began on June 30, 1892, in Homestead, Pennsylvania, as steelworkers protested against wage cuts and poor working conditions. This labor dispute escalated into a violent confrontation between strikers and private security agents, marking a significant moment in American labor history.
events.name: Homestead Strike begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1892, Samoa made a significant change to its time zone, shifting from being 4 hours ahead of Japan to 3 hours behind California. This adjustment resulted in the unique occurrence of July 4 being celebrated twice in the islands, illustrating the complexities of timekeeping in the Pacific.
events.name: Samoa changes time zone

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1892, the British general election resulted in the Conservative and Liberal Unionist coalition government losing its majority in the House of Commons. This political shift ultimately led to the resignation of Prime Minister Lord Salisbury on August 12, marking a significant change in British governance.

image.caption: Portrait of Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 3rd Marquess of Salisbury.
image.credit: Elliott & Fry — This image has been extracted from another file
image.date_qualification: A portrait of Salisbury, not a photograph of the 1892 election. The image is dated before 21 August 1886; no supported display date is provided.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: British general election

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1892, Dr. José Rizal, a prominent Filipino nationalist and reformist, was arrested by Spanish authorities in Manila for his involvement with La Liga Filipina, a progressive organization advocating for political reforms in the Philippines. His arrest marked a pivotal moment in the Philippine struggle for independence.
events.name: Dr. José Rizal's arrest

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1892, a devastating fire swept through St. John's, Newfoundland, destroying a significant portion of the city. This disaster led to widespread destruction and prompted a major rebuilding effort in the aftermath.
events.name: The Great Fire of 1892

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1892, a hidden lake burst from a glacier on Mont Blanc, causing catastrophic flooding in the valley below and resulting in the deaths of approximately 200 villagers and holidaymakers in Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. This natural disaster underscored the dangers posed by glacial lakes.
events.name: Flooding in Saint-Gervais-les-Bains

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1892, the United International Bureau for the Protection of Intellectual Property (BIRPI) was established in Bern, Switzerland. This organization aimed to facilitate international cooperation in the protection of intellectual property rights, laying the groundwork for future global agreements.
events.name: Establishment of the United International Bureau for the Protection of Intellectual Property

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1892, the Community of the Resurrection, an Anglican religious community for men, was founded in Oxford, England, by Charles Gore and Walter Frere. This community aimed to promote spiritual renewal and social justice within the Anglican Church.
events.name: Foundation of the Community of the Resurrection

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1892, the bodies of Andrew and Abby Borden were discovered in their home in Fall River, Massachusetts. Their daughter, Lizzie Borden, was later accused of the murders but was acquitted, leading to one of the most famous and controversial cases in American criminal history.
events.name: Lizzie Borden murders

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1892, Andrew Borden and his wife Abby were found brutally murdered in their home in Fall River, Massachusetts. Their daughter Lizzie Borden was accused of the crime but was acquitted after a highly publicized trial, which remains one of the most infamous cases in American criminal history.
events.name: The murders of Andrew and Abby Borden

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1892, Thomas Edison was awarded a patent for his invention of a two-way telegraph. This innovation allowed for simultaneous sending and receiving of messages, significantly advancing communication technology.
events.name: Thomas Edison receives patent

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1892, Santiago Wanderers, the first football team in Valparaíso, Chile, was founded. This marked a significant development in the history of sports in the region, contributing to the growth of football culture in Chile.
events.name: Founding of Santiago Wanderers

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1892, William Ewart Gladstone took office as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, leading a Liberal government supported by the Irish Nationalist Party. His premiership was marked by significant political reforms and challenges.
events.name: William Ewart Gladstone assumes premiership

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1892, the Pledge of Allegiance was recited for the first time in the United States, during a public school celebration of Columbus Day. This event marked the beginning of a tradition that would become a significant part of American culture and patriotism.

image.caption: Portrait of George Thatcher Balch.
image.credit: Unknown photographer — Balch, George T. and Wallace Foster (1898) A Patriotic Primer for the Little Citizen (3rd ed.), Levy Bros. & Co.
image.date_qualification: Dated by 1894 in the supplied image metadata; not a photograph of the 1892 recitation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1892, astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard discovered Amalthea, the fifth moon of Jupiter. This discovery contributed to the understanding of the Jovian system and expanded knowledge of celestial bodies.
events.name: Discovery of Amalthea

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1892, Sergei Witte was appointed as the new finance minister of Russia, replacing Ivan Vyshnegradsky. Witte's tenure would later be marked by significant economic reforms and modernization efforts in the Russian Empire.
events.name: Sergei Witte replaces Ivan Vyshnegradsky

events.enhanced_description: The University of Chicago, founded in 1890, commenced its first classes on October 1, 1892. It quickly became a leading institution in higher education, known for its rigorous scholarship and influential faculty.
events.name: The University of Chicago holds its first classes

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1892, the Dalton Gang attempted to rob two banks in Coffeyville, Kansas. The robbery turned deadly when townspeople fought back, resulting in the deaths of several gang members, while Emmett Dalton survived with 23 wounds and was later imprisoned for 14 years.
events.name: Coffeyville bank robbery

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1892, to commemorate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas, the Pledge of Allegiance was recited for the first time in unison by students in U.S. public schools, marking a significant moment in American patriotic culture.
events.name: Pledge of Allegiance recited

events.enhanced_description: The Historical American Exposition opened in Madrid on October 30, 1892, showcasing the cultural and historical ties between Spain and the Americas. This event was part of the celebrations marking the 400th anniversary of Columbus's voyage.
events.name: Historical American Exposition opens

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1892, Arthur Conan Doyle's first collection of Sherlock Holmes stories, titled 'The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes', was published in London. This collection introduced readers to the iconic detective and solidified Holmes's place in literary history.
events.name: Publication of The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1892, Slavia Praha was established as the first football club in Bohemia, originally named Akademický cyklistický odbor Slavia. The club initially focused on cycling before expanding into football, becoming one of the most successful clubs in Czech history.
events.name: Establishment of Slavia Praha

events.enhanced_description: In the 1892 United States presidential election held on November 8, Grover Cleveland defeated incumbent Benjamin Harrison and third-party candidate James B. Weaver. This victory marked Cleveland's return to the presidency, making him the only U.S. president to serve two non-consecutive terms.
events.name: 1892 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1892, French troops occupied Abomey, the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey, as part of their colonial expansion in West Africa. This occupation marked a significant step in the French conquest of Dahomey, which would eventually lead to its incorporation into French West Africa.
events.name: French occupation of Abomey

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1892, a devastating fire broke out at the Hotel Zinzendorf in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, resulting in the tragic deaths of 45 people. This incident highlighted the need for improved fire safety regulations in hotels and public buildings.
events.name: Hotel Zinzendorf fire

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1892, John Thompson was sworn in as the fourth Prime Minister of Canada. His leadership was marked by efforts to promote national unity and economic development during a time of significant growth for the country.
events.name: John Thompson becomes Prime Minister of Canada

events.enhanced_description: The first issue of Vogue magazine was published in the United States on December 17, 1892. This publication would go on to become a leading fashion and lifestyle magazine, influencing trends and culture for over a century.
events.name: First issue of Vogue published

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1892, Tchaikovsky's ballet 'The Nutcracker' premiered at the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg, Russia. This enchanting performance, based on E.T.A. Hoffmann's story, has since become a beloved holiday classic worldwide.
events.name: Premiere of The Nutcracker ballet

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1892, Newcastle East End F.C. was renamed Newcastle United F.C. following the demise of Newcastle West End F.C. This rebranding marked a new era for the club, which would go on to become one of the most recognized football teams in England.

locations.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Newcastle East End F.C. renamed Newcastle United F.C.

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, the Alpha Xi Delta Sorority was founded at Lombard College in Galesburg, Illinois, marking an important development in women's collegiate organizations in the United States. This sorority aimed to promote sisterhood and academic excellence among women.
events.name: The Alpha Xi Delta Sorority is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, Lizzie Borden was acquitted of the axe murder of her parents in Fall River, Massachusetts, a case that captured national attention and remains one of America's most infamous murder trials. The trial highlighted issues of gender and class in the late 19th century.
events.name: Lizzie Borden acquitted of axe murder

events.enhanced_description: José Santos Zelaya, a prominent Liberal general and politician, successfully led a revolt in Nicaragua, which resulted in significant political changes and the establishment of his presidency.
events.name: José Santos Zelaya leads a successful revolt in Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: Kōkichi Mikimoto successfully developed the method for cultivating pearls, revolutionizing the pearl industry and establishing Japan as a leader in pearl production.
events.name: Kōkichi Mikimoto develops cultured pearl cultivation

events.enhanced_description: Frederick Jackson Turner presented his influential lecture titled 'The Significance of the Frontier in American History' to the American Historical Association in Chicago, which would shape the understanding of American identity and expansion.
events.name: Frederick Jackson Turner delivers a lecture

events.enhanced_description: Dundee F.C., a professional football club based in Dundee, Scotland, was established, contributing to the rich sporting culture of the region.

image.caption: Dens Park and Tannadice Park football stadiums viewed from Dundee Law.
image.credit: FHL2 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2014-11-30; it shows the stadiums, not Dundee F.C.’s formation in 1893.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Dundee F.C. is formed

events.enhanced_description: The Russian monitor Rusalka sank in a storm in the Gulf of Finland, resulting in the tragic loss of all 177 crew members, with the wreckage discovered decades later.

locations.name: Gulf of Finland, near Helsinki, Finland

events.name: Rusalka sinks in the Gulf of Finland

events.enhanced_description: The Genoa Cricket & Athletic Club was established, becoming the oldest Italian football club and a significant part of Italy's sports history.
events.name: Genoa Cricket & Athletic Club is formed

events.enhanced_description: Swami Vivekananda delivered a powerful paper at the World Parliament of Religions in Chicago, advocating for the acceptance of all religions and promoting the idea of universal brotherhood.
events.name: Swami Vivekananda delivers a paper at the World Parliament of Religions

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, St Hilda's College, Oxford, was founded by Dorothea Beale, and the first students entered the college, which was established to provide higher education for women. This institution played a crucial role in advancing women's education in the UK.
events.name: First Students Enter St Hilda's College

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, the Franco-Siamese Treaty was signed, resulting in the Kingdom of Siam ceding all territories east of the Mekong River to France, which subsequently established the territory of Laos. This treaty significantly altered the political landscape of Southeast Asia.
events.name: Franco-Siamese Treaty of 1893

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, Carl Anton Larsen became the first person to ski in Antarctica, marking a significant moment in the exploration of the continent. His pioneering efforts contributed to the understanding of the harsh Antarctic environment.
events.name: Carl Anton Larsen's Skiing in Antarctica

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, the first recumbent bicycle, known as the Fautenil Vélociped, was manufactured in France. This innovative design represented a significant advancement in cycling technology.
events.name: Invention of the Fautenil Vélociped

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, Sudbury, Ontario, was incorporated as a town, marking its official recognition as a municipality. This development was part of the broader growth of communities in Canada during this period.
events.name: Incorporation of Sudbury, Ontario

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, German physicist Wilhelm Wien formulated Wien's displacement law, which describes the relationship between the temperature of a black body and the wavelength of its emitted radiation. This law was a significant contribution to the field of thermodynamics and black body radiation.

image.caption: Graph illustrating Planck blackbody spectra at 6000 K across wavelength, fractional bandwidth, and frequency.
image.credit: Rhwentworth — Own work
image.date_qualification: Modern explanatory graph published in 2023, not a contemporary depiction of the law’s formulation in 1893.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Wien's Displacement Law Formulated

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, TMI Episcopal was founded in San Antonio as 'The West Texas School for Boys', later renamed 'West Texas Military Academy'. This institution was established by Bishop James S. Johnston to provide education with a military focus.
events.name: Founding of TMI Episcopal

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, Booker T. Washington High School was founded in Houston, Texas, originally named 'Colored High'. It became the first African-American high school in the city, serving as a vital educational institution for the African-American community.
events.name: Founding of Booker T. Washington High School

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, a 16th-century Ardabil Carpet from Persia was added to the collection of the South Kensington Museum in London. This acquisition highlighted the museum's commitment to showcasing global art and culture.
events.name: Acquisition of Ardabil Carpet

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, American pharmacist Caleb Bradham invented the recipe for what would later become known as Pepsi, initially selling it as 'Brad's Drink' at his pharmacy in New Bern, North Carolina. This invention marked the beginning of a major soft drink brand.
events.name: Invention of Pepsi

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, the Girls' Brigade was founded in Dublin, Ireland, establishing an international Christian youth organization aimed at empowering young girls through faith and community service. This organization has since expanded globally.
events.name: Founding of the Girls' Brigade

events.enhanced_description: In 1893, approximately 8,000 Chinese immigrants arrived in Cuba, contributing to the island's cultural diversity and labor force. This migration was part of a larger trend of Chinese emigration during this period.
events.name: Arrival of Chinese in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: The Independent Labour Party (ILP) held its inaugural meeting in Manchester, marking a significant moment in British political history as it aimed to represent the interests of the working class and advocate for social reforms.
events.name: The Independent Labour Party of the United Kingdom has its first meeting

events.enhanced_description: The Telefon Hírmondó service, an early form of telephone broadcasting, commenced operations in Budapest with around 60 subscribers, representing a pioneering step in telecommunications.
events.name: The Telefon Hírmondó service starts

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1893, Lorrin A. Thurston and the Citizen's Committee of Public Safety, supported by U.S. Marines, orchestrated the overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani's government, leading to the eventual annexation of Hawaii by the United States.
events.name: Overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii

events.enhanced_description: The Tati Concessions Land, previously part of Matabeleland, was formally annexed to the Bechuanaland Protectorate, marking a significant expansion of British colonial interests in southern Africa.
events.name: Annexation of Tati Concessions Land

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Edison completed the construction of the first motion picture studio in West Orange, New Jersey, a pivotal development in the history of cinema that would lead to the creation of numerous films and innovations in filmmaking.

locations.name: West Orange, New Jersey, United States

events.name: Thomas Edison finishes construction of the first motion picture studio

events.enhanced_description: The White Star Line cargo liner SS Naronic sank without a trace in heavy seas during its transatlantic passage from Liverpool to New York, highlighting the perils of maritime travel in the 19th century.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: SS Naronic sinks

events.enhanced_description: Rudolf Diesel was granted a patent for his innovative diesel engine, a significant advancement in engine technology that would later revolutionize transportation and industry.
events.name: Rudolf Diesel receives a patent for the diesel engine

events.enhanced_description: The American University was established by an Act of Congress in Washington, D.C., aiming to provide higher education and promote the values of democracy and service.
events.name: The American University is established

events.enhanced_description: The USS Indiana was launched, becoming the first battleship in the United States Navy that was comparable to contemporary battleships of other nations, marking a significant advancement in naval power.
events.name: USS Indiana launched

events.enhanced_description: The Liverpool Overhead Railway opened, becoming the first elevated electric railway in the world, showcasing advancements in urban transportation and engineering.

image.caption: Cap badge belonging to Liverpool Overhead Railway Chief Inspector Joe Harrison.
image.credit: Photograph by Mike Peel ( www.mikepeel.net ). — Own work
image.date_qualification: A photograph of a railway-related object on display at the Museum of Liverpool, not a photograph of the railway's opening. Image date: 2014-02-23.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Liverpool Overhead Railway opens

events.enhanced_description: The Ivory Coast was officially declared a French colony, marking a significant expansion of French colonial rule in West Africa and impacting the region's political and social landscape.
events.name: Ivory Coast becomes a French colony

events.enhanced_description: In Belgium, notorious criminal Adam Worth was sentenced to seven years in prison for robbery, a significant event in the history of crime in Europe during that period.

image.caption: Portrait of Adam Worth from an American magazine.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — The American Magazine (1905). American Illustrated Magazine . Volume LX. New York: Colver Publishing House, p. 206
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Adam Worth reproduced in an American magazine published in 1905. The original portrait date is not established; it is not a depiction of the sentencing.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Adam Worth sentenced in Belgium

events.enhanced_description: The United States Navy established the rank of Chief Petty Officer, creating a new level of leadership and responsibility within the naval hierarchy.
events.name: The rank of Chief Petty Officer established

events.enhanced_description: The Salt Lake Temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was dedicated after 40 years of construction, symbolizing the faith and perseverance of the early Mormon pioneers.

locations.name: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

events.name: Salt Lake Temple dedicated

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded college basketball game took place in Beaver Falls, Pennsylvania, between the Geneva College Covenanters and the New Brighton YMCA, marking a significant moment in the history of collegiate sports.
events.name: First recorded college basketball game

events.enhanced_description: The Belgian general strike of 1893 began with riots in Mons, leading to significant political changes, including the approval of universal male suffrage by the Belgian Parliament the following day. This event highlighted the growing labor movement and demands for social reform in Belgium.
events.name: Belgian general strike of 1893

events.enhanced_description: The Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland was formed, reflecting a significant movement within Scottish Christianity that sought to uphold traditional values and practices.
events.name: Formation of the Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: The 1893 World's Fair, also known as the World's Columbian Exposition, opened to the public in Chicago, celebrating the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the New World and showcasing advancements in technology and culture.
events.name: 1893 World's Fair opens

events.enhanced_description: The Panic of 1893 began with a crash on the New York Stock Exchange, leading to a severe economic depression that affected the United States and had lasting impacts on the economy.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Panic of 1893

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Edison's 1½ inch system of Kinetoscope was first demonstrated in public at the Brooklyn Institute, marking a significant milestone in the development of motion picture technology.
events.name: Edison's Kinetoscope demonstrated

events.enhanced_description: Mahatma Gandhi arrived in South Africa, where he would live until 1914, leading non-violent protests on behalf of Indian immigrants and developing his philosophy of non-violent resistance.
events.name: Gandhi arrives in South Africa

events.enhanced_description: The Anti-Saloon League was incorporated in Oberlin, Ohio, originally as a state organization, and would later become a nationwide movement advocating for the prohibition of alcohol in the United States.
events.name: Anti-Saloon League incorporated

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1893, Prince George, Duke of York, later known as King George V, married Princess Mary of Teck at St James's Palace in London. This royal union was significant as it solidified the connection between the British monarchy and various European royal families.
events.name: Wedding of Prince George, Duke of York, and Princess Mary of Teck

events.enhanced_description: In the German federal election held on June 15, 1893, small anti-Semitic parties managed to secure 2.9% of the vote, reflecting the growing political tensions and the rise of nationalist sentiments in the German Empire during this period.
events.name: 1893 German federal election

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1893, gold was discovered in Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, leading to a gold rush that significantly impacted the local economy and population growth. This discovery marked a pivotal moment in Australia's mining history.

image.caption: The Super Pit gold mine near Kalgoorlie, Western Australia.
image.credit: Chris Olszewski — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2023-07-31; not contemporaneous with the 1893 discovery.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Gold is found in Kalgoorlie, Western Australia

events.enhanced_description: The Wengernalpbahn railway was inaugurated on June 20, 1893, in Wengen, Switzerland, enhancing access to the scenic Jungfrau region. This railway played a crucial role in the development of tourism in the Swiss Alps.
events.name: The Wengernalpbahn railway is opened

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1893, the flagship HMS Victoria of the British Mediterranean Fleet collided with HMS Camperdown and sank within ten minutes, resulting in the death of Vice-admiral Sir George Tryon. This incident raised significant questions about naval command and ship handling.
events.name: HMS Victoria sinks

events.enhanced_description: The Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain, featuring the statue of Anteros, was unveiled at Piccadilly Circus in London on June 29, 1893. This fountain serves as a tribute to the philanthropic work of Lord Shaftesbury and has become an iconic landmark in the city.
events.name: Unveiling of the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1893, U.S. President Grover Cleveland underwent a secret operation to remove a cancerous growth from his mouth aboard a yacht. This event was kept from the public to avoid political fallout and concerns about his health.
events.name: Grover Cleveland's secret operation

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1893, a devastating tornado struck the small town of Pomeroy, Iowa, resulting in the deaths of 71 people and injuring over 200. This disaster highlighted the vulnerability of communities to severe weather events.
events.name: Tornado in Pomeroy, Iowa

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1893, Liberal general and politician José Santos Zelaya led a successful revolt in Nicaragua, which resulted in his rise to power. This event marked a significant shift in Nicaraguan politics and the ongoing struggle between Liberal and Conservative factions.
events.name: José Santos Zelaya's revolt in Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1893, the Paknam Incident occurred when two French Navy ships were fired upon by Siamese cannons stationed at Paknam Fort, guarding the Chao Phraya River. This conflict escalated tensions between France and Siam, leading to territorial concessions.
events.name: Paknam Incident

events.enhanced_description: The Corinth Canal was completed on July 25, 1893, providing a crucial shortcut for maritime traffic between the Aegean and Ionian Seas. This engineering marvel significantly reduced travel time for ships and boosted trade in the region.
events.name: Completion of the Corinth Canal

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1893, France introduced the world's first driving licenses under the Paris Police Ordinance, marking a significant step in regulating motor vehicle use. This legislation laid the groundwork for modern driving laws and vehicle registration.
events.name: Introduction of the world's first driving licenses

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1893, the Ibadan area became a British protectorate following a treaty signed by Fijabi, the Baale of Ibadan, with George C. Denton, the British acting Governor of Lagos. This event marked a significant expansion of British colonial influence in Nigeria.
events.name: Ibadan becomes a British protectorate

events.enhanced_description: The Sea Islands hurricane struck on August 27, 1893, affecting Savannah, Georgia, Charleston, South Carolina, and the surrounding Sea Islands, resulting in the deaths of 1,000 to 2,000 people. This catastrophic event highlighted the vulnerability of coastal communities to hurricanes.
events.name: Sea Islands hurricane

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1893, William Ewart Gladstone's Government of Ireland Bill, which aimed to grant self-government to Ireland, was rejected by the U.K. Parliament. This defeat underscored the ongoing political struggles regarding Irish home rule.

image.caption: An Ulster loyalist sticker protesting Irish Home Rule.
image.credit: Unknown. Obviously an Ulster loyalist person or organisation. — A sticker on the book published by Internet Archive at https://archive.org/details/ahistorysiegelo00grahgoog/page/n16
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1919, 26 years after the 1893 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: William Ewart Gladstone's Government of Ireland Bill 1893 rejected

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1893, under pressure from a general strike, the Belgian Federal Parliament enacted general multiple suffrage, a significant step towards expanding voting rights in Belgium. This reform was a response to the growing demands for democratic representation.
events.name: Belgian Federal Parliament enacts general multiple suffrage

events.enhanced_description: The World Parliament of Religions opened on September 11, 1893, in Chicago as part of the World's Columbian Exposition. Bengali Hindu monk Swami Vivekananda received a standing ovation for his address, which emphasized the importance of religious tolerance and understanding.
events.name: World Parliament of Religions opens

events.enhanced_description: American Temperance University began classes on September 12, 1893, in Harriman, Tennessee, aiming to promote temperance and moral education. The institution would operate for 15 years before closing in May 1908.
