events.name: American Temperance University begins classes

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1893, settlers participated in a land run for prime land in the Cherokee Strip in Oklahoma, marking a significant moment in the westward expansion of the United States. This event exemplified the push for settlement in newly available territories.

image.caption: Silver gelatin prints documenting the Cherokee Strip land rush, including “One Minute Before the Start.”
image.credit: The former with verso hand stamp of photographer L.D. Hodge, Arkansas City, KS, and the latter known to be from a negative made by W.S. Prettyman, also of Arkansas City. — Cowan's Auctions
image.date_qualification: The supplied image description identifies photographs documenting the rush and gives September 16, 1893 as their date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Land run in the Cherokee Strip

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1893, New Zealand became the first country in the world to grant women's suffrage, allowing women to vote in parliamentary elections. This landmark decision was a significant milestone in the global women's rights movement.
events.name: New Zealand grants women's suffrage

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1893, brothers Charles and Frank Duryea drove the first gasoline-powered motorcar on public roads in Springfield, Massachusetts. This event marked a pivotal moment in automotive history and the beginning of the motor vehicle era in America.
events.name: First gasoline-powered motorcar in America

events.enhanced_description: The Bahá'í Faith was first publicly introduced in the United States during the World Parliament of Religions held in Chicago, marking a significant moment for interfaith dialogue and the promotion of religious tolerance.
events.name: The Bahá'í Faith is first publicly mentioned in the United States

events.enhanced_description: The World Parliament of Religions concluded its sessions in Chicago, bringing together diverse religious leaders and promoting dialogue among various faiths, significantly influencing the future of interfaith relations.
events.name: The World Parliament of Religions holds its closing meeting

events.enhanced_description: Futebol Clube do Porto, one of the most successful and storied football clubs in Portugal, was founded, marking the beginning of a significant chapter in Portuguese sports history.
events.name: Futebol Clube do Porto is founded

events.enhanced_description: The first car number plates were introduced in Paris, marking a significant development in vehicle registration and identification.
events.name: The first car number plates appear

events.enhanced_description: St Hilda's College, founded for women by Dorothea Beale, welcomed its first students in Oxford, representing a significant advancement in women's education.
events.name: First students enter St Hilda's College, Oxford

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic levee collapse, flash flood, and landslide caused by a strong typhoon struck Kyushu, Shikoku, and western Honshū in Japan, resulting in the tragic loss of 2,044 lives.
events.name: Devastating natural disaster in Japan

events.enhanced_description: American sisters Patty and Mildred J. Hill copyrighted their book 'Song Stories for the Kindergarten,' which included the melody for 'Good Morning to All,' later adapted into the famous 'Happy Birthday to You.'
events.name: Hill sisters copyright their book

events.enhanced_description: The Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization (IMRO) was founded in Thessaloniki by Bulgarians, aiming to liberate Macedonia from Ottoman rule, which would play a crucial role in the Balkan struggles.
events.name: IMRO is founded

events.enhanced_description: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky conducted the first performance of his Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Pathétique, in Saint Petersburg, just nine days before his death, marking a poignant moment in classical music history.
events.name: Tchaikovsky conducts Symphony No. 6

events.enhanced_description: The 1893 World's Fair, also known as the World's Columbian Exposition, closed after showcasing innovations and cultures from around the world, leaving a lasting legacy on American society.
events.name: World's Columbian Exposition closes

events.enhanced_description: During the First Matabele War, the British South Africa Company achieved a decisive victory against the Matabele forces at the Battle of Bembezi, solidifying British control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Bembezi

events.enhanced_description: Colorado became the first state in the United States to grant women the right to vote, a landmark achievement in the women's suffrage movement.
events.name: Colorado women granted the right to vote

events.enhanced_description: The Durand Line was established as the boundary between British India and Afghanistan through a memorandum signed by Sir Mortimer Durand and Abdur Rahman Khan, a decision that would have lasting geopolitical implications.
events.name: The Durand Line is established

events.enhanced_description: FC Basel, one of Switzerland's most successful football clubs, was founded, contributing significantly to the country's football culture.
events.name: FC Basel is founded

events.enhanced_description: The athletic club Královské Vinohrady, which would later be known as Sparta Prague, was founded, marking an important development in Czech sports history.
events.name: Athletic club Královské Vinohrady is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 'The Adventure of the Final Problem', published in December 1893, Arthur Conan Doyle shocked readers by revealing the apparent death of his iconic character Sherlock Holmes at the Reichenbach Falls. This story marked a significant moment in literary history, as it led to widespread public outcry and speculation about the fate of Holmes.
events.name: The Adventure of the Final Problem

events.enhanced_description: In December 1893, Mark Twain's novel 'Pudd'nhead Wilson' began serialization in The Century Magazine, captivating readers with its exploration of identity and race in America. This work is notable for its innovative narrative structure and social commentary.
events.name: Pudd'nhead Wilson Serialization

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1893, during the First Matabele War, the Shangani Patrol of British South Africa Company soldiers was ambushed and annihilated by over 3,000 Matabele warriors. This event highlighted the fierce resistance of the Matabele people against colonial encroachment.
events.name: Shangani Patrol Ambush

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1893, New South Wales abolished plural voting, a significant reform aimed at ensuring fairer representation in elections. This change was part of a broader movement towards electoral reform in Australia.
events.name: Abolition of Plural Voting in New South Wales

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1893, Antonín Dvořák's Symphony No. 9, known as 'From the New World', premiered at Carnegie Hall in New York City, conducted by the composer himself. The symphony received immediate acclaim and has since become one of the most popular orchestral works.
events.name: Premiere of Dvořák's Symphony No. 9

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1893, Evergreen Park, Illinois, was incorporated as a village, marking its establishment as a distinct community. This incorporation was part of the suburban expansion occurring in the Chicago area during this period.
events.name: Incorporation of Evergreen Park

events.enhanced_description: In early 1894, the Donghak Peasant Revolution erupted in Korea, driven by widespread discontent among peasants against oppressive taxation and foreign influence. The uprising prompted military interventions from both China and Japan, escalating tensions in the region.
events.name: Donghak Peasant Revolution begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1894, French anarchist Martial Bourdin died from an accidental detonation of his own bomb near the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. His death highlighted the violent tactics employed by anarchists during this period and the tensions surrounding political dissent.
events.name: Martial Bourdin dies in Greenwich

events.enhanced_description: In May 1894, the Third Plague Pandemic struck Hong Kong, with the bubonic plague breaking out in the Tai Ping Shan area. By the end of the year, the death toll reached 2,552, marking one of the deadliest outbreaks in history.
events.name: Bubonic plague outbreak in Hong Kong

events.enhanced_description: The May Day Riots erupted in Cleveland, Ohio, resulting in the deaths of two individuals, injuries to 40 others, and the arrest of 116 people. The riots were a manifestation of the labor unrest and social tensions prevalent in the post-World War I era.
events.name: May Day Riots in Cleveland

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1894, Sanford B. Dole proclaimed the establishment of the short-lived Republic of Hawaii. This event marked a significant shift in Hawaiian governance following the overthrow of the monarchy.
events.name: Proclamation of the Republic of Hawaii

events.enhanced_description: In 1894, the football club FC La Chaux-de-Fonds was founded in Switzerland. This club has since become an important part of Swiss football history.
events.name: Foundation of FC La Chaux-de-Fonds

events.enhanced_description: In 1894, the discovery of oil on the Osage Indian Reservation transformed the Osage Nation into one of the wealthiest groups in the world. This wealth led to significant changes in their social structure and attracted attention from various external interests, ultimately resulting in exploitation and legal battles over their resources.
events.name: Oil is discovered on the Osage Indian reservation

events.enhanced_description: In 1894, Edward B. Marks and Joe Stern published 'The Little Lost Child,' which became a significant cultural phenomenon in the United States. This waltz was notable for being accompanied by projected images, marking an early form of the music video known as the illustrated song.
events.name: Publication of The Little Lost Child

events.enhanced_description: Spillers Records, founded in 1894 in Cardiff, Wales, is recognized as the world's oldest record shop still in operation. It has played a significant role in the music industry, serving as a cultural hub for music lovers and artists alike.
events.name: Founding of Spillers Records

events.enhanced_description: The Liga Femeilor Române, established in 1894, was the first women's organization in Romania, advocating for women's rights and social issues. This organization marked a significant step towards gender equality in Romanian society.
events.name: Founding of Liga Femeilor Române

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1894, a military alliance was established between the French Third Republic and the Russian Empire, aimed at countering the growing influence of Germany in Europe. This alliance would play a significant role in the geopolitical landscape leading up to World War I.
events.name: Military Alliance between France and Russia

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1894, William Kennedy Dickson received a patent for motion picture film in the United States, marking a pivotal moment in the development of cinema. This invention laid the groundwork for the film industry as we know it today.
events.name: Patent for Motion Picture Film

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1894, New England Telephone and Telegraph installed the first battery-operated telephone switchboard in Lexington, Massachusetts. This innovation represented a significant advancement in telecommunications technology.
events.name: First Battery-Operated Telephone Switchboard

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1894, French anarchist Émile Henry set off a bomb in a Paris café, resulting in one death and twenty injuries. This act of violence was part of a broader wave of anarchist terrorism in Europe during this period.
events.name: Bombing in Paris Café

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1894, peasant unrest erupted in Korea, leading to the Donghak Peasant Revolution, a massive revolt by followers of the Donghak movement. Both China and Japan sent military forces to intervene, claiming to support the Joseon dynasty government.
events.name: Donghak Peasant Revolution

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1894, the Local Government Act came into effect in Britain, reforming local governance by creating urban and rural districts with elected councils. This act also granted women the right to vote and stand in local elections, marking a significant step towards gender equality in politics.
events.name: Local Government Act in Britain

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1894, William Gladstone resigned as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom for the fourth time, marking the end of a significant political career that spanned over four decades. His resignation was influenced by various political pressures and the challenges of managing the Liberal Party during a period of internal strife.
events.name: William Gladstone resigns as British Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1894, Coca-Cola was sold in bottles for the first time, allowing the beverage to reach a wider audience beyond soda fountains. This innovation marked a pivotal moment in the history of soft drinks, contributing to Coca-Cola's rise as a global brand.
events.name: Coca-Cola is sold in bottles for the first time

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1894, a rare astronomical event occurred where Mercury transited the Sun as seen from Venus, and both Mercury and Venus transited the Sun as observed from Saturn. This complex alignment of planets provided valuable data for astronomers studying planetary motion.
events.name: Syzygy of planets occurs

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1894, Jacob Coxey led Coxey's Army, a march of unemployed workers, from Massillon, Ohio, to Washington, D.C. This event marked the first significant protest march in the United States, advocating for government action to address unemployment and economic distress.
events.name: Coxey's Army departs for Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1894, Britain formally established a protectorate over Uganda, marking a significant step in the expansion of British colonial rule in East Africa. This move was part of a broader strategy to control trade routes and resources in the region.
events.name: Britain establishes a protectorate over Uganda

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1894, Manchester City Football Club was officially formed, establishing itself as a prominent football club in England. The club's formation marked the beginning of a rich history in English football, contributing to the sport's development in the region.
events.name: Manchester City Football Club is formed

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1894, a significant strike by bituminous coal miners occurred, leading to the closure of mines across the central United States. This strike was part of a broader labor movement advocating for better working conditions and wages.
events.name: Bituminous coal miners' strike

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1894, Canada's largest known landslide occurred in Saint-Alban, Quebec, displacing approximately 185 million cubic meters of rock and dirt. This geological event left a significant scar on the landscape, highlighting the power of natural forces.
events.name: Canada's largest landslide occurs

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1894, Sanford B. Dole proclaimed the establishment of the Republic of Hawaii, following the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy. This event marked a significant shift in Hawaiian governance and set the stage for eventual annexation by the United States.
events.name: Republic of Hawaii proclaimed

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1894, a devastating fire broke out at the site of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, destroying most of the remaining buildings. This incident marked the end of an important chapter in Chicago's architectural history.
events.name: Fire at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition site

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1894, the United Kingdom and Japan signed the Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, which marked a significant diplomatic milestone. This treaty established a framework for trade and mutual respect, with the UK being the first Western nation to relinquish extraterritorial rights in Japan.
events.name: Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1894, the Paris–Rouen Competition for Horseless Carriages took place, marking the first automobile competition in history. This event showcased the burgeoning technology of motor vehicles and set the stage for the future of automotive innovation.
events.name: Paris–Rouen Competition for Horseless Carriages held

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1894, war was declared between the Qing Empire of China and the Empire of Japan, primarily over their competing interests in Korea. This conflict marked the beginning of the First Sino-Japanese War, which would significantly alter the balance of power in East Asia.
events.name: First Sino-Japanese War Declaration

events.enhanced_description: The double homicide at Schagen on August 11, 1894, was a notable criminal case in the Netherlands that shocked the local community. The investigation and trial that followed became a topic of public interest and discussion regarding crime and justice in Dutch society.
events.name: Double homicide at Schagen

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1894, Italian anarchist Sante Geronimo Caserio was executed by guillotine in Lyon for the assassination of French President Sadi Carnot. This event highlighted the tensions between anarchist movements and state authority in late 19th-century Europe.
events.name: Execution of Sante Geronimo Caserio

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1894, New Zealand enacted the world's first minimum wage law through the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act. This landmark legislation aimed to improve working conditions and set a precedent for labor rights globally.
events.name: New Zealand Minimum Wage Law

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1894, the Great Hinckley Fire swept through Hinckley, Minnesota, resulting in the deaths of over 450 people. This catastrophic event was one of the deadliest forest fires in U.S. history, leading to significant changes in fire management and prevention policies.
events.name: Great Hinckley Fire

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1894, approximately 12,000 tailors in New York City went on strike to protest against sweatshop working conditions. This significant labor action highlighted the growing movement for workers' rights and better labor standards in the United States.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Tailors' Strike in New York City

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1894, composer Richard Strauss married soprano Pauline De Ahna in Munich. Their partnership would significantly influence Strauss's musical career and the development of German opera.
events.name: Marriage of Richard Strauss and Pauline De Ahna

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1894, the SS Ohio collided with the schooner barge Ironton in Lake Huron, resulting in the sinking of the Ironton. While the crew of the Ohio was rescued, five members of the Ironton's crew, including the captain, tragically lost their lives.
events.name: Collision of SS Ohio and Ironton

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1894, Petrópolis was designated as the capital of the Brazilian state of Rio de Janeiro, a status it would hold until 1902. This change reflected the city's growing importance in the region.
events.name: Petrópolis Becomes Capital of Rio de Janeiro

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1894, French Army officer Alfred Dreyfus was arrested on charges of spying, marking the beginning of the Dreyfus Affair. This scandal would expose deep-seated anti-Semitism in France and lead to significant political and social upheaval.
events.name: Dreyfus Affair: Arrest of Alfred Dreyfus

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1894, Domenico Menegatti obtained a patent for a procedure to produce pandoro industrially. This innovation contributed to the popularization of this traditional Italian Christmas cake.
events.name: Domenico Menegatti's Patent for Pandoro

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1894, Republicans achieved a landslide victory in the United States House of Representatives elections, setting the stage for the pivotal presidential election of 1896. This shift in political power reflected growing discontent with the Democratic administration.
events.name: Republicans Win House Elections

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1894, the Masonic Grande Loge de France was founded, splitting from the older Grand Orient de France. This event marked a significant moment in the history of Freemasonry in France.
events.name: Foundation of the Grande Loge de France

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1894, during the First Sino-Japanese War, Japanese troops secured a decisive victory at the Battle of Lushunkou, capturing the port city and initiating the Port Arthur massacre, which resulted in the deaths of over 1,000 Chinese servicemen and civilians.
events.name: Battle of Lushunkou

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1894, Nicholas II of Russia married Alix of Hesse in a grand ceremony at the Grand Church of the Winter Palace in Saint Petersburg. This royal union would have significant implications for the Russian monarchy and its future.
events.name: Wedding of Nicholas II and Alix of Hesse

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1894, Kate Chopin's feminist short story 'The Story of an Hour' was first published in the American magazine Vogue. This work is now considered a classic of feminist literature, exploring themes of freedom and identity.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Publication of 'The Story of an Hour'

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1894, women in South Australia became the first in Australia to gain the right to vote and to be elected to Parliament, effective from 1895. This milestone was the result of decades of activism and set a precedent for women's rights in the country.
events.name: Women's Suffrage in South Australia

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1894, Mackenzie Bowell was appointed as Canada's fifth prime minister. His tenure was marked by political challenges and internal divisions within the Conservative Party.
events.name: Mackenzie Bowell Becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1894, Alfred Dreyfus was convicted of treason in a highly publicized trial that revealed deep-seated anti-Semitism within the French military and society. This event sparked widespread controversy and became a pivotal moment in French history.
events.name: Dreyfus Affair: Conviction of Alfred Dreyfus

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in United States v. E. C. Knight Co. that Congress could not regulate manufacturing under the Sherman Antitrust Act. This landmark decision limited federal power over monopolies and shaped future antitrust legislation.
events.name: United States v. E. C. Knight Co.

events.enhanced_description: The S.S. Chicora sank in a storm on Lake Michigan in 1895, resulting in the loss of all 21 crew members and one passenger. This maritime disaster highlighted the perils of navigation on the Great Lakes.
events.name: Sinking of S.S. Chicora

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, U.S. President Grover Cleveland signed a bill advocating for arbitration to resolve the territorial dispute between Venezuela and Great Britain. This event underscored the United States' growing role in international diplomacy and its commitment to the Monroe Doctrine.
events.name: Venezuelan crisis of 1895

events.enhanced_description: Bridget Cleary was murdered by her husband, Michael Cleary, in a tragic case that highlighted the intersection of folklore and domestic violence in late 19th-century Ireland. Michael claimed he believed he had killed a changeling, a fairy substitute for his wife, after she had been abducted by fairies, leading to his conviction for manslaughter.
events.name: Bridget Cleary is killed

events.enhanced_description: The Heian Shrine, a significant Shinto shrine in Kyoto, was completed in 1895 to commemorate the 1100th anniversary of the founding of the city. The shrine is known for its beautiful gardens and architecture that reflects the Heian period style.
events.name: Heian Shrine is completed

events.enhanced_description: In December 1895, Ottoman troops committed a horrific massacre in Urfa, where they burned approximately 3,000 Armenians alive. This event marked a significant and tragic moment in the history of the Armenian people and foreshadowed the larger atrocities that would occur in the years to come.
events.name: Ottoman troops burn 3,000 Armenians alive in Urfa

events.enhanced_description: In January 1895, Rudyard Kipling published the story 'Mowgli Leaves the Jungle Forever' in The Cosmopolitan illustrated magazine in the United States. This story was later included in his collection 'The Second Jungle Book', which was published in England in November of the same year.
events.name: Publication of 'Mowgli Leaves the Jungle Forever'

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the London School of Economics (LSE) held its first classes in London, England. Founded by Beatrice and Sidney Webb, LSE became a leading institution for social sciences and economics education.
events.name: London School of Economics holds first classes

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, George Washington Vanderbilt II officially opened his Biltmore Estate, inviting family and guests to celebrate his new home in Asheville, North Carolina. This estate is renowned for its architecture and gardens, becoming a significant tourist attraction.
events.name: George Washington Vanderbilt II opens Biltmore Estate

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, brothers Wilhelm and Carl Fein developed the world's first portable handheld electric drill in Germany. This innovation revolutionized construction and manufacturing processes, making drilling tasks more efficient.
events.name: Development of the first portable handheld electric drill

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, Konstantin Tsiolkovsky proposed the concept of a space elevator, a revolutionary idea that suggested a structure extending from the Earth's surface into space. This concept has inspired future generations of scientists and engineers in the field of space exploration.
events.name: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky proposes a space elevator

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the Swarovski Company was founded in the Austrian Tyrol by Armand Kosman, Franz Weis, and Daniel Swarovski for the production of crystal glass. This company would grow to become a leading name in luxury crystal products.
events.name: Foundation of Swarovski Company

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the name 'HP Sauce' was first registered in the United Kingdom for a brown sauce. This condiment has since become a staple in British cuisine.

image.caption: HP Sauce signage from the former Aston factory, exhibited at the Midlands Arts Centre.
image.credit: Andy Mabbett — Own work
image.date_qualification: The sign is contextual evidence of HP Sauce and its former factory, not a depiction of the 1895 registration. Image date: 2010-06-24.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Registration of HP Sauce

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the Duck Reach Power Station opened in Tasmania, becoming the first publicly owned hydroelectric plant in the Southern Hemisphere. This facility marked a significant advancement in renewable energy production.

image.caption: Archival photograph of Duck Reach Power Station, attributed to the Spurling cabinet.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — National Library of Australia. nla.pic-an21697618-176 PIC LOC RR
image.date_qualification: A historical site photograph dated 1906–1930 in the image description; the supplied date metadata specifies before 1930. It does not establish that the photograph records the 1895 opening.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Duck Reach Power Station opens

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the first sample fair (Mustermesse) was held in Leipzig, Germany. This event showcased various products and innovations, contributing to Leipzig's reputation as a center for trade and commerce.
events.name: First sample fair held at Leipzig

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the first Boxer dog club was established in Germany, marking the formal recognition and promotion of the Boxer breed. This club played a crucial role in the breed's development and popularity.
events.name: First Boxer dog club established

events.enhanced_description: In 1895, the Raiffeisen model of Cooperative Credit and Saving Bank was founded in the Netherlands. This model laid the groundwork for cooperative banking and has influenced financial services worldwide.
events.name: Raiffeisen model of Cooperative Credit and Saving Bank founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1895, French officer Alfred Dreyfus was wrongfully stripped of his rank and sentenced to life imprisonment on Devil's Island due to a false charge of treason. This event sparked a major political scandal in France, leading to widespread debates about anti-Semitism and justice.

image.caption: Portrait of Alfred Dreyfus.
image.credit: Aron Gerschel — http://media.web.britannica.com/eb-media/45/8245-050-75EEC0A6.jpg
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated circa 1894, preceding his January 1895 sentencing; it is not a depiction of the sentencing event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Dreyfus Affair: Alfred Dreyfus sentenced

events.enhanced_description: The Wilcox Rebellion began on January 6, 1895, when royalist troops, led by Robert Wilcox, landed at Waikiki Beach in an attempt to overthrow the Republic of Hawaii and restore the monarchy. The rebellion lasted three days before the royalists were captured, marking a significant moment in Hawaiian history.

locations.name: Waikiki Beach, Oahu, Hawaii, United States

events.name: Wilcox Rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1895, Britain's National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty was founded by Octavia Hill, Robert Hunter, and Canon Hardwicke Rawnsley. This organization aimed to preserve historic sites and natural beauty in the UK, setting a precedent for conservation efforts worldwide.
events.name: Founding of Britain's National Trust

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1895, during the First Italo-Ethiopian War, Italian forces achieved a decisive victory over Ethiopian troops at the Battle of Coatit. This battle was part of Italy's efforts to expand its colonial presence in East Africa.
events.name: Battle of Coatit

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1895, a catastrophic warehouse fire and subsequent dynamite explosion in Butte, Montana, resulted in the deaths of 57 individuals, including 13 firefighters. This tragic event highlighted the dangers of industrial accidents during this period.
events.name: Butte warehouse fire and explosion

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1895, a devastating 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck near Quchan in northeastern Iran, resulting in at least 1,000 fatalities. This natural disaster had a profound impact on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Earthquake in Iran

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1895, former Queen Liliʻuokalani of Hawaii abdicated her claim to the throne and pledged allegiance to the Republic of Hawaii. This marked the end of efforts to restore the Hawaiian monarchy following the overthrow of her government in 1893.

image.caption: Sepia-toned gelatin silver portrait of Liliʻuokalani, the last sovereign of the Hawaiian Kingdom.
image.credit: James J. Williams / Adam Cuerden — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ppmsca.53150 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated circa 1891, two years before the overthrow and several years before her 1895 abdication; it is not a depiction of the abdication itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Abdication of Queen Liliʻuokalani

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1895, the German ocean liner SS Elbe sank after colliding with the British steamer SS Crathie, resulting in the deaths of 334 people. The tragedy underscored the dangers of maritime travel during this era.

locations.name: North Sea, near the coast of Germany

events.name: Sinking of SS Elbe

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1895, J. P. Morgan and the Rothschild banking family loaned $65 million worth of gold to the U.S. Treasury, averting a financial crisis. This event demonstrated the influence of private banking on government finances during this period.
events.name: J. P. Morgan and Rothschilds loan to U.S. Treasury

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1895, the first rebellions of the Cuban War of Independence erupted, marking a significant struggle against Spanish colonial rule. This conflict would eventually lead to Cuba's independence.
events.name: First rebellions of the Cuban War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1895, Munich implemented regulations requiring bicyclists to pass a test and display license plates. This was one of the early instances of traffic regulation in urban areas, reflecting the growing popularity of bicycles.
events.name: Bicyclist regulations in Munich

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1895, Japanese troops captured Liaoyang during the First Sino-Japanese War, marking a significant advance in Japan's military campaign against China. This victory contributed to Japan's emergence as a major world power.
events.name: Japanese capture of Liaoyang

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1895, Bridget Cleary was murdered by her husband, Michael, in County Tipperary, Ireland. He claimed to have killed a changeling, believing that fairies had abducted his wife and replaced her with a doppelgänger, highlighting the intersection of folklore and domestic violence.
events.name: Bridget Cleary murder case

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1895, the world's first gasoline bus route was inaugurated in Germany, connecting the towns of Siegen and Netphen. This marked a significant advancement in public transportation and the use of motor vehicles.
events.name: First gasoline bus route

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière presented what is considered the first projected celluloid film, 'Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory,' in Paris. This event is often regarded as the birth of cinema and had a lasting impact on the film industry.
events.name: First projected film presentation by Lumière brothers

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1895, Rudolf Diesel patented the Diesel engine in Germany, a revolutionary advancement in engine technology. This invention would later transform transportation and industry worldwide.
events.name: Rudolf Diesel patents the Diesel engine

events.enhanced_description: Oscar Wilde was arrested in London for 'gross indecency' after losing a libel case against the Marquess of Queensberry, who had accused him of being homosexual. This event marked a significant moment in Wilde's life, leading to his imprisonment and the eventual decline of his literary career.

image.caption: Retrospective newspaper illustration depicting scenes from Oscar Wilde’s trial.
image.credit: Illustrated Police News , a newspaper from the 19th century. — https://blog.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/2020/06/09/trial-of-oscar-wilde/
image.date_qualification: Published 20 April 1895, after the arrest; depicts trial scenes, not the arrest itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Oscar Wilde is arrested

events.enhanced_description: Fridtjof Nansen's Fram expedition reached a record latitude of 86°13.6'N in the Arctic, surpassing previous records for northern exploration. This achievement contributed significantly to the understanding of Arctic geography and climate.
events.name: Nansen's Fram expedition reaches Farthest North

events.enhanced_description: A significant earthquake struck Ljubljana, the capital of Carniola (now Slovenia), causing extensive damage to buildings and infrastructure. This event highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: Major earthquake damages Ljubljana

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed, formally ending the First Sino-Japanese War. Under the terms of the treaty, China recognized Korea's independence and ceded Taiwan and the Pescadores Islands to Japan, marking a significant shift in power in East Asia.
events.name: Treaty of Shimonoseki is signed

events.enhanced_description: The Gongche Shangshu movement saw 603 candidates sign a petition against the Treaty of Shimonoseki, expressing widespread discontent with the terms imposed on China. This movement was part of a larger wave of nationalism and reform in late Qing China.
events.name: Gongche Shangshu movement petition

events.enhanced_description: The Spiral Bridge was constructed to carry U.S. Route 61 over the Mississippi River at Hastings, Minnesota. This unique bridge design became a notable landmark before its demolition in 1951.
events.name: Spiral Bridge construction

events.enhanced_description: Thousands of scholars and citizens in Beijing protested against the Treaty of Shimonoseki as part of the Gongche Shangshu movement. This demonstration reflected the growing nationalist sentiments and opposition to foreign influence in China.
events.name: Gongche Shangshu movement protests

events.enhanced_description: During the Yaroslavl Great Manufacture strike, thirteen workers were killed by soldiers of the Russian Empire, highlighting the tensions between labor movements and the state. This incident underscored the growing unrest in Russia leading up to the 1905 Revolution.
events.name: Yaroslavl Great Manufacture strike

events.enhanced_description: The first motor race in Italy took place on a course from Turin to Asti and back, covering a total of 93 km. It was a landmark event in automotive history, with Simone Federman winning in a Daimler Omnibus at an average speed of 15.5 km/h.
events.name: First motor race in Italy

events.enhanced_description: Anti-Japanese officials in Taiwan, led by Tang Jingsong, declared independence from the Qing dynasty, forming the short-lived Republic of Formosa. This declaration was a response to Japan's victory in the First Sino-Japanese War and the subsequent Treaty of Shimonoseki.
events.name: Republic of Formosa declared

events.enhanced_description: Oscar Wilde was convicted in London of 'unlawfully committing acts of gross indecency' under the Labouchere Amendment, receiving a two-year sentence of hard labor. This conviction had a profound impact on his life and work, leading to his eventual decline.
events.name: Oscar Wilde convicted

events.enhanced_description: The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in In re Debs that the federal government had the right to regulate interstate commerce, thereby legalizing the military suppression of the Pullman Strike. This decision underscored the government's stance against labor movements during this period.

image.caption: Group portrait of the Fuller Court justices of the United States Supreme Court.
image.credit: Clarence Dodge (1847-1914) — https://www.supremecourt.gov/visiting/exhibitions/GroupPhotoExhibit/Section2.aspx
image.date_qualification: The portrait depicts the Supreme Court justices in 1894, before the In re Debs decision; it is contextual, not a photograph of the decision.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: In re Debs decision

events.enhanced_description: The Liberal Revolution began in Ecuador, intensifying the ongoing civil war in the country. This movement aimed to challenge conservative power and promote liberal reforms, significantly shaping Ecuador's political landscape.
events.name: Liberal Revolution begins in Ecuador

events.enhanced_description: Britain annexed Tongaland, a territory located between Zululand and Mozambique, as part of its imperial expansion in Southern Africa. This annexation was part of the broader context of colonial rule and the establishment of British authority in the region.
events.name: Britain annexes Tongaland

events.enhanced_description: The Kiel Canal, which connects the North Sea to the Baltic Sea across the base of the Jutland peninsula, was officially opened in 1895. This engineering marvel significantly shortened maritime travel times and enhanced trade routes in Northern Europe.
events.name: Kiel Canal officially opened

events.enhanced_description: The United States Court of Private Land Claims ruled that James Reavis's claim to the Barony of Arizona was 'wholly fictitious and fraudulent.' This ruling was significant in the context of land claims and property rights in the American West.
events.name: James Reavis's claim ruled fictitious

events.enhanced_description: Oldham Athletic A.F.C. was established in 1895, becoming one of the oldest professional football clubs in England. The club has a rich history and has played a significant role in the development of football in the region.
events.name: Oldham Athletic A.F.C. founded

events.enhanced_description: The Doukhobors, a spiritual and pacifist group, culminated their protests against military conscription in the South Caucasus with the 'burning of the arms' event. This act of defiance was emblematic of their commitment to non-violence and resistance to state authority.
events.name: Doukhobors' pacifist protests

events.enhanced_description: Archie MacLaren set a record for the highest innings in the English County Championship by scoring 424 runs for Lancashire against Somerset at Taunton. This remarkable achievement stood as a record until 1994.
events.name: Archie MacLaren's cricket record

events.enhanced_description: The Basque Nationalist Party (Euzko Alderdi Jeltzalea) was founded by Sabino Arana in 1895, marking a significant moment in the political history of the Basque Country. This party aimed to promote Basque nationalism and self-determination.
events.name: Basque Nationalist Party founded

events.enhanced_description: The Aljaž Tower, a symbol of Slovenian national identity, was erected on Mount Triglav in 1895. This tower serves as a testament to the cultural heritage and natural beauty of Slovenia.
events.name: Aljaž Tower erected

events.enhanced_description: The first indoor promenade concert, which would evolve into The Proms, was held at Queen's Hall in London on August 10, 1895. Conducted by Henry Wood, this event marked a significant moment in the history of classical music in Britain.
events.name: First indoor promenade concert

events.enhanced_description: John Wesley Hardin, a notorious American outlaw and murderer, was killed on August 19, 1895, by an off-duty policeman in a saloon in El Paso, Texas. His violent life and death reflect the tumultuous nature of the American frontier during that era.
events.name: John Wesley Hardin killed

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1895, the Northern Rugby Football Union was formed at a meeting of 21 rugby clubs at the George Hotel in Huddersfield. This event laid the foundation for the professional sport of rugby league football in England.
events.name: Northern Rugby Football Union formed

events.enhanced_description: Shelbourne F.C. was founded in Dublin, Ireland, in 1895, becoming one of the oldest and most successful football clubs in the country. The club has a storied history and has contributed significantly to Irish football.
events.name: Shelbourne F.C. founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1895, the first professional American football game was played in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, between the Latrobe YMCA and the Jeannette Athletic Club, marking a significant milestone in the history of American sports.
events.name: First professional American football game

events.enhanced_description: The first game of what would become known as rugby league football was played on September 7, 1895, in England, marking the beginning of the 1895-96 Northern Rugby Football Union season and the establishment of a new era in rugby.
events.name: First rugby league football game

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1895, Daniel David Palmer performed the first chiropractic spinal adjustment on Harvey Lillard, who had been suffering from partial deafness. This event marked the inception of chiropractic care as a recognized health practice.
events.name: First chiropractic spinal adjustment

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1895, French troops captured Antananarivo, the capital of Madagascar, marking a significant step in the French colonization of the island. This event led to the establishment of French rule over Madagascar.
events.name: French troops capture Antananarivo

events.enhanced_description: Peiyang University, the predecessor of Tianjin University, was founded on October 2, 1895, as an institution of higher education in Qing dynasty China. It played a crucial role in modernizing Chinese education.
events.name: Peiyang University founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1895, the Automobile Club de France sponsored the longest race to date, a 1,710 km event from Bordeaux to Agen and back. This event is considered the first rally and showcased the burgeoning automobile industry.
events.name: Automobile Club de France race

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1895, Queen Min, the queen consort of Joseon Korea, was assassinated by Japanese agents at her residence within Gyeongbokgung Palace. This event marked a significant moment in Korean history, reflecting the tensions between Korea and Japan.
events.name: Queen Min assassinated

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1895, the city of Tainan, the last stronghold of the Republic of Formosa, capitulated to Japanese forces. This event marked the end of the short-lived republic and the beginning of Taiwan's era under Japanese rule.
events.name: Tainan capitulates to Japan

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1895, a major earthquake occurred near Charleston, Missouri, in the New Madrid Seismic Zone. This earthquake raised awareness of seismic activity in the region, which continues to be monitored for earthquake risk.
events.name: 1895 Charleston earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1895, Max Skladanowsky and his brother Emil presented a short film at the Berlin Wintergarten theatre using their developed movie projector. This event is considered a significant milestone in the history of cinema.
events.name: Skladanowsky brothers present short film

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1895, George B. Selden was granted the first U.S. patent for an automobile. This patent laid the groundwork for the automotive industry in the United States.
events.name: George B. Selden granted patent

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered the type of electromagnetic radiation that would later be known as X-rays. This groundbreaking discovery revolutionized medical imaging and diagnostics.
events.name: Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1895, Flamengo, a well-known professional football club, was officially founded in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The club has since become one of the most successful and popular teams in Brazilian football.
events.name: Flamengo founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1895, Oscar Hammerstein opened the Olympia Theatre, the first theatre to be built in New York City's Times Square district. This venue played a significant role in the development of American theater.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Olympia Theatre opens

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1895, Alfred Nobel signed his last will and testament at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, setting aside his estate to establish the Nobel Prize after his death. This act would have a lasting impact on the fields of science, literature, and peace.
events.name: Alfred Nobel signs will

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1895, the Chicago Times-Herald sponsored the first American automobile race in history, which sparked significant interest in the automobile industry across the United States.
events.name: Chicago Times-Herald race

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1895, during the First Italo-Ethiopian War, a corps of 2,350 Italian troops, primarily composed of Askari soldiers, faced a crushing defeat against an overwhelming force of 30,000 Abyssinian troops at Amba Alagi. This battle significantly impacted Italy's colonial ambitions in Africa.
events.name: Battle of Amba Alagi

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1895, Svante Arrhenius presented his groundbreaking paper titled 'On the Influence of Carbonic Acid in the Air Upon The Temperature of the Ground' to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. This work laid the foundation for understanding the greenhouse effect and its implications for global climate change.
events.name: Svante Arrhenius presents paper on Greenhouse effect

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1895, the railways of the Cape of Good Hope, Colony of Natal, the Orange Free State, the South African Republic, and southern Mozambique were linked at Union Junction near Alberton. This significant railway development facilitated trade and transportation across the region.
events.name: Union Junction railway linking

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1895, the Laurin & Klement automobile brand was founded in central Bohemia, initially as a bicycle manufacturer. This company would later evolve into Škoda Auto, becoming one of the leading automobile manufacturers in Europe.
events.name: Foundation of Laurin & Klement

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1895, the Kingstown lifeboat disaster occurred when a lifeboat capsized while attempting to rescue the crew of the Palme off the coast of Kingstown (modern-day Dún Laoghaire), resulting in the loss of 15 crew members. This tragedy highlighted the dangers faced by lifeboat crews in maritime rescue operations.
events.name: Kingstown lifeboat disaster

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière conducted what is considered the first commercial public screening of projected moving picture films at the Salon Indien du Grand Café in Paris. This event marked a pivotal moment in the history of cinema and entertainment.
events.name: First commercial public screening of films

events.enhanced_description: The Yaqui Uprising was a series of armed conflicts between the Yaqui people and the Mexican government, primarily occurring in the states of Sonora and Arizona. This conflict was rooted in the Yaqui's resistance to land dispossession and cultural assimilation, leading to a prolonged struggle for autonomy.
events.name: Yaqui Uprising

events.enhanced_description: Svante Arrhenius published his groundbreaking 'greenhouse law', predicting that emissions of carbon dioxide from fossil fuels could lead to global warming. This early insight into climate science laid the groundwork for future research on climate change.
events.name: Svante Arrhenius publishes greenhouse law

events.enhanced_description: In 1896, a group of 12 purely industrial stocks was selected to form the Dow Jones Industrial Average, marking a pivotal moment in the history of stock market indices. This index was the first to exclusively represent industrial shares, reflecting the economic landscape of the time.
events.name: Formation of the Dow Jones Industrial Average

events.enhanced_description: In January 1896, following the conclusion of the Fourth Anglo-Ashanti War, Britain established a Protectorate over the Ashanti people, effectively ending their sovereignty. This marked a significant step in British colonial expansion in West Africa.
events.name: Britain establishes a Protectorate over the Ashanti people concluding the Fourth Anglo-Ashanti War

events.enhanced_description: In 1896, Italy and France signed a treaty that effectively recognized Tunisia as a French protectorate, marking a significant shift in colonial power dynamics in North Africa. This agreement was part of a broader strategy by both nations to solidify their influence in the region.
events.name: Italy and France sign a treaty whereby Italy virtually recognizes Tunisia as a French dependency

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1896, the Jameson Raid came to an end when Leander Starr Jameson surrendered to the Boers in Johannesburg. This failed raid aimed to incite an uprising among British settlers in the Transvaal and had significant political repercussions for Cecil Rhodes.
events.name: Jameson Raid ends

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1896, Utah was admitted as the 45th state of the United States. This admission followed a long struggle for statehood, influenced by the region's unique cultural and religious history.
events.name: Utah admitted as 45th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1896, an Austrian newspaper reported Wilhelm Röntgen's groundbreaking discovery of a type of electromagnetic radiation, which would later be known as X-rays. This discovery revolutionized medical imaging and diagnostics.
events.name: Wilhelm Röntgen's discovery of X-rays reported

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1896, Cecil Rhodes was forced to resign as Prime Minister of the Cape of Good Hope due to his involvement in the failed Jameson Raid. This event marked a significant turning point in his political career and the history of British colonialism in southern Africa.
events.name: Cecil Rhodes resigns as Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: Fannie Farmer, an influential American culinary expert, published her first cookbook, which standardized recipes and cooking techniques, making them accessible to the general public. Her work laid the foundation for modern American cooking and culinary education.
events.name: Fannie Farmer publishes her first cookbook

events.enhanced_description: H. L. Smith made history by taking the first X-ray photograph, marking a significant advancement in medical imaging and diagnostics. This innovation paved the way for the use of X-rays in medicine, revolutionizing how doctors diagnose and treat patients.
events.name: H. L. Smith takes the first X-ray photograph

events.enhanced_description: Devonport High School for Boys was established in Plymouth, England, providing a new educational institution for boys in the area. The school has since become known for its academic excellence and contribution to the local community.
events.name: Devonport High School for Boys is founded

events.enhanced_description: During the Fourth Anglo-Ashanti War, British forces entered the Ashanti capital of Kumasi, leading to the deposition of Asantehene Agyeman Prempeh I. This event marked a significant moment in the British colonial expansion in West Africa.
events.name: Fourth Anglo-Ashanti War: British redcoats enter Kumasi

events.enhanced_description: Walter Arnold became the first person to be fined for speeding in East Peckham, Kent, when he was caught driving at 8 mph, exceeding the urban speed limit of 2 mph. This incident marked the beginning of traffic law enforcement in the United Kingdom.

locations.name: East Peckham, Kent, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Walter Arnold fined for speeding

events.enhanced_description: Giacomo Puccini's opera 'La bohème' premiered in Turin, Italy, captivating audiences with its poignant story of love and loss among young artists in Paris. The opera has since become one of the most performed works in the operatic repertoire.
events.name: Puccini's opera La bohème premieres

events.enhanced_description: Oscar Wilde's play 'Salomé' premiered in Paris while he was imprisoned, showcasing his literary genius and the themes of desire and betrayal. The play's bold content and innovative structure contributed to its lasting impact on theater.
events.name: Oscar Wilde's play Salomé premieres

events.enhanced_description: The Braamfontein Explosion occurred when a train carrying 56 tons of dynamite exploded in Johannesburg, resulting in the deaths of over 78 people. This tragic event highlighted the dangers of industrial transportation and led to increased safety regulations.
events.name: Braamfontein Explosion

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Adwa was a decisive conflict in which Ethiopian forces, led by Emperor Menelik II, successfully defended their independence against Italian invasion, marking a significant victory for African sovereignty. This battle ended the First Italo-Ethiopian War.
events.name: Battle of Adwa

events.enhanced_description: Adolf Brand began publishing 'Der Eigene', the world's first magazine oriented towards male homosexuality, in Berlin. This publication played a crucial role in the early LGBTQ+ rights movement and provided a platform for gay culture and discourse.
events.name: Publication of Der Eigene

events.enhanced_description: In response to national outrage following the defeat at the Battle of Adwa, Italian Prime Minister Francesco Crispi resigned from his position. His resignation reflected the political turmoil and public dissatisfaction with the government's handling of the war.

image.caption: Henri Meyer’s caricature of Francesco Crispi, depicting him in connection with the failure at Makallè.
image.credit: H. Meyer (1844-1899) — http://it.wahooart.com/@@/9DHDEC-Henri-Meyer-Caricatura-di-Francesco-Crispi
image.date_qualification: Image dated 1896; it is not established as depicting the resignation itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francesco Crispi resigns

events.enhanced_description: The Royal College of St Patrick in Maynooth was granted the status of pontifical university by the Holy See, enhancing its reputation and authority in theological education. This recognition marked a significant milestone in the institution's history.
events.name: Royal College of St Patrick granted pontifical status

events.enhanced_description: The first known women's basketball game was played between Stanford University and the University of California, Berkeley, marking a significant moment in the history of women's sports. This event helped to promote women's participation in athletics and paved the way for future developments in women's basketball.
events.name: First known women's basketball game

events.enhanced_description: The opening ceremonies of the 1896 Summer Olympics were held in Athens, Greece, marking the revival of the ancient Olympic Games. This event was significant in promoting international sports and fostering a spirit of global unity.
events.name: Opening ceremonies of the 1896 Summer Olympics

events.enhanced_description: The National Farm School, which later became Delaware Valley College, was chartered in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, to provide agricultural education. This institution has played a vital role in advancing agricultural practices and education in the region.
events.name: National Farm School chartered

events.enhanced_description: Blackpool Pleasure Beach, a popular amusement park known as 'Britain's Biggest Tourist Attraction', was founded by Alderman William George Bean. The park has since become a staple of British seaside culture, attracting millions of visitors each year.
events.name: Blackpool Pleasure Beach founded

events.enhanced_description: In a remarkable cricket match against Warwickshire, Yorkshire set a still-standing County Championship record by accumulating an innings total of 887. This achievement remains a highlight in the history of English cricket.
events.name: Yorkshire sets County Championship record

events.enhanced_description: The Franchise Bill was passed by the Legislative Assembly of the Colony of Natal, which effectively disfranchised natives of other countries. This legislation reflected the racial tensions and discriminatory practices prevalent in colonial South Africa.
events.name: Franchise Bill passed in Natal

events.enhanced_description: In the landmark case Plessy v. Ferguson, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the doctrine of 'separate but equal', legitimizing racial segregation in public facilities. This ruling had profound implications for civil rights in the United States for decades to come.
events.name: Plessy v. Ferguson decision

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1896, during the coronation festivities of Emperor Nicholas II, a crowd crush at Khodynka Field resulted in the deaths of at least 1,200 people. This tragic event highlighted the dangers of large public gatherings and had a lasting impact on Russian society.

locations.name: Khodynka Field, Moscow, Moscow Oblast, Russia

events.name: Khodynka Tragedy

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Nicholas II and Alexandra Feodorovna took place in the Dormition Cathedral in Moscow, marking the last coronation of the Russian monarch. This event was attended by various dignitaries, including Chinese official Li Hongzhang, symbolizing international relations of the time.
events.name: Coronation of Nicholas II and Alexandra Feodorovna

events.enhanced_description: The St. Louis–East St. Louis tornado struck, becoming the costliest and third deadliest tornado in U.S. history. It devastated a mile-wide swath of downtown St. Louis, resulting in over 255 fatalities and significant property damage.
events.name: St. Louis–East St. Louis tornado

events.enhanced_description: Henry Ford completed the Ford Quadricycle, his first vehicle, which marked the beginning of his journey to revolutionize the automotive industry. This invention laid the groundwork for Ford's future success and the mass production of automobiles.
events.name: Completion of the Ford Quadricycle

events.enhanced_description: During the Mahdist War, British and Egyptian troops achieved victory at the Battle of Ferkeh. This battle was part of the larger conflict against the Mahdist forces in Sudan, contributing to British colonial control in the region.

image.caption: Illustration of Egyptian troops storming a Mahdist-held village at Ferkeh.
image.credit: Archibald Forbes , Arthur Griffiths and others. — This file is from the Mechanical Curator collection , a set of over 1 million images scanned from out-of-copyright books and released to Flickr Commons by the British Library in London, England. View image on Flickr View all images from book View catalogue entry for book .
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1895; it is an illustration, not a contemporary photograph of the 7 June 1896 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Ferkeh

events.enhanced_description: J. T. Hearne set a record for the earliest date of taking 100 wickets in cricket, a milestone in the sport's history. This achievement was later equalled by Charlie Parker in 1931, showcasing Hearne's exceptional talent.
events.name: J. T. Hearne sets cricket record

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1896, a massive 8.5 Mw earthquake struck off the Sanriku Coast of northeastern Japan, triggering a devastating tsunami that resulted in the deaths of approximately 22,000 people. This disaster highlighted the vulnerability of coastal communities to seismic activity and tsunamis in the region.
events.name: Sanriku earthquake and tsunami

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1896, the New York Telephone Company was established, succeeding the Metropolitan Telephone and Telegraph Company. This company was created to consolidate and control telephone service within New York City, marking a significant development in telecommunications.
events.name: Formation of the New York Telephone Company

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1896, Liberal leader Wilfrid Laurier defeated Conservative leader Charles Tupper in the Canadian federal elections, becoming the first Francophone Prime Minister of Canada. His leadership marked a significant shift in Canadian politics and representation.
events.name: Wilfrid Laurier's election victory

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1896, an explosion occurred in the Newton Coal Company's Twin Shaft Mine in Pittston, Pennsylvania, leading to a catastrophic cave-in that killed 58 miners. This disaster underscored the dangers of coal mining during this period.
events.name: Twin Shaft disaster

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1896, William Jennings Bryan delivered his famous 'Cross of Gold' speech at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, advocating for bimetallism and earning him the party's nomination for president. This speech became a defining moment in American political history.
events.name: William Jennings Bryan's Cross of Gold speech

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1896, Wilfrid Laurier was sworn in as Canada's seventh prime minister, becoming the first French-speaking individual to hold the office. His leadership was significant in shaping the future of Canada.

image.caption: Portrait photograph of Sir Wilfrid Laurier by William James Topley.
image.credit: William James Topley — This file has been provided by the British Library from its digital collections. Links to the British Library's website may be broken as the library recovers from a October 2023 cyber attack, and will be updated once material becomes accessible online. For more information on the attack see: https://www.bl.uk/about/cyber-attack It is also made available on a British Library website . Catalogue entry: HS85/10/16871
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Laurier, dated 1906, ten years after he became prime minister; it is not a photograph of the 1896 swearing-in.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Wilfrid Laurier becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1896, the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs was organized in Washington, D.C., in response to a call issued by Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin. This organization aimed to address the social issues faced by women of color in America.
events.name: Formation of the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1896, the International Socialist Workers and Trade Union Congress convened in London, bringing together labor leaders and activists from various countries to discuss workers' rights and international solidarity.
events.name: International Socialist Workers and Trade Union Congress

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1896, a causeway was opened between the islands of Saaremaa and Muhu in Estonia, facilitating transportation and trade between the two islands. This engineering feat was significant for the local economy and connectivity.
events.name: Opening of the causeway between Saaremaa and Muhu

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1896, a tragic rail crash occurred just west of Atlantic City, New Jersey, when two trains collided, resulting in the deaths of 50 people and injuring approximately 60 others. This incident raised concerns about rail safety and regulations.
events.name: Atlantic City rail crash

events.enhanced_description: In August 1896, a severe heat wave swept across Eastern North America, claiming the lives of approximately 1,500 people from Chicago to Boston. This extreme weather event highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban populations to heat-related illnesses.
events.name: Eastern North America heat wave

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1896, the Park Seung-jik shop was founded in Joseon, which later evolved into the Doosan Group, one of South Korea's largest conglomerates. This marked the beginning of a significant business legacy in the region.
events.name: Foundation of the Park Seung-jik shop

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1896, the Uganda Railway Act was approved in the United Kingdom, authorizing the construction of a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria in Africa. This project was pivotal for trade and transportation in the region.
events.name: Approval of the Uganda Railway Act

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1896, gold was discovered in the Klondike region of Yukon by Skookum Jim Mason, George Carmack, and Dawson Charlie. This discovery sparked the Klondike Gold Rush, leading to a massive influx of prospectors and settlers to the area.
events.name: Discovery of gold in Klondike

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1896, Bridget Driscoll was struck and killed by a Benz car on the grounds of the Crystal Palace in London, marking the world's first recorded motoring fatality. This incident raised awareness about road safety and the dangers of motor vehicles.
events.name: Bridget Driscoll's motoring fatality

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1896, the Cry of Pugad Lawin was a significant event that initiated the Philippine Revolution against Spanish colonial rule. This uprising marked the beginning of a struggle for independence in the Philippines.
events.name: Cry of Pugad Lawin

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1896, the Anglo-Zanzibar War commenced at 9:00 AM and lasted only 45 minutes, making it the shortest war in recorded history. The conflict arose from a succession dispute in Zanzibar, leading to British intervention.
events.name: Anglo-Zanzibar War

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1896, Clarkson University held its first classes in Potsdam, New York, with an initial enrollment of 17 students. This marked the beginning of the university's long-standing commitment to engineering and technology education.
events.name: Clarkson University first classes

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1896, the Crash at Crush train wreck stunt was held in Crush, Texas, where two trains were deliberately crashed into each other as a spectacle for the public. This event attracted large crowds and became a notable example of early American entertainment.
events.name: Crash at Crush train wreck stunt

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1896, Queen Victoria surpassed her grandfather, King George III, to become the longest-reigning monarch in British history up to that time. This milestone was celebrated across the British Empire, reflecting her significant influence.
events.name: Queen Victoria's longest reign

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1896, Pathé Frères, one of the oldest film companies in the world, was founded in Paris by the Pathé brothers. This company played a crucial role in the development of the film industry and cinema.
events.name: Foundation of Pathé Frères

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1896, Italy and France signed a treaty in Rome, whereby Italy effectively recognized Tunisia as a French dependency. This agreement was part of the broader context of European colonialism in North Africa.
events.name: Italy and France treaty on Tunisia

events.enhanced_description: In October 1896, Gottlieb Daimler constructed the first gasoline-powered truck, marking a significant advancement in automotive technology. This innovation laid the groundwork for the future of commercial transportation.
events.name: Gottlieb Daimler builds the first gasoline truck

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1896, the Victorian Football League (VFL) was established in Melbourne, Australia, as a governing body for Australian rules football. This league would evolve into what is now known as the Australian Football League (AFL), becoming a cornerstone of Australian sporting culture.
events.name: The Victorian Football League is established

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1896, the cornerstone for Augusta High School was laid in Augusta, Kentucky, marking the end of the Augusta Methodist College. This event symbolized a shift in the educational landscape of the region.
events.name: The Augusta High School cornerstone is laid

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1896, William McKinley won the United States presidential election against William Jennings Bryan. This election is often viewed as a pivotal moment in American politics, signaling a realignment of the Republican Party and the nation’s economic policies.
events.name: 1896 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1896, Richard Strauss conducted the first performance of his orchestral tone poem Also sprach Zarathustra in Frankfurt. This work would later gain immense popularity, particularly due to its use in film and popular culture.
events.name: Richard Strauss's Also sprach Zarathustra is first performed

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1896, Udinese Calcio, an association football club, was founded in Udine, Italy. The club has since become one of the prominent teams in Italian football.
events.name: Udinese Calcio Association football club is founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1896, archaeologist Alois Anton Führer, alongside Nepalese General Khadga Samsher Rana, rediscovered the great stone pillar of Ashoka at Lumbini, a site traditionally recognized as the birthplace of Gautama Buddha. This rediscovery was significant for Buddhist history and archaeology.
events.name: Rediscovery of the great stone pillar of Ashoka at Lumbini

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1896, the New York Aquarium opened in Brooklyn, New York. It became a significant cultural and educational institution, showcasing marine life and promoting conservation efforts.
events.name: New York Aquarium opens

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1896, the Glasgow Subway, the third-oldest underground metro system in the world, officially opened in Glasgow, Scotland. This development marked a significant advancement in urban transportation.
events.name: The Glasgow Subway opens

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1896, composer John Philip Sousa completed The Stars and Stripes Forever, which would become the national march of the United States. This piece is celebrated for its patriotic themes and has become a staple in American music.

image.caption: Page 1 of the sheet music for John Philip Sousa’s “The Stars and Stripes Forever.”
image.credit: John Philip Sousa — Library of Congress - ( Archived link )
image.date_qualification: Image dated 1897, after the stated composition date of December 25, 1896.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: John Philip Sousa composes The Stars and Stripes Forever

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1896, Filipino nationalist and reformist José Rizal was executed by Spanish authorities in Bagumbayan, Manila. His death sparked widespread outrage and became a catalyst for the Philippine Revolution against Spanish colonial rule.

image.caption: The catafalque carrying José Rizal’s remains is marched through Manila to Luneta, accompanied by Knights of Rizal honor guards.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://pinoyhistorian.blogspot.com/2012/12/1912-transfer-of-rizals-mortal-remains.html
image.date_qualification: Depicts the 1912 transfer of Rizal’s remains, not his 1896 execution.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: José Rizal is executed by Spanish authorities

events.enhanced_description: The Lasithi massacres were a series of violent events in 1897 during the Cretan revolt against Ottoman rule, where ethnic Turkish and Cretan Muslim civilians were targeted. This conflict highlighted the ethnic tensions in Crete and the broader struggle for autonomy from the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Lasithi massacres

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1897, drillers struck oil at the Nellie Johnstone Number One well in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, marking the first significant oil discovery in the region. This event initiated a boom in oil production that transformed the local economy and contributed to the growth of the petroleum industry in the United States.
events.name: Drillers near Bartlesville, Oklahoma strike oil for the first time

events.enhanced_description: Yamaichi Securities was founded in 1897 in Tokyo, Japan, becoming one of the country's leading financial institutions. It played a significant role in the development of Japan's modern financial markets until it ceased trading in 1997.
events.name: Yamaichi Securities founded in Japan

events.enhanced_description: The Stars and Stripes Forever, a patriotic march composed by John Philip Sousa, was performed for the first time in 1897. This piece has since become a staple of American patriotic music and is often played at national celebrations.
events.name: The Stars and Stripes Forever is performed for the first time

events.enhanced_description: Belo Horizonte, the first planned city in Brazil, was officially created on January 1, 1897. Designed to accommodate a growing population, it became a model for urban planning in the country.
events.name: Belo Horizonte is created

events.enhanced_description: The USS Baltimore (Cruiser # 3, later CM-1) was recommissioned on January 1, 1897, for several months of duty in the Hawaiian Islands. This recommissioning was part of the U.S. Navy's efforts to strengthen its presence in the Pacific.
events.name: USS Baltimore is recommissioned

events.enhanced_description: The first electric bicycle was invented in 1897 by Gustav Trouvé, showcasing early advancements in electric vehicle technology. This invention paved the way for future developments in personal transportation.
events.name: The first electric bicycle is invented

events.enhanced_description: Karl Lueger was elected mayor of Vienna in 1897, serving until 1910. His tenure was marked by significant urban development and controversial policies, including his use of populist rhetoric.

image.caption: Portrait of Karl Lueger, mayor of Vienna, by Wenzl Weis.
image.credit: Wenzl Weis — Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Bildarchiv Austria, Inventarnr. 167964-D
