image.date_qualification: Dated 1897 in the supplied image metadata; this is a portrait, not evidence of the mayoral election or appointment itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Karl Lueger becomes mayor of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: Zhejiang University, one of the oldest and most prestigious universities in China, was founded in 1897 in Hangzhou. It has played a crucial role in the development of higher education in China.
events.name: Zhejiang University is founded

events.enhanced_description: Émile Durkheim published his seminal sociological study, Suicide, in 1897, which analyzed the social factors contributing to suicide rates. This work laid the foundation for modern sociology and the study of social behavior.
events.name: Émile Durkheim publishes Suicide

events.enhanced_description: The pan-African anthem "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika" was composed as a Xhosa hymn by South African teacher Enoch Sontonga in 1897. It has since become a symbol of the struggle for freedom and equality in Africa.
events.name: Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika composed

events.enhanced_description: Dos Equis beer was first brewed in 1897 in Monterrey, Mexico, as a response to the growing demand for quality beer in the region. It has since become one of Mexico's most recognized beer brands.
events.name: Dos Equis beer is first brewed

events.enhanced_description: In 1897, Alexander Scriabin published his Piano Sonata No. 2, also known as Sonata-Fantasia, in G sharp minor. This work is notable for its innovative harmonic language and emotional depth, marking a significant contribution to piano literature.
events.name: Alexander Scriabin publishes Piano Sonata no. 2

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1897, Lady Flora Shaw proposed the name 'Nigeria' in a newspaper contest, which was intended for the British Niger Coast Protectorate. This name was derived from the Niger River and would later become the official name of the country.
events.name: Proposal of the name 'Nigeria'

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1897, the term 'computer' was first used in the journal Engineering to refer to a mechanical calculation device. This marked a significant moment in the evolution of computing technology.
events.name: First use of the word 'computer'

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1897, the Czechoslovak Trade Union Association was founded in Prague, marking a significant step in the labor movement in the region. This organization aimed to represent the interests of workers in Czechoslovakia.
events.name: Foundation of the Czechoslovak Trade Union Association

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1897, freedom of religion was proclaimed in Madagascar, reflecting a significant shift in the legal and cultural landscape of the island. This proclamation allowed for greater religious diversity and expression.
events.name: Proclamation of freedom of religion in Madagascar

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1897, the French military conquered the island of Raiatea and captured the rebel chief Teraupo'o, effectively ending the Leeward Islands War. This event solidified French control over the Society Islands.
events.name: French conquest of Raiatea

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1897, the British Army's Benin Expedition resulted in the burning of Benin City, leading to the exile of Ovonramwen, the Oba of Benin. This event marked a significant moment in British colonial expansion in West Africa.
events.name: Benin Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1897, the Sigma Pi fraternity was founded in Vincennes, Indiana. This organization has since grown to become one of the prominent collegiate fraternities in the United States.
events.name: Foundation of Sigma Pi fraternity

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1897, Joseph Gallieni, the French military governor of Madagascar, exiled Queen Ranavalona III to Réunion, effectively abolishing the monarchy the following day. This marked a significant moment in the French colonial rule over Madagascar.

image.caption: A Le Petit Journal cover illustration of Queen Ranavalona III in Algiers with her aunt Ramasindrazana and niece Marie-Louise.
image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist — Back Cover of Le Petit Journal, Paris (France), published March 19, 1899.
image.date_qualification: Published 19 March 1899; depicts the queen in Algiers after her relocation there, not the 27 February 1897 exile event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Exile of Queen Ranavalona III

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1897, William McKinley was sworn in as the 25th president of the United States. His presidency would see significant events, including the Spanish-American War and the economic prosperity of the late 1890s.
events.name: William McKinley sworn in as president

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1897, San Diego State University was founded, establishing it as one of the oldest institutions of higher education in California. It has since grown into a major public research university.

image.caption: College West at San Diego State University.
image.credit: Roman Eugeniusz — https://web.archive.org/web/20161102213106/http://www.panoramio.com/photo/128454253
image.date_qualification: Photographed on 28 February 2016; the image documents the later campus, not the 1897 founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of San Diego State University

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1897, at the Tejeros Convention, Emilio Aguinaldo unseated Andrés Bonifacio, becoming the new leader of the Filipino revolutionary group Katipunan. This event was pivotal in the Philippine Revolution against Spanish rule.
events.name: Tejeros Convention

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1897, drillers near Bartlesville, Oklahoma, struck oil for the first time in the designated Indian Territory, leading to a significant oil boom and rapid population growth in the region.
events.name: First oil strike in Oklahoma

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1897, the first Boston Marathon was held, featuring fifteen male competitors, with John McDermott emerging as the winner. This event has since become an iconic annual race.
events.name: First Boston Marathon

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1897, representatives of the Chickasaw Nation, Choctaw Nation, and the U.S. Dawes Commission signed the Atoka Agreement, which was a crucial step toward the creation of the State of Oklahoma.
events.name: Signing of the Atoka Agreement

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1897, J. J. Thomson announced his discovery of the electron as a subatomic particle at a lecture at the Royal Institution in London. This groundbreaking discovery significantly advanced the field of atomic physics.
events.name: Discovery of the electron

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1897, the Battle of Velestino occurred during the Greco-Turkish War of 1897. This battle was part of the larger conflict between Greece and the Ottoman Empire over territorial disputes.

image.caption: Greek painting by Karl Haupt depicting the Battle of Velestino.
image.credit: Karl Haupt — Εθνικό και Ιστορικό Μουσείο (Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους . Τόμος ΙΔ', σελ.142. Αθήνα 1980. ISBN 960-213-110-1 )
image.date_qualification: 1897 is supplied as the image date; this is a painting, not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Velestino

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1897, John Jacob Abel announced the successful isolation of epinephrine (adrenaline) in a paper presented before the Association of American Physicians. This discovery had significant implications for medicine and pharmacology.
events.name: Isolation of epinephrine

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1897, a tragic accident at Snaefell Mine on the Isle of Man resulted in the deaths of 19 zinc miners due to carbon monoxide poisoning. This incident highlighted the dangers of mining during this period.
events.name: Snaefell Mine disaster

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1897, a patent was awarded for the invention of the first automotive muffler to Milton Reeves and his brother Marshall T. Reeves of the Reeves Pulley Company in Columbus, Indiana. This invention significantly contributed to the development of quieter automobiles.
events.name: Patent for automotive muffler

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1897, 'The Stars and Stripes Forever,' an American patriotic march composed by John Philip Sousa, was performed for the first time. This piece has since become a staple of American patriotic music.
events.name: First performance of 'The Stars and Stripes Forever'

events.enhanced_description: Founded in May 1897, the Scientific-Humanitarian Committee in Berlin was the first LGBT advocacy organization in history. It aimed to combat the criminalization of homosexuality and promote the rights of sexual minorities.

image.caption: Vita homosexualis, a 1902 collection of August Fleischmann’s pamphlets, from the Scientific-Humanitarian Committee’s library.
image.credit: Wikiwlh — Own work
image.date_qualification: The depicted book dates to 1902; its confiscation is described as occurring on 6 May 1933. The image itself was photographed in 2013, not at the committee’s 1897 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Scientific-Humanitarian Committee is founded in Berlin

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1897, Oscar Wilde was released from prison in England after serving a sentence for 'gross indecency.' Following his release, he went into voluntary exile on the continent, marking a significant turn in his life and career.
events.name: Oscar Wilde released from prison

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1897, the Blackwall Tunnel, then the longest underwater road tunnel in the world, was opened for traffic beneath the River Thames in East London by the Prince of Wales. This engineering feat significantly improved transportation in the area.
events.name: Opening of the Blackwall Tunnel

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1897, Bram Stoker's Gothic horror novel 'Dracula' was first published in London. This novel would go on to have a profound influence on vampire literature and popular culture.
events.name: Publication of 'Dracula'

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1897, the Robert Gould Shaw Memorial was dedicated in Boston on Decoration Day (later Memorial Day). This bronze bas relief by Augustus St. Gaudens honors the 54th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment, one of the first African American units in the Civil War.
events.name: Dedication of the Robert Gould Shaw Memorial

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1897, an earthquake with a magnitude of 8.0 struck Assam, India, resulting in the deaths of over 1,500 people. This devastating natural disaster had a lasting impact on the region.

image.caption: Map 1 from Richard D. Oldham’s report on the 1897 Assam earthquake.
image.credit: Oldham, Richard Dixon, 1858-1936 — https://archive.org/details/memoirsofgeologi29geol/page/n546/mode/thumb
image.date_qualification: A map published in 1899 in Oldham’s report on the earthquake, not a contemporary photograph of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 1897 Assam earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Kyoto University, one of Japan's most prestigious institutions, was officially established on June 18, 1897. It has since become a leading center for research and higher education in Asia.
events.name: Kyoto University is officially established in Japan

events.enhanced_description: The Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria was celebrated on June 22, 1897, marking her 60 years on the throne. This event was a significant moment in British history, showcasing the empire's global reach and the queen's enduring popularity.
events.name: The Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria is celebrated in the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1897, S. A. Andrée's Arctic Balloon Expedition commenced with the aim of reaching the North Pole. Unfortunately, the expedition ended tragically with the loss of all team members within months due to harsh conditions.

locations.name: S. A. Andrée's Arctic Balloon Expedition

events.name: S. A. Andrée's Arctic Balloon Expedition begins

events.enhanced_description: The Klondike Gold Rush began on July 17, 1897, when the first successful prospectors arrived in Seattle, Washington, after discovering gold in the Klondike region of Canada. This event sparked a massive influx of fortune seekers to the Yukon, significantly impacting the region's development.
events.name: The Klondike Gold Rush begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1897, writer Jack London set sail to join the Klondike Gold Rush. His experiences during this period inspired some of his most famous literary works, including 'The Call of the Wild.'
events.name: Writer Jack London sails to join the Klondike Gold Rush

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1897, British troops were besieged by Pashtun tribesmen in Malakand, located on the Northwest frontier of British India. This siege was part of the larger context of British colonial military engagements in the region.
events.name: Siege of Malakand

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1897, Mount Saint Elias, the second highest peak in the United States and Canada, was first ascended. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the history of mountaineering in North America.
events.name: Mount Saint Elias is first ascended

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1897, pharmacist Felix Hoffmann successfully synthesized acetylsalicylic acid at the Bayer pharmaceutical company, leading to the creation of the widely used pain reliever, Aspirin. This innovation revolutionized pain management and established Bayer as a major player in the pharmaceutical industry.
events.name: Felix Hoffmann synthesizes acetylsalicylic acid

events.enhanced_description: The Olds Motor Vehicle Co. was founded on August 21, 1897, in Lansing, Michigan, by Ransom E. Olds. This company played a crucial role in the early automotive industry, introducing assembly line production techniques.

image.caption: Portrait of Ransom E. Olds, founder of Oldsmobile.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Unknown
image.date_qualification: The image is a portrait of the company’s founder, not a depiction of the company’s 1897 founding. The image date is approximate.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Olds Motor Vehicle Co. is founded

events.enhanced_description: The First Zionist Congress convened in Basel, Switzerland, on August 29, 1897, marking a pivotal moment in the Zionist movement. Led by Theodor Herzl, the congress aimed to establish a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.

image.caption: The Basel Program adopted at the First Zionist Congress, a document outlining the aims and methods of Zionism.
image.credit: Max Nordau (1849-1923) Epson291 ( talk ) — JAFI:Zionist Congresses: First Congress - Basle (Basel), 1897 , Jewish Virtual Library: The First Zionist Congress and the Basel Program , 3 September 1897 “At Basel I founded the Jewish State” writes Herzl
image.date_qualification: The image metadata dates the document to 1897; it does not establish that this is a photograph made during the congress.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The First Zionist Congress convenes

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1897, Thomas Edison was granted a patent for the Kinetoscope, a device that allowed for the viewing of moving pictures. This invention was a precursor to modern film projectors and played a significant role in the development of the film industry.
events.name: Thomas Edison is granted a patent for the Kinetoscope

events.enhanced_description: The Tremont Street subway, the first underground subway system in the United States, was opened in Boston, Massachusetts, on September 1, 1897. This groundbreaking project marked the beginning of modern public transportation in American cities.
events.name: The Tremont Street subway is opened

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1897, the Lattimer massacre occurred when a sheriff's posse killed 19 unarmed immigrant miners during a labor dispute in Lattimer, Pennsylvania. This tragic event highlighted the tensions between labor movements and law enforcement during the industrial era.
events.name: Lattimer massacre

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1897, Ethiopian forces under Menelik II captured Gaki Sherocho, the last king of Kaffa, effectively ending the ancient kingdom of Kaffa. This event was part of Menelik II's broader campaign to consolidate power in Ethiopia.

locations.name: Kaffa
locations.region: Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples' Region

events.name: Capture of Gaki Sherocho

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1897, the Battle of Saragarhi took place, where 21 Sikhs of the 36th Sikhs regiment defended their post against 10,000 Afghan and Orakzai tribesmen. This battle is celebrated for the bravery and sacrifice of the Sikh soldiers.
events.name: Battle of Saragarhi

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1897, Greece and Turkey signed a peace treaty to formally end the Greco-Turkish War. This treaty marked a significant moment in the history of relations between the two nations.
events.name: Greece and Turkey sign a peace treaty

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1897, Francis P. Church anonymously responded to a letter in The Sun, famously stating, 'Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus.' This response has since become a cherished part of American Christmas folklore.
events.name: Francis P. Church responds to letter about Santa Claus

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1897, after a prolonged siege, Brazilian government troops captured Canudos, effectively crushing the resistance led by Antônio Conselheiro and his followers. This conflict highlighted the tensions between the Brazilian state and its rural populations.
events.name: Brazilian government troops take Canudos

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1897, Ethiopia adopted its tricolor flag, symbolizing the land (green), wealth (yellow), and the blood shed for freedom (red). This flag has become a significant emblem of Ethiopian national identity.
events.name: Ethiopia adopts the tricolor flag

events.enhanced_description: The Korean Empire was proclaimed on January 1, 1897, marking the end of the Joseon dynasty after over 500 years of rule. This significant event represented Korea's efforts to assert its sovereignty and modernize in the face of foreign pressures.
events.name: The Korean Empire is proclaimed

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1897, HMS Canopus, a pre-dreadnought battleship of the Royal Navy, was launched in Portsmouth, England. This ship would later see extensive service during World War I.
events.name: HMS Canopus is launched

events.enhanced_description: The Kappa Delta sorority was founded on October 23, 1897, at Longwood University in Farmville, Virginia, by four women who aimed to create a sisterhood focused on personal growth and community service. It has since grown into a national organization with chapters across the United States.
events.name: The Kappa Delta sorority is founded

events.enhanced_description: Juventus Football Club, one of the most successful and storied football clubs in the world, was founded on November 1, 1897, in Turin, Italy. The club has since become a symbol of Italian football, known for its rich history and numerous championships.
events.name: Juventus FC is founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1897, Spain granted autonomy to Puerto Rico, allowing for a degree of self-governance under the Spanish crown. This was part of a broader movement in Spain to reform its colonial policies amid growing pressures for independence.
figures: Antonio de la Torre y Miranda
events.name: Spain grants Puerto Rico autonomy

events.enhanced_description: The feminist newspaper La Fronde, founded by Marguerite Durand, published its first issue on December 9, 1897, in Paris. It aimed to advocate for women's rights and social issues, becoming a significant voice in the feminist movement of the time.
events.name: First issue of La Fronde published

events.enhanced_description: The comic strip The Katzenjammer Kids, created by Rudolph Dirks, debuted on December 12, 1897, in the New York Journal. It became one of the first successful comic strips in American history, influencing the genre significantly.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The Katzenjammer Kids debuts

events.enhanced_description: The Pact of Biak-na-Bato, signed on December 14, 1897, marked a truce in the Philippine Revolution against Spanish colonial rule. The agreement included promises of reforms from the Spanish government and the temporary exile of revolutionary leaders.
events.name: Pact of Biak-na-Bato

events.enhanced_description: The play Cyrano de Bergerac, written by Edmond Rostand, premiered on December 28, 1897, in Paris. This romantic drama, featuring the iconic character Cyrano, has since become a classic of French literature and theatre.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Cyrano de Bergerac, after a painting by Zacharie Heince.
image.credit: ZH, pinxit (Zacharie Heince, 1611-1669) LAH, delin. et Sculpsit — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID [1]
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the 17th-century writer, not an image of the 1897 premiere. Image date: 1654.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Cyrano de Bergerac premieres

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1897, the British colony of Natal formally annexed Zululand, a region inhabited by the Zulu people. This annexation was part of the broader British imperial expansion in southern Africa during the late 19th century.
events.name: Natal annexes Zululand

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1898, New York City annexed land from surrounding counties, creating the City of Greater New York. This consolidation made it the second-largest city in the world at the time, significantly altering its political and social landscape.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: New York City annexes land

events.enhanced_description: In 1898, the Rheinisch-Westfälisches Elektrizitätswerk (RWE) was founded in Essen, Germany. This company would grow to become one of the largest energy providers in Europe, playing a significant role in the development of the electricity market.
events.name: In Essen, German company Rheinisch-Westfälisches Elektrizitätswerk RWE is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1898, Geert Adriaans Boomgaard, born on April 8, 1788, in Groningen, Netherlands, was recognized as the world's first validated supercentenarian, living to the age of 110 years. His longevity sparked interest in the study of aging and the factors contributing to a long life.
events.name: Geert Adriaans Boomgaard of Groningen in the Netherlands becomes the world's first validated supercentenarian

events.enhanced_description: In 1898, the first volume of the Linguistic Survey of India was published in Kolkata, marking a significant contribution to the field of linguistics. This comprehensive survey aimed to document the diverse languages and dialects spoken across India, providing valuable insights into the country's linguistic heritage.
events.name: The first volume of the Linguistic Survey of India is published in Calcutta

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1898, Émile Zola published his open letter 'J'Accuse…!' in the newspaper L'Aurore, accusing the French government of antisemitism and wrongful imprisonment of Alfred Dreyfus. This bold act sparked widespread public debate and became a pivotal moment in the Dreyfus Affair.
events.name: Émile Zola's J'Accuse published

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1898, Henry Lindfield became the first person to die in an automobile accident on a public highway when his car rolled out of control in Purley, London. This tragic event highlighted the dangers of early motor vehicles and the need for traffic regulations.
events.name: First automobile fatality

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1898, the USS Maine exploded in Havana Harbor, Cuba, killing 266 men. The cause of the explosion was never definitively established, but it served as a catalyst for the Spanish-American War, leading to U.S. intervention in Cuba.
events.name: USS Maine explosion

events.enhanced_description: After publishing his open letter 'J'Accuse…!', Émile Zola was imprisoned on February 23, 1898, in France. His imprisonment was a significant moment in the Dreyfus Affair, highlighting the tensions surrounding justice and antisemitism in French society.
events.name: Émile Zola imprisoned

events.enhanced_description: In March 1898, Vladimir Lenin founded the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) in Minsk, aiming to unite various socialist factions in Russia. This party would later play a crucial role in the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the establishment of the Soviet state.

image.caption: Image of the Social Democrats of the Second State Duma.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://viewer.rsl.ru/ru/rsl01009008489?page=69&rotate=0&theme=white Альбом по истории ВКП(б). 1874-1917 / Общая редакция С. И. Мицкевича и Н. М. Дружинина. - Москва : [б. и.], 1928.
image.date_qualification: Image date stated as 1907; the credit identifies a 1928 album as the source. Neither date depicts the party's 1898 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Vladimir Lenin creates the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1898, the Fussballclub Young Boys was established in Bern, Switzerland. This club would go on to become one of the most successful football teams in Swiss history, known for its vibrant fan base and competitive spirit.
events.name: BSC Young Boys is established

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1898, representatives from five Australian colonies convened in Melbourne to adopt a constitution that would lay the groundwork for the Commonwealth of Australia. This significant step towards federation marked the beginning of a unified Australian nation.
events.name: Constitution adopted in Melbourne

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1898, Robert Allison of Port Carbon, Pennsylvania, made history by purchasing the first American-built automobile, a Winton, which had been advertised in Scientific American. This marked a significant milestone in the automotive industry in the United States.
events.name: Robert Allison buys first American-built automobile

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1898, the Sabie Game Reserve was established in South Africa, marking it as the first officially designated game reserve in the country. This initiative was a pioneering step towards wildlife conservation in South Africa.
events.name: Creation of the Sabie Game Reserve

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1898, renowned sharpshooter Annie Oakley wrote a letter to President McKinley, offering to organize a company of 50 'lady sharpshooters' to serve in the military should war break out with Spain. This act highlighted her advocacy for women's roles in combat.
events.name: Annie Oakley promotes women in combat

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1898, during the Spanish-American War, the United States Navy initiated a blockade of Cuban ports, effectively cutting off supplies to Spanish forces. This strategic move was crucial in the lead-up to the conflict's major battles.
events.name: U.S. Navy blockade of Cuban ports

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1898, a conference of senior Spanish Navy officers, led by naval minister Segismundo Bermejo, convened to decide on the deployment of Admiral Pascual Cervera's squadron to Cuba and Puerto Rico. This decision was pivotal in the Spanish-American War.
events.name: Spanish Navy conference on Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1898, the United States Congress officially declared war on Spain, stating that a state of war had existed since April 21. This declaration marked the formal entry of the U.S. into the Spanish-American War.
events.name: U.S. declares war on Spain

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1898, the United States Congress declared war on Spain, officially marking the beginning of the Spanish–American War. This declaration followed the sinking of the USS Maine and was backdated to April 20.
events.name: Spanish–American War: The United States declares war on Spain

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1898, a tragic explosion occurred at the California Powder Works in Santa Cruz, resulting in the deaths of 13 workers. This incident highlighted the dangers associated with the production of explosives during this era.
events.name: Explosion at California Powder Works

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1898, the first large-scale commercial vehicle exhibition, the Paris Auto Show, was held in Tuileries Garden, showcasing the latest innovations in the automotive industry. This event marked a significant moment in the history of automobile exhibitions.
events.name: First Paris Auto Show

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1898, during the Spanish-American War, Commodore George Dewey led the U.S. Navy to a decisive victory at the Battle of Manila Bay, destroying the Spanish fleet. This battle was the first major engagement of the war and a pivotal moment in the Philippines Campaign.

image.caption: Painting of the Battle of Manila Bay by James Gale Tyler.
image.credit: James Gale Tyler (1855–1931) — Geographicus , accessed 21 September 2024
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration dated 1898; the battle took place on May 1, 1898. It is not established here as a contemporary photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Manila Bay

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1898, thousands of scholars and citizens in Beijing protested in front of the capital control yuan, demanding reforms in response to the growing influence of foreign powers in China. This protest was part of a larger movement advocating for modernization and reform.
events.name: Protests in Beijing

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1898, during a rally in Milan, General Fiorenzo Bava Beccaris ordered troops to fire on demonstrators, resulting in hundreds of deaths. This tragic event highlighted the tensions between the government and the populace during a period of social unrest in Italy.
events.name: Bava Beccaris massacre

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1898, the first games of the Italian Football Federation were played, featuring a match between Genoa and Torino. This event marked the beginning of organized football in Italy, which would grow to become a significant part of the country's culture.
events.name: First games of the Italian Football Federation

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1898, the Puerto Rican Campaign commenced with the Bombardment of San Juan, marking a significant military operation during the Spanish-American War. This campaign aimed to secure Puerto Rico for the United States.
events.name: Puerto Rican Campaign begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1898, the German football club SV Darmstadt 98 was formed. This club has since become an important part of German football history, contributing to the development of the sport in the region.
events.name: Formation of SV Darmstadt 98

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1898, China leased the territory of Kwang-Chou-Wan to France as part of the Treaty of 12 April 1892. This area would later become part of French Indochina, reflecting the imperialist ambitions of European powers in Asia.
events.name: Leasing of Kwang-Chou-Wan

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1898, Secondo Pia took the first photographs of the Shroud of Turin, revealing that the image appeared as a photographic negative. This discovery sparked significant interest and debate regarding the authenticity of the shroud.
events.name: First photographs of the Shroud of Turin

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1898, the Trans-Mississippi Exposition World's Fair opened in Omaha, Nebraska, showcasing the resources and culture of the American West. This event attracted visitors from across the nation and highlighted the region's development.
events.name: Trans-Mississippi Exposition opens

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1898, chemists William Ramsay and Morris Travers discovered neon at their laboratory at University College London, after extracting it from liquid nitrogen. This discovery contributed to the understanding of noble gases and their properties.
events.name: Discovery of neon

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1898, the British government arranged a 99-year lease of Hong Kong from China, significantly expanding British colonial influence in the region. This lease would shape the political landscape of Hong Kong for nearly a century.
events.name: Lease of Hong Kong

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1898, Tuone Udaina, the last known speaker of the Dalmatian language, was killed in an explosion. His death marked the end of a linguistic heritage that had persisted for centuries in the Adriatic region.
events.name: Death of Tuone Udaina

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1898, the Guangxu Emperor announced the creation of what would later become Peking University, aiming to modernize education in China. This institution has since become one of the leading universities in Asia.
events.name: Creation of Peking University

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1898, General Emilio Aguinaldo declared the Philippines' independence from Spanish colonial rule after 333 years of dominance. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the Philippine Revolution and the fight for national sovereignty.
events.name: Philippine Declaration of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1898, the Yukon Territory was officially established in Canada, with Dawson City designated as its capital. This formation was a direct result of the Klondike Gold Rush, which attracted thousands of prospectors and settlers to the region.
events.name: Yukon Territory is formed in Canada, with Dawson chosen as its capital

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1898, Nabisco, originally known as the National Biscuit Company, was founded in East Hanover, New Jersey. The company became famous for its innovative baking techniques and iconic products, including Oreos and Ritz crackers.
events.name: Food processing giant Nabisco is founded in New Jersey

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1898, during the Spanish–American War, the United States captured Guam, marking it as the first U.S. overseas territory. This event significantly expanded American influence in the Pacific region.
events.name: Spanish–American War: The United States captures Guam

events.enhanced_description: In 1898, Joshua Slocum became the first person to sail solo around the world, completing his journey in Fairhaven, Massachusetts. His remarkable voyage, which began in 1895, covered over 46,000 miles and was documented in his book 'Sailing Alone Around the World', inspiring future generations of sailors and adventurers.

image.caption: Illustration of Joshua Slocum, published in Century Magazine.
image.credit: Hollinger & Co. — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID cph.3b46344 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration published after Slocum completed his circumnavigation; the saved image date is 1899-09.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: American adventurer Joshua Slocum completes a 3-year solo circumnavigation of the world

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1898, the Curtis Act was enacted, leading to the dissolution of tribal and communal lands in Indian Territory. This act paved the way for the eventual creation of the State of Oklahoma in 1907.
events.name: Effective date of the Curtis Act of 1898

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1898, during the Spanish–American War, U.S. troops, including Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders, fought for and captured San Juan Hill near Santiago de Cuba. This pivotal battle was a significant victory for the United States.

locations.name: San Juan Hill, Santiago de Cuba

events.name: Spanish–American War: Battle of San Juan Hill

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1898, during the Spanish–American War, the United States Navy decisively defeated the Spanish Navy at the Battle of Santiago de Cuba. This victory effectively destroyed Spanish naval power in the Caribbean.
events.name: Spanish–American War: Battle of Santiago de Cuba

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Santiago de Cuba, fought in July 1898, was a decisive naval engagement during the Spanish–American War, where the United States Navy, under Admiral William T. Sampson, effectively destroyed the Spanish Caribbean Squadron led by Admiral Pascual Cervera. This victory played a crucial role in the U.S. victory in the war and the subsequent Treaty of Paris.
events.name: Spanish–American War: Battle of Santiago de Cuba – The United States Navy destroys the Spanish Navy's Caribbean Squadron

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1898, the ocean liner SS La Bourgogne collided with another vessel and sank off the coast of Sable Island, resulting in the tragic loss of 549 lives. This incident remains one of the deadliest maritime disasters in Canadian history.
events.name: SS La Bourgogne disaster

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1898, the United States formally annexed the Hawaiian Islands, following the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy. This annexation was part of the broader expansionist policies of the U.S. during this period.
events.name: The United States annexes the Hawaiian Islands

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1898, during the Spanish–American War, U.S. forces under General William R. Shafter captured Santiago de Cuba, marking a significant victory that contributed to the end of Spanish colonial rule in the Americas.
events.name: Spanish–American War: Battle of Santiago Bay

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1898, the first installment of 'The Adventures of Louis de Rougemont' was published in The Wide World Magazine. This series captivated readers with its tales of adventure and exploration, contributing to the era's fascination with travel narratives.
events.name: The Adventures of Louis de Rougemont first appear in The Wide World Magazine

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1898, U.S. forces landed at Guánica Bay, Puerto Rico, marking the beginning of the American invasion of the island during the Spanish–American War. This operation aimed to secure Puerto Rico as a U.S. territory.
events.name: Spanish–American War: The United States invasion of Puerto Rico begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1898, hostilities officially ended between American and Spanish forces in Cuba, concluding the military operations of the Spanish–American War in the region. This marked a significant turning point in U.S.-Cuba relations.
events.name: Spanish–American War: Hostilities end between American and Spanish forces in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1898, the Spanish commander in Manila surrendered the city to U.S. forces, effectively ending hostilities in the Philippines during the Spanish–American War. This strategic victory prevented the city from falling into the hands of Filipino rebels.
events.name: Spanish–American War: Battle of Manila

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1898, the Gornergrat railway was inaugurated, connecting Zermatt to the Gornergrat in Switzerland. This railway became a significant engineering achievement, facilitating access to the stunning views of the Matterhorn and surrounding Alps.
events.name: The Gornergrat railway opens

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1898, Clube de Regatas Vasco da Gama was founded in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This sports club has since become one of the most prominent football clubs in Brazil, with a rich history in various sports.
events.name: Clube de Regatas Vasco da Gama is founded in Rio de Janeiro

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1898, the Southern Cross Expedition, led by Sir Ernest Shackleton, set sail from London. This expedition marked the beginning of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, aiming to explore the Antarctic region.
events.name: The Southern Cross Expedition sets sail from London

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1898, the Chickasaw and Choctaw tribes signed the Atoka Agreement, which was a requirement of the Curtis Act of 1898. This agreement aimed to reorganize tribal governance and land ownership in Indian Territory.
events.name: Chickasaw and Choctaw tribes sign the Atoka Agreement

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1898, a tragic massacre occurred in Heraklion, Crete, where 700 Greeks and 15 Englishmen were killed by Turkish forces. This event contributed to the international response that led to the establishment of the autonomous Cretan State.
events.name: 700 Greeks and 15 Englishmen are slaughtered by the Turks in Heraklion, Greece

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1898, American pharmacist Caleb Bradham officially named his soft drink Pepsi-Cola. This beverage would go on to become one of the most recognized brands in the world.
events.name: Caleb Bradham names his soft drink Pepsi-Cola

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1898, British and Egyptian troops led by General Horatio Kitchener defeated Sudanese tribesmen at the Battle of Omdurman. This decisive victory established British dominance in Sudan, with significant casualties on both sides.
events.name: Battle of Omdurman (Mahdist War)

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1898, Italian anarchist Luigi Lucheni assassinated Empress Elisabeth of Austria in Geneva. This act was part of a broader wave of political violence aimed at royalty and was motivated by anarchist ideology.
events.name: Luigi Lucheni assassinates Empress Elisabeth of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1898, the Fashoda Incident occurred when a British flotilla arrived at the French-occupied fort of Fashoda on the White Nile. This standoff between British and French forces highlighted the imperial rivalries in Africa and led to a diplomatic resolution.
events.name: Fashoda Incident

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1898, Empress Dowager Cixi orchestrated a coup d'état that marked the end of the Hundred Days' Reform in China. The Guangxu Emperor was arrested, and Cixi reasserted her control over the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Empress Dowager Cixi of China engineers a coup d'état

events.enhanced_description: In September 1898, Empress Dowager Cixi orchestrated a coup d'état that effectively ended the Hundred Days' Reform, a series of radical reforms aimed at modernizing China. The Guangxu Emperor was placed under house arrest, and Cixi reasserted her control over the Qing dynasty, leading to a period of conservative governance.
events.name: Empress Dowager Cixi of China engineers a coup d'état, marking the end of the Hundred Days' Reform; the Guangxu Emperor is arrested

events.enhanced_description: The Vienna University of Economics and Business, originally established as the K.u.K. Exportakademie in 1898, has grown to become one of Europe's leading institutions for business education. Its founding marked a significant development in higher education focused on economics and international trade.

image.caption: Northwest area of the Vienna University of Economics and Business campus, including Departments 3 and 4 and the Administration Department.
image.credit: C.Stadler/Bwag — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2018-05-26; depicts the later campus, not the university’s 1898 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Vienna University of Economics and Business is founded, under the name K.u.K. Exportakademie

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1898, the Battle of Sugar Point occurred in northern Minnesota, where Ojibwe tribesmen, led by Chief Hole-in-the-Day, successfully defeated U.S. government troops. This battle was part of the ongoing tensions between Native Americans and the U.S. government over land and rights.

image.caption: Front page of The St. Paul Globe showing images of U.S. Army casualties associated with the Battle of Sugar Point.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn90059523/1898-10-09/ed-1/seq-1/#date1=10%2F09%2F1898&index=0&rows=20&searchType=advanced&language=&sequence=0&words=EDWARD+LOWE&proxdistance=5&date2=10%2F09%2F1898&ortext=&proxtext=Edward+Lowe&phrasetext=&andtext=&dateFilterType=range&page=1
image.date_qualification: Newspaper page dated 1898-10-09; it is not a photograph of the battle itself. The article excerpt dates the battle to October 5, 1898.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Sugar Point: Ojibwe tribesmen defeat U.S. government troops

events.enhanced_description: Founded on October 6, 1898, at the New England Conservatory of Music in Boston, the Sinfonia Club was established by Ossian Everett Mills as a fraternity for male musicians. It later evolved into the Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia fraternity, which promotes music and brotherhood among its members.
events.name: The Sinfonia Club, later to become the Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia fraternity, is founded at the New England Conservatory of Music in Boston by Ossian Everett Mills

events.enhanced_description: The Fork Union Military Academy was founded in 1898 in Fork Union, Virginia, as a private military school. It has since developed a reputation for academic excellence and character development, serving students in a structured military environment.
events.name: The Fork Union Military Academy is founded, in Fork Union, Virginia

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1898, the Lutheran Church of the Redeemer was dedicated in Jerusalem, marking a significant moment for the Lutheran community in the Holy Land. The church serves as a symbol of Protestant presence and heritage in a city of profound religious significance.
events.name: The Lutheran Church of the Redeemer, Jerusalem, is dedicated

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1898, the Negros Revolution erupted as Filipinos on Negros Island revolted against Spanish colonial rule, leading to the establishment of the short-lived Republic of Negros. This uprising was part of the broader struggle for independence from Spain in the Philippines.
events.name: Negros Revolution: Filipinos on the island of Negros revolt against Spanish rule and establish the short-lived Republic of Negros

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on November 10, 1898, the Wilmington insurrection marked a violent coup d'état orchestrated by white Democrats in North Carolina, resulting in the overthrow of the elected biracial government. This event is a significant moment in the history of racial violence and political power struggles in the United States.
events.name: The Wilmington insurrection of 1898, a coup d'état by the white Democratic Party of North Carolina, begins

events.enhanced_description: The Portland Gale, a severe blizzard that struck from November 26 to 27, 1898, brought heavy snowfall and strong winds to Boston and surrounding areas, significantly disrupting the Massachusetts fishing industry and coastal towns. The storm caused extensive damage and highlighted the vulnerability of the region to extreme weather events.
events.name: A two-day blizzard known as the Portland Gale piles snow in Boston, severely impacting the Massachusetts fishing industry and several coastal New England towns

events.enhanced_description: In December 1898, John Henry Patterson, a British engineer, shot the first of the infamous Tsavo Man-Eaters, lions that terrorized railway construction workers in Kenya, killing over 135 men. The second lion was killed three weeks later, and the events surrounding these attacks became legendary, inspiring numerous books and films.
events.name: The first of the two Tsavo Man-Eaters is shot by John Henry Patterson; the second is killed 3 weeks later, after 135 railway construction workers have been killed by the lions

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1898, the Treaty of Paris was signed, officially ending the Spanish–American War. The treaty resulted in Spain ceding Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States, marking a significant shift in colonial power and the emergence of the U.S. as a global player.
events.name: The Treaty of Paris is signed, ending the Spanish–American War

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1898, Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat set the first official land speed record in an automobile, achieving an average speed of 63.15 km/h (39.24 mph) over a distance of 1 km in Acheres, France. This milestone marked a significant achievement in automotive engineering and paved the way for future speed records.
events.name: Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat sets the first official land speed record in an automobile, averaging 63.15 km/h (39.24 mph) over 1 km (0.62 mi) in France

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1898, Marie and Pierre Curie announced the discovery of radium, a highly radioactive element, which they isolated from uranium ore. This groundbreaking discovery contributed significantly to the field of radioactivity and laid the foundation for future research in nuclear physics and medicine.
events.name: Marie and Pierre Curie announce the discovery of an element that they name radium

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1898, the Moscow Art Theatre premiered Anton Chekhov's play 'The Seagull', which marked a pivotal moment in modern theatre. The production was innovative in its use of naturalism and character development, influencing the direction of drama in the 20th century.
events.name: The Moscow Art Theatre production of The Seagull by Anton Chekhov opens

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1898, Joseph Vacher, a notorious French serial killer, was executed in Bourg-en-Bresse. His crimes, which included the murder of several young men, shocked the nation and highlighted issues of mental health and criminal justice in France.
events.name: French serial killer Joseph Vacher is executed at Bourg-en-Bresse

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1899, Spanish rule officially ended in Cuba, marking the conclusion of 400 years of Spanish colonial presence in the Americas. This transition was a significant moment in the history of Cuba, leading to its eventual independence and the establishment of a new political landscape in the region.
events.name: Spanish rule ends in Cuba, concluding 400 years of the Spanish Empire in the Americas

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1899, Spanish rule officially ended in Cuba, concluding nearly 400 years of Spanish colonial presence in the Americas. This marked a significant shift in the region's political landscape following the Spanish-American War.
events.name: Spanish rule ends in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1899, Queens and Staten Island were officially incorporated into New York City, expanding the city's boundaries and population. This consolidation was part of a broader trend of urbanization in the late 19th century.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Queens and Staten Island become part of New York City

events.enhanced_description: In early 1899, the British four-masted sailing ship Andelana capsized during a storm in Commencement Bay, Washington, resulting in the tragic loss of all 17 crew members aboard. This incident highlighted the dangers of maritime navigation in treacherous weather conditions.
events.name: The British four-masted sailing ship Andelana capsizes

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1899, the Malolos Constitution was ratified by the Revolutionary Government of the Philippines, establishing the First Philippine Republic. This constitution was significant as it represented the first republican constitution in Asia.
events.name: The Malolos Constitution is ratified

events.enhanced_description: In early 1899, Ranavalona III, the last Queen of Madagascar, was sent into exile by English colonial authorities along with her royal family, following her deposition in 1897. This marked the end of the Merina monarchy and a significant shift in Madagascar's political landscape.
events.name: Ranavalona III exiled

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, Shinjiro Torii established the Suntory whisky distiller in Osaka, initially as a store selling imported wines. This company would later grow to become a global leader in the alcoholic beverage industry.
events.name: Establishment of Suntory

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, Knattspyrnufélag Reykjavíkur was established in Reykjavík, becoming the first association football club in Iceland. This marked the beginning of organized football in the country.
events.name: Establishment of Knattspyrnufélag Reykjavíkur

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the Vicksburg National Military Park was established in Mississippi to preserve the battlefield of the Battle of Vicksburg, a significant site from the American Civil War. The park serves as a memorial to the soldiers who fought there.
events.name: Establishment of Vicksburg National Military Park

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1899, the world's first wireless distress signal was sent via wireless telegraphy to the East Goodwin light vessel when the German barquentine Elbe ran aground in fog in the English Channel. This event marked a significant advancement in maritime safety and communication.
events.name: First Wireless Distress Signal

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, Waldemar Jungner filed a patent application for the first alkaline battery in Sweden, which would later revolutionize portable power sources. This innovation played a crucial role in the development of modern batteries.

image.caption: Portrait of Swedish inventor Waldemar Jungner.
image.credit: Svenska dagbladets årsbok 1924 — https://runeberg.org/svda/1924/0191.html
image.date_qualification: Dated 1924-12-31; a portrait of Jungner, not a depiction of the 1899 patent application.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Patent for Alkaline Battery

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the Battle of Taguig occurred as the USS Laguna de Bay bombarded the Katipunan stronghold during the Philippine–American War. This battle was part of the larger conflict for Philippine independence.
events.name: Battle of Taguig

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, during the Philippine–American War, American forces captured Malolos, the capital of the First Philippine Republic. This event marked a significant turning point in the conflict as American control expanded.

image.caption: The national flag of the Philippines.
image.credit: See File history below for details. — The design was taken from [1] and the colors were also taken from a Government website CONSTRUCTION SHEET:
image.date_qualification: The image_date is 1898-06-12; it is not the date of the Capture of Malolos, which the article excerpt dates to March 31, 1899.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Invasion of the Philippines

events.enhanced_description: The Greek ship Maria sank after a collision in the Mediterranean Sea, resulting in the tragic drowning of 45 individuals.
events.name: Sinking of the Greek ship Maria

events.enhanced_description: A tragic train wreck occurred near Reading, Pennsylvania, resulting in the deaths of 28 individuals and injuring 50 others. This incident highlighted the dangers of rail travel during this period.
events.name: Train wreck near Reading, Pennsylvania

events.enhanced_description: Esporte Clube Vitória, a prominent football club in Brazil, was founded in Salvador, Bahia. The club has a rich history in Brazilian football and has won numerous state and national championships.
events.name: The Esporte Clube Vitória football club is founded

events.enhanced_description: Maurice Ravel conducted the first public performance of his orchestral work Shéhérazade, ouverture de féerie in Paris. This piece is known for its lush orchestration and exotic themes.
events.name: Maurice Ravel conducts Shéhérazade

events.enhanced_description: The Bloemfontein Conference was held between Paul Kruger, President of the South African Republic, and Sir Alfred Milner, Governor of the Cape Colony. The conference aimed to resolve tensions between the British and the Boers but ultimately ended in failure after six days.
events.name: The Bloemfontein Conference commences

events.enhanced_description: France's Court of Cassation orders the reopening of the treason conviction of Captain Alfred Dreyfus, revealing evidence of a wrongful conviction. This pivotal moment in the Dreyfus affair ignites public debate over anti-Semitism and justice in France.
events.name: Dreyfus affair: Reopening of conviction

events.enhanced_description: The United States and Spain resume diplomatic relations following the appointment of the Duke of Arcos as the new Minister for Spain. This marks a significant step in the post-Spanish-American War era.
events.name: Resumption of diplomatic relations between the United States and Spain

events.enhanced_description: Sweden's Department of Foreign Affairs hosts a significant conference with delegates from multiple countries to negotiate fishing rights in the Arctic Ocean, Baltic Sea, and North Sea. This conference aims to establish cooperative agreements for sustainable fishing practices.
events.name: Fishing conference hosted by Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Cycle & Carriage is founded in Singapore, eventually becoming one of the largest automotive companies in the region. This establishment marks a significant development in the automotive industry in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Founding of Cycle & Carriage

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan is established as a joint territory governed by Egypt and the United Kingdom, although it effectively operates as a British colony. This arrangement reflects the complexities of colonial governance in Africa.
events.name: Creation of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan

events.enhanced_description: Edward Elgar's Enigma Variations are premiered in London, showcasing his innovative orchestral composition that explores themes of friendship and mystery. This work becomes one of Elgar's most celebrated pieces.
events.name: Premiere of Edward Elgar's Enigma Variations

events.enhanced_description: A. E. J. Collins, a 13-year-old schoolboy, sets a remarkable cricket record by scoring 628 not out, a feat that remains unmatched for 117 years. This achievement highlights the extraordinary talent and potential in youth sports.

locations.name: The Oval, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: A. E. J. Collins' cricket record

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the German domestic appliance company Miele was founded in Gütersloh. The company has since become renowned for its high-quality home appliances and has a significant presence in the global market.

image.caption: A Miele 1913 automobile displayed at the Miele Museum in Gütersloh.
image.credit: Buch-t — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed in 2011; depicts a 1913 Miele vehicle at the museum, not the 1899 founding event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of Miele

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the Battle of Togbao took place in Chad, where the French Bretonnet–Braun mission was destroyed by the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr. This event highlighted the resistance against French colonial expansion in the region.
events.name: Battle of Togbao

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation took effect in 1899, effectively ending extraterritoriality and the unequal status of Japan in foreign commerce. This treaty marked a significant step in Japan's emergence as a modern nation.
events.name: Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation

events.enhanced_description: The retrial of Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer wrongfully convicted of treason, opened in Paris in January 1899, igniting a national scandal that would expose deep-seated anti-Semitism in France. This event was pivotal in shaping modern French politics and civil rights.
events.name: Dreyfus Affair: Retrial of Alfred Dreyfus

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the governance of Guam began under the administration of the United States Department of the Navy, marking a significant shift in the island's political landscape following the Spanish-American War. This period laid the groundwork for Guam's future as a U.S. territory.
events.name: Governance of Guam under U.S. Navy

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the French Army invaded the Sultanate of Zinder in Niger, resulting in the death of its ruler, Amadou Kouran Daga. This event marked a significant step in the French colonial expansion in West Africa.
events.name: French invasion of Zinder

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, Edwin Ford was granted the patent for the first water meter, a significant innovation that would impact water management and billing practices in urban areas. This invention laid the groundwork for modern water usage tracking.
events.name: Patent for first water meter granted

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the Dominion Line steamer Scotsman sank in the Strait of Belle Isle, resulting in the tragic loss of 15 women and children. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during that era.

locations.name: Strait of Belle Isle, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Sinking of the Scotsman

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Angeles City was a significant engagement during the Philippine-American War, where U.S. forces successfully captured the capital of the Philippine Republic after intense fighting. This battle marked a pivotal moment in the U.S. campaign to assert control over the Philippines following the Spanish-American War.
events.name: Battle of Angeles City

events.enhanced_description: The Belgian Antarctic Expedition, led by Gerard De Gerlache, concluded its journey after significant contributions to the exploration of Antarctica. This expedition was notable for its scientific research and for being one of the first to spend an entire winter in the Antarctic.

image.caption: Belgica in the ice, reproduced in Quinze mois en Antarctique.
image.credit: Adrien de Gerlache — Adrien de Gerlache (1902), Quinze mois en Antarctique , p171
image.date_qualification: Dated 1902; later than the expedition’s 1897–1899 dates.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Conclusion of the Belgian Antarctic Expedition

events.enhanced_description: Representatives from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany signed a treaty to arbitrate claims regarding the Samoan Islands, with King Oscar II of Sweden appointed as the neutral arbitrator. This agreement aimed to resolve tensions and disputes over territorial claims in the Pacific.
events.name: Treaty for Arbitration of Samoa

events.enhanced_description: Joshua Lionel Cohen was awarded a U.S. patent for the flash-lamp, a significant innovation in the field of photography and lighting. This invention contributed to advancements in both amateur and professional photography.
events.name: Patent for Flash-Lamp

events.enhanced_description: Anton Chekhov's play 'Uncle Vanya' premiered at the Moscow Art Theatre, marking a significant moment in Russian theatre. The play is celebrated for its deep exploration of human emotions and relationships, and it remains a classic in the world of drama.
events.name: Premiere of Uncle Vanya

events.enhanced_description: In early 1899, a near-grand conjunction of classical planets occurred during the new moon, where the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Mars, and Saturn aligned closely, with Venus and Jupiter positioned nearby. This astronomical event fascinated observers and was noted for its rarity.
events.name: Near-grand conjunction of planets

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, four-month-old Sobhuza II ascended to the throne as King of Swaziland, beginning a reign that would last for 82 years. His long rule witnessed significant changes in the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Sobhuza II begins reign

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Stormberg occurred during the Second Boer War in December 1899, where the British Army suffered a disastrous defeat while attempting to surprise Boer positions in Natal, resulting in 687 casualties. This battle was part of a series of setbacks for British forces during what was termed 'Black Week.'
events.name: Battle of Stormberg

events.enhanced_description: Delta Sigma Phi, a college fraternity, was founded at the City College of New York in 1899. The fraternity has since grown to become a significant organization in American collegiate life, promoting brotherhood and leadership among its members.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Foundation of Delta Sigma Phi

events.enhanced_description: The Glasgow School of Art, designed by renowned architect Charles Rennie Mackintosh, opened in 1899 and became a pivotal institution in the development of art and design education in Scotland. The building itself is celebrated for its distinctive architectural style and remains a significant cultural landmark.
events.name: Opening of Glasgow School of Art

events.enhanced_description: In a tragic incident on January 1, 1899, more than 40 schoolchildren from Belgium drowned when their boat capsized near Frelinghien, France. This event shocked the local communities and drew attention to the safety of children during excursions.
events.name: Drowning of Belgian schoolchildren

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1899, a devastating fire in Quincy, Illinois, resulted in the tragic deaths of 16 children. This incident raised awareness about fire safety and the need for better regulations to protect vulnerable populations.
events.name: Fire in Quincy, Illinois

events.enhanced_description: Riro, the last king of Easter Island, died in 1899 during a visit to Valparaíso, Chile. His death, shrouded in mystery, was attributed either to alcohol poisoning or a conspiracy by the Chilean government, marking a significant moment in the history of Easter Island.
events.name: Death of Riro, last King of Easter Island

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, Oxo beef stock cubes were introduced by Liebig's Extract of Meat Company, revolutionizing the way cooks prepared flavorful broths and soups. This innovation became a staple in kitchens around the world.
events.name: Introduction of Oxo beef stock cubes

events.enhanced_description: The Giros-Loucheur Group, which would later become known as Vinci, was founded in 1899 in France, marking the beginning of a significant player in the global construction and infrastructure industry.
events.name: Foundation of Giros-Loucheur Group

events.enhanced_description: In 1899, the Timken Roller Bearing Company was founded in Missouri, laying the groundwork for what would become a leading global brand in bearing manufacturing and engineering solutions.
events.name: Foundation of Timken Roller Bearing Company

events.enhanced_description: The cholera pandemic that began in 1923 spread rapidly across Europe, Asia, and Africa, causing widespread illness and death. This pandemic highlighted the need for improved public health measures and sanitation practices.
events.name: Start of the 1923 cholera pandemic

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1899, a fierce battle erupted between American troops and Filipino defenders in Pililla, Luzon, as part of the Philippine–American War. This conflict was indicative of the broader struggle for independence by Filipinos against American colonial rule.
events.name: A fierce battle is fought between American troops and Filipino defenders at the town of Pililla on the island of Luzon

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1899, SK Rapid Wien, one of Austria's most successful football clubs, was founded in Vienna. The club has since become a significant part of Austrian football history, contributing to the sport's development in the country.
events.name: The Association football club SK Rapid Wien is founded in Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1899, following a successful revolt against Ottoman rule, the island of Crete joined Greece and established its first constitution. This event marked a significant step in the island's long struggle for autonomy and integration into the Greek state.
events.name: After a successful revolt against the Ottoman Empire by the inhabitants of the island of Crete, the area, which joins Greece, gets its first constitution

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1899, the Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity was founded at Illinois Wesleyan University in Bloomington, Illinois. The fraternity has since grown into one of the largest collegiate fraternities in North America, promoting brotherhood and academic excellence.
events.name: The Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity is founded, at Illinois Wesleyan University in Bloomington, Illinois

events.enhanced_description: In January 1899, the Canadian Northern Railway was established, marking a significant development in Canada's transportation infrastructure. This railway played a crucial role in connecting various regions of Canada and facilitating economic growth.
events.name: The Canadian Northern Railway is established

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1899, the RMS Oceanic, a transatlantic ocean liner of the White Star Line, was launched from the shipyards in Belfast. At the time of her launch, she was the largest ship afloat, measuring 704 feet in length and weighing 17,272 gross register tons.
events.name: The White Star Line's transatlantic ocean liner RMS Oceanic is launched

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1899, the United States formally took possession of Wake Island in the Pacific Ocean. This acquisition was part of the U.S. strategy to expand its territories and influence in the Pacific region.
events.name: The United States takes possession of Wake Island

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1899, the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan was officially formed, marking a joint British-Egyptian administration over Sudan. This arrangement lasted until Sudan's independence in 1956.
events.name: The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan is formed

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1899, Opel Motors was founded in Rüsselsheim, Germany, by Adam Opel. The company initially produced sewing machines before transitioning to manufacturing bicycles and eventually automobiles.
events.name: Opel Motors opens for business

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1899, leaders from six Australian colonies convened in Melbourne to discuss the potential confederation of Australia. This meeting was a crucial step towards the eventual establishment of the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901.
events.name: Australian colonies meet to discuss confederation

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1899, Emilio Aguinaldo was sworn in as the President of the First Philippine Republic in Malolos. This event marked a significant moment in Philippine history as Aguinaldo led the country during its struggle for independence from colonial rule.
events.name: Emilio Aguinaldo is sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1899, the Philadelphia College of Osteopathic Medicine was founded in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. This institution played a pivotal role in the development of osteopathic medicine in the United States.

image.caption: Anatomy dissection class in the basement at 33rd and Arch Street, Philadelphia.
image.credit: PCOM — PCOM Facebook Site
image.date_qualification: Depicted image dated 1908, nine years after the founding in 1899.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Philadelphia College of Osteopathic Medicine is founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1899, German inventor Karl Ferdinand Braun received a British patent for his wireless radio invention, 'Telegraphy without directly connected wire.' This innovation laid the groundwork for future developments in wireless communication.
events.name: Karl Ferdinand Braun receives British patent for wireless radio invention

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1899, Camille Jenatzy of France became the first person to drive an automobile at a speed exceeding 80 kilometers per hour, reaching a speed of 80.35 kph in his CGA Dogcart racecar. This achievement marked a significant milestone in automotive history.
events.name: Camille Jenatzy drives an automobile over 80 kilometers per hour

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1899, the League of Peja, organized by Haxhi Zeka, held its first convention in Peja, Kosovo. The league aimed to lobby for the establishment of a Kosovar Albanian state within the Ottoman Empire, attracting 450 delegates.
events.name: The League of Peja convenes

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1899, Ranavalona III, the last queen of Madagascar, was sent into exile by English colonial authorities, along with her royal family. This event marked the end of the Merina monarchy and the consolidation of colonial rule in Madagascar.
events.name: Ranavalona III is sent into exile

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1899, participants in the Australian Premiers' Conference reached an agreement that Australia's capital should be located between Sydney and Melbourne. This decision ultimately led to the establishment of Canberra as the capital city.
events.name: Australian Premiers' Conference agrees on capital location

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1899, the Philippine–American War began as hostilities broke out in Manila. This conflict arose from the struggle for independence of the Philippines from American colonial rule.
events.name: The Philippine–American War begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1899, the first major battle of the Philippine–American War concluded with the capture of the San Juan River Bridge by U.S. forces. This strategic victory connected Manila with San Juan and marked a significant escalation in the conflict.

locations.name: San Juan River Bridge, Metro Manila, Philippines

events.name: First major battle of the Philippine–American War

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1899, the United States Senate ratified a peace treaty with Spain to officially end the Spanish–American War. This treaty marked the conclusion of hostilities and the beginning of American colonial rule over former Spanish territories.
events.name: Peace treaty ratified to end the Spanish–American War

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1899, U.S. Army troops, supported by bombardment from the warships Charleston and Monadnock, defeated Filipino forces in the Battle of Caloocan. This battle was crucial for U.S. control over the Manila to Dagupan railway during the Philippine–American War.
events.name: Battle of Caloocan

events.enhanced_description: Cipriano Castro, a Venezuelan military leader, initiated the Restorative Liberal Revolution by leading a small group of exiles across the Colombia–Venezuela border to challenge the government of President Ignacio Andrade. This marked the beginning of a significant political upheaval in Venezuela.
events.name: Cipriano Castro starts the Restorative Liberal Revolution

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1899, Emperor Nicholas II of Russia issued the February Manifesto, which allowed the Diet of Finland to be overruled in legislative matters concerning the interests of all Russia. This decree was a significant step in the centralization of power and the erosion of Finnish autonomy.
events.name: The February Manifesto issued by the Emperor of Russia

events.enhanced_description: Félix Faure, the President of France since 1895, died unexpectedly on February 16, 1899, in his office at the Élysée Palace while engaged in a private moment with his mistress, Marguerite Steinheil. His sudden death led to a political transition in France.
events.name: Death of Félix Faure

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1899, the research vessel SS Southern Cross, under the command of Carsten Borchgrevink, arrived at Cape Adare, marking a significant moment in Antarctic exploration. The expedition unloaded 90 sledge dogs, the first ever on the continent, and established a temporary settlement.
events.name: SS Southern Cross arrives at Cape Adare

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1899, the National Assembly of France elected Émile Loubet as the new President to complete the term of the late Félix Faure. Loubet's election marked a shift in French politics during a period of instability.
events.name: Election of new President of France

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1899, Ramón Guerra, the former Minister of War in Venezuela, declared the state of Guárico an independent territory in response to President Ignacio Andrade's reforms. This act of defiance led to military actions as Andrade sought to suppress the rebellion.
events.name: Ramón Guerra proclaims independence in Guárico

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1899, discussions among a joint Anglo-American commission, aimed at resolving the Alaska boundary dispute, ended abruptly when it became clear that the U.S. would not make any concessions. This impasse led to heightened tensions between the U.S. and Canada.
